News.title: 'Like knives inside me': Women hit out at 'barbaric' NHS womb procedure
News.content:
'Like knives inside me': Women hit out at 'barbaric' NHS womb procedure

EXCLUSIVE: A disjointed approach to treating women's health in the UK means many women are suffering painful procedures unnecessarily

View 3 Images Emma Jane Taylor passed out during the painful procedure

Screaming in pain, denied adequate pain relief, and passing out in the chair - this is the traumatic reality for hundreds of women subjected to routine NHS gynaecological procedures.

‌



While health concerns naturally bring anxiety, women across the UK are highlighting the true extent of the agony they are expected to endure just to stay healthy.

‌



At the centre of the controversy is a hysteroscopy - a procedure used to examine the inside of the womb. A petition calling for an end to the "barbaric" manner in which the procedure is typically carried out has amassed nearly 70,000 signatures from desperate women demanding urgent reform.

‌



Classed as a minimally invasive procedure, the procedure involves passing a thin telescope (a hysteroscope) through the vagina and cervix into the womb, which is pumped open with fluid. It is routinely carried out in an outpatient department, to investigate abnormal bleeding, diagnose health conditions, or remove polyps, fibroids, and tissue biopsies.

Patients are usually awake and told the procedure will cause only "mild discomfort," but for thousands of women, the reality has been excruciating.

Not checking one body part 'regularly' increases risk of dementia by 500 per cent READ MORE :

View 3 Images Emma Jane had no idea how painful the procedure was going to be

‌



Emma Jane Taylor, a 53-year-old from Oxfordshire, was told she needed a hysteroscopy to investigate a polyp. She assumed it would feel similar to a routine smear test.

"They said it wasn't going to hurt but I just couldn't complete it," she told the Daily Mirror. "It felt like there was someone inside me with knives cutting through my body.

She blacked out, after being overwhelmed by nausea and pain. "The pain is just beyond what women are told to expect. "We're told it's a routine procedure, but in reality there is no way. It's degrading and it feels like you've been butchered. I was so embarrassed and ashamed.

‌



"Women are being gaslit into having these types of procedures that are so painful."

Emma Jane's nightmare is echoed by 52-year-old Dawn Lord, from Hartlepool. In 2023, Dawn attended what she believed was a routine attempt to review tests results, only to undergo an unexpected hysteroscopy without any informed consent or warning.

"Nothing was explained. They just said I'd feel a few cramps, but that was the biggest lie," Dawn told the Daily Mirror.

‌



"I was screaming in pain and ignored. Even when my husband asked for pain relief, we were told there wasn't any available - and then I blacked out."

Afterwards, staff apologised for failing to warn her about fainting, but added that "most patients can tolerate it."

The experience left Dawn shattered. Left bedbound for a month afterwards with heavy bleeding, severe depression and PTSD, she sought therapy to process the trauma.

‌



"My therapist told me my memories connected the lack of control from a traumatic control to the lack of control in the procedure and that's when the PTSD happened," Dawn added.

Determined to help others, Dawn launched a support group called Hysteroscopy Trauma, which now has over 200 members sharing their experiences. Unlike other internal examinations, such as colonoscopies and gastroscopies - patients having a hysterescopy aren't offered sedation as standard practice.

Instead , women are advised to take over the counter medication like paracetamol or ibruprofen before arriving. During the procedure, some are offered nothing more than a stress ball to squeeze, while electro-surgical tools remove tissue, and nurses attempt to make light conversation.

‌



"One of the nurses was just chatting about holidays while giving me gas and air," Dawn said. "I couldn't chat about holidays - I was in too much pain."

View 3 Images Dawn Lord was left needing therapy after her procedure

Recent research led by the University of Reading analysed 4,644 posts on the parenting forum Mumsnet, which showed a chaotic postcode lottery in how patients are being treated across the country. Susanne Cromme, lead author of the study, told the Daily Mirror that pain management was "completely unstandardised across NHS trusts."

‌



"Every hospital, every clinician just does what works best for them, rather than one standardised approach with set pain relief protocols and informed consent procedures," Susanne said.

"Currently, it's very binary. You either go in with paracetamol that you have to take yourself before the procedure, or you're offered a general anaesthetic, which is quite extreme. But there's research coming out of Chelsea and Westminster Hospital where they've been researching conscious sedation for hysteroscopy, and they've got a great set of data."

The findings mirror a searing report by the Commons' Women and Equalities Committee, which slammed widespread "medical misogyny" and a systemic failure to take women's pain seriously. It found women suffering from conditions like endometriosis, adenomyosis and heavy menstrual bleeding frequently have their agonising symptoms "normalised" and their "pain dismissed" - forcing many to leave careers, relationships, or even contemplate suicide.

‌



Organisers of the petition are now calling on the Secretary State for Health to overhaul how hysteroscopies are delivered across the NHS. The three focus points include:

Advanced training in pain medicine for all NHS hysteroscopists

Clear written information given to patients before procedures, detailing the risks and benefits and explaining that local anaesthetic may be painful and ineffective against the severity of pain from cervical dilation, womb distension

Dedicated funding to ensure patients can choose between local anaesthetic, conscious sedation, or general anaesthetic before the procedure begins

Justine Roberts, founder of Mumsnet and Gransnet, said: "This research makes clear that too many women are still experiencing severe pain during hysteroscopy, and that problem is compounded by unclear information, inconsistent pain relief and a lack of proper consent.

‌



"These are not one-off failures - they form a repeated pattern and that’s exactly what Mumsnet’s medical misogyny campaign is highlighting: systemic failings in women's healthcare.

"Nothing encapsulates that more clearly than the expectation that women should endure avoidable pain during gynaecological procedures. If the NHS is serious about tackling medical misogyny, this has to change.”

Sign the petition here

News.title: France wildfires live: Inferno threatens Bordeaux as Macron holds crisis meeting
News.content:
More than 250,000 people have been evacuated in south-west France due to raging wildfires heading towards Bordeaux and its airport

Fierce wildfires are raging less then seven miles the French city of Bordeaux and its airport, with more than 250,000 people evacuated from the area.

Firefighters are struggling to contain the flames, which have burned 42,000 hectares - an area four times the size of Paris - leaving two firefighters dead and 84 injured. Volunteers, including local farmers, are helping by towing huge water tankers to the scene.

President Emmanuel Macron is holding a crisis meeting as shifting winds and arid conditions have made the blaze impossible to control. The main fire has caused an unprecedented "pyrocumulonimbus" - a huge fire thunderstorm fuelled by its own winds and lightning, the National Firefighters Federation of France said.

The flames have now forced the closure of the hotel zone at Bordeaux Airport, while travellers have been advised to find accommodation outside the evacuation zones.

Meanwhile in Spain, 25,000 people have been ordered to evacuate and almost 40,000 told to stay indoors. Wildfires near Madrid "slowed their advance" overnight but remain active, the regional government said today.

News.title: Most polluted neighbourhoods in UK revealed - see how yours fares
News.content:
Most polluted neighbourhoods in UK revealed - see how yours fares

An interactive map reveals the worst pollution hotspots across Britain, with almost every neighbourhood exceeding recommended levels of harmful PM2.5 particles that can cause cancer

View 2 Images Some residents are breathing in an annual average of pollutants that far exceed safety levels (Image: Getty Images)

The parts of Britain with the dirtiest air have been revealed, with some neighbourhoods seeing levels of potentially deadly pollutants more than four times the recommended limit.

‌



Figures from the Geographic Data Service show that an area in Camden, London, covering parts of Holborn, St Giles, and Covent Garden was the most polluted in the country. Residents are breathing in an annual average of nearly 21 micrograms of fine particulate matter and more than 34 micrograms of nitrogen dioxide.

‌



The World Health Organisation recommends levels should not exceed an annual average of five micrograms of PM2.5 and 15 micrograms of NO2. However, scientists have stressed that even these limits are not “safe”, as pollutants can cause damage at any level.

‌



View 2 Images London was home to Britain's most polluted neighbourhoods (Image: Getty Images)

PM2.5 is particularly harmful. These microscopic particles can bypass the body's natural defences and travel deep into the lungs and bloodstream, posing serious health risks. As well as potentially causing stinging eyes, coughing, and shortness of breath, exposure increases the risk of lung cancer, respiratory infections, and cardiovascular diseases.

Similarly, exposure to NO2 can inflame airways, trigger asthma attacks, and reduce lung function, as well as increasing the risk of respiratory infections. A shocking 99% of neighbourhood's in Britain had levels of PM2.5 that were over the recommended amount, and 51% had excess levels of NO2.

‌



Urban areas are the worst affected, seeing significantly higher levels of both pollutants but NO2 in particular, compared to rural neighbourhoods. All of the hardest-hit areas in Britain are in London, but the figures also reveal the places in each region with the dirtiest air.

These include a neighbourhood located in the Stone area of Dartford, Kent, an inner-city neighbourhood in the Aston Park area of Birmingham, and parts of the North Evington area of Leicester. Other regional hotspots include parts of Bootle and Seaforth in Sefton, West Thurrock in Essex, the Sheepscars and Lovell Park neighbourhoods in Leeds, and a neighbourhood in the Splott district of Cardiff.

‌



Also ranking highly were parts of North Shields in North Tyneside, Upper Montpelier in Bristol and a neighbourhood in the city centre of Glasgow. At the other end of the scale, the areas with the cleanest air are largely in remote, rural parts of Scotland and Wales, while in England parts of Devon in the south and Cumberland and Northumberland in the north also have particularly low levels of air pollution.

Jonathan Blades, head of policy and public affairs at Asthma + Lung UK, said: “It’s unacceptable that communities across the UK are being exposed to unsafe levels of air pollution, which is linked to up to 43,000 deaths across the UK every year.

"This will be especially worrying for the 12 million people living with a lung condition who are particularly vulnerable to the impact of poor air quality. These statistics show that current UK guidelines on air pollution are outdated and failing to protect our communities.”

Article continues below

The charity would like to see the Labour Party recommit its support for a new Clean Air Act that sets legally binding air quality targets in line with World Health Organization guidelines, as well as a national public awareness campaign to help people better understand the health impact of air pollution and how to reduce their exposure.

A Defra spokesperson said: “Poor air quality robs people of their health and costs the NHS millions in extra treatments for lung conditions and asthma. That is why the government remains committed to improving air quality to deliver benefits for public health, the environment, and the economy.

“The action we've taken includes setting new air quality targets to cut exposure to harmful particles by nearly a third by 2030. Alongside this, we are taking steps to reform areas like simpler industrial permits to reduce emissions and have consulted on exploring tightening standards for new wood burning appliances to help reduce health impacts.”

News.title: Boy, one, fighting for his life after horror 'fall from window' in Gillingham
News.content:
Boy, one, fighting for his life after horror 'fall from window' in Gillingham

‌

It is understood the fall was from a flat above a shop.

News.title: 'Donald Trump's meeting with Benjamin Netanyahu meeting is a nailbiter that affects us all'
News.content:
This week Israeli leader Benjamin Netanyahu faces one of his most decisive meetings with US President Donald Trump.

He is one of Washington’s most frequent flyers but Netanyahu’s trip could leave his political career shattered, along with hopes of a quick end to the Iran crisis.

All the time he has to maintain pressure on Iran’s nuclear programme upon which Trump and Netanyahu’s defence of the war rests. It all has major implications for the UK in terms of the economy, future military back-up to secure the Strait of Hormuz, the growing terror threat from Iran’s proxies and elusive Middle East peace, which affects us all.

War in Iran, domestic strife, Gaza and escalations in the West Bank, the neighbouring Hezbollah threat and growing anger with Netanyahu’s government make this a crucial event.

‌



US President Donald Trump was sold a nightmare, a quagmire war, falling for what no other President has fallen for. He was convinced and told the world that it was the case, that the Iran nuclear threat was just around the corner and that the conflict could easily be won.

Domestically it is a disaster for Trump with three-quarters of Americans surveyed in a recent poll saying they thought the Trump administration has had more difficulty navigating the conflict than expected.

View 4 Images US B1 Bomber parks up at RAF Fairford, UK (Image: Tom Wren / SWNS)

Latest casualty analysis lists 14 troops killed and 417 wounded during Operation Epic Fury. A new and manipulative “Overseas Operations” category covering incidents since July 7 lists four additional deaths and 207 wounded.

‌



Both categories combined produces a total of 18 dead and 624 wounded but the Pentagon has not confirmed that all 207 wounded listed in the new category were wounded by Iran.

Against all of this Netanyahu has to appear strong, best friends with Trump, getting just the right amount of fawning in without overdoing it and securing Israel’s powerful ally.

All the time with everyone in the same room knowing that Trump fell for it last time and is far less willing to do it again. He will try to convince Trump that latest intelligence suggests Iranian leader Motjaba Khamenei is seeking nuclear weapons - more so than his slain father.

He has a monumental task ahead of him, an audience with Trump he has long been lobbying for weeks for whilst claiming his visit is really about attending the funeral for late Senator Lyndsey Graham.

‌



Netanyahu will have been briefed almost to the point of derision by his diplomats on Trumps’ mood, his mercurial views and talking points, intelligence assessments of what is really happening inside Iran.

View 4 Images Benjamin Netanyahu will attend funeral services for US Senator Lindsey Graham - the pair met in Jerusalem earlier this year (Image: Maayan Toaf/Israel Gpo/ZUMA Press Wire/Shutterstock)

Even Trump’s bellicose hubris cannot protect him against the truth, that Iran is by many metrics winning the crisis over the Strait of Hormuz.

Trump has beefed up America’s military presence in the region massively in the past week, his finger poised on the button to escalate and Netanyahu will be trying to force it downward, to keep pressure on Tehran, both men knowing the war is an immensely difficult prospect domestically.

‌



Netanyahu knows he has to get the tone right, to bolster military pressure on Iran, least convincing of all, suggesting the war can be won on Trump’s terms.

This meeting could be masterful, the arch manipulator and vastly superior political intellect of Netanyahu rubbing up against Trump’s fragile ego.

An ego through which the bloody truth about the Iran conflict, that it is winning and Netanyahu only uses the truth when convenient, must surely have penetrated.

Israel’s domestic elections in October, which are seemingly touch and go for Netanyahu mean he is struggling against a powerful opposition.

‌



Britain Israel Communication and Research Centre - BICOM - this morning said: “For some supporters, he is the greatest leader the country has ever had, combining supreme intellect, communications skills and unmatched experience. For others he is a lying manipulator that places self-interest above those of the country.”

View 4 Images US President Donald Trump has beefed up America's military presence in the Middle East (Image: Getty Images)

Both of these aspects of his character will be used to the maximum tomorrow and the outcome will have implications for us all. Britain, as the US’s junior and vulnerable partner, is in the firing line and Iran has said as much.

This is in response to Britain’s RAF Fairford, in Gloucestershire, being identified as the air force base from where B1 bombers took off last week for a raid on Iran.

‌



There is real concern in Washington that Trump may still give the go-ahead for a major escalation in Iran and Netanyahu will want to influence that. The fascinating theatre of tomorrow’s meeting with Trump has implications well beyond the political ambitions of both leaders.

News.title: Newquay deaths: Man and woman dead after night time Fistral Beach drowning
News.content:
Beachgoers bravely tried to rescue a man and woman after they reportedly fell from a cliff and died in the choppy sea at Britain's most popular surfing spot.

Scene at Fistral beach where witnesses say man and woman fell into water

A woman in her 30s and a man in his 60s have tragically died after rescue crews pulled them from the water at Britain's most famous surfing beach in Cornwall.

People at Fistral Beach, in Newquay, bravely attempted to rescue the pair - reportedly a father and daughter - with witnesses suggesting they had fallen from a cliff.

Witnesses said nine emergency vehicles and a helicopter rushed to the 750-metre long sands, known as the 'home of British surfing' ,last night. mPolice, coastguard and the ambulance service were deployed at around 9.30pm. Images from Fistral last night showed people crowding on the sands trying to help with the rescue effort.

The incident happened just days before the location was about to be used for the annual Boardmasters festival.

The area is well-known for having extremely strong and dangerous rip currents, particularly during outgoing tides. Locals said the sea currents were "very strong" last night.

The Mirror has launched the Save Lives For Sam water safety campaign to tackle the UK's growing drowning crisis. Backed by MPs, Olympic champions, national water safety organisations and bereaved families, the campaign is calling for urgent action to make our waters safer.

Find out more about the campaign and how you can support it here.

News.title: 'Andy Burnham must fix social care - we're already paying the price and it's time we admitted it'
News.content:
Social care is the most intractable problem faced by generations of British politicians due to our aging population.

So much so that for decades they have all managed to put off making the difficult decision - how do we pay for it? That is the multi-billion dollar question, but currently we are paying heavily for the crisis in pounds as well as human cost.

The financial costs are largely hidden from view - paid for by the NHS, local councils and families whose life savings are wiped out because they're unfortunate enough to have a relative with complex needs.

Also hidden behind closed doors is the human cost, in the miserable existence of lonely elderly people living with what the system terms “unmet need”.

‌



Andy Burnham issues dire warning NHS will collapse if social care isn't finally fixed READ MORE :

Pensioner discharged from hospital is in budget hotel for five weeks as rate of bed blocking soars READ MORE :

View 4 Images Many elderly people are living with unmet need relating to daily living (Image: Getty Images)

Hidden also is the lost potential of thousands of middle aged carers who have to quit their jobs to care for a parent. Not so hidden are the thousands of elderly and vulnerable people lining our hospital corridors every day who shouldn’t be there.

When Andy Burnham says the NHS will collapse if we don’t sort social care he is referring to is the issue of delayed discharges that are crippling hospitals.

Last month 14,000 medically fit patients were stuck in hospital every day in England, mainly because they could not get social care to be safely discharged somewhere else.

‌



This was up 12% since June 2024 when it was 12,000 and is up 70% since 2021. And there is a huge cost to this already. Delayed discharges are now costing the NHS £230 a month. The annual cost in 2025/26 was £2.7 billion.

The human cost of that was spelled out in a recent report from Age UK. The charity collated heartbreaking accounts from elderly people who lost their health and independence as their home care visits were cancelled because they were in hospital - which meant they then couldn’t be discharged home.

Any prolonged stay in a hospital bed for an elderly person risks irreversible loss of muscle mass and mobility. One 70-year-old told the Mirror how she had to discharge herself to a budget hotel and had been living there for five months.

View 4 Images The Mirror has launched the Fair Care for All campaign

‌



The Mirror has launched the Fair Care for All campaign calling for a government to finally bite the bullet. The campaign calls for all older people to be treated with dignity and respect.

Our demands include the creation of national care service to run alongside the NHS, the appointment of minister for the elderly and a properly-funded care system that works for everyone.

The campaign also calls for a fair deal for care workers. We are calling for carers to be paid the real Living Wage, an end to home visits of 15 minutes or less and an increase in the allowance for unpaid carers.

Mr Burnham - whose dad Roy has Alzheimer's disease and lives in a care home - is expected to give a major speech on social care this week. He told the BBC: "Whatever political capital I have, I will put in to fixing broken social care.”

‌



This isn't without political risk given the salutary tale of one former Prime Minister in Theresa May who - to her credit - actually attempted to tackle the issue with a plan that was criticised as a "dementia tax". The solution must lie in a new system where the risk of catastrophic care home costs is shared across the population.

View 4 Images A hospital stay for a relatively minor illness can result in some elderly people never going home (Image: Getty Images/iStockphoto)

A kind of insurance against losing your family’s entire savings, sometimes built up over generations, simply because you were unlucky enough to develop dementia and live a long time with it. However, the cost of that will be your insurance premium - likely in the form of a tax.

But let’s not pretend this is an entirely new cost to the taxpayer - because the nation is already paying a heavy price.

News.title: How wildfires in France and Spain may affect your travel plans
News.content:
The UK government has not specifically warned against travel to anywhere in France or Spain, but it does advise caution.

In France, it says access to affected areas may be restricted and roads may close at short notice. It adds that further evacuations may take place.

It has also issued a general warning about the high risk of wildfires in France during the summer season from April to October.

For those in an affected area in France or Spain or planning to travel there, the UK government recommends following instructions and updates from local authorities and emergency services at all times.

Those needing emergency help in France or Spain can call 112.

Travellers should also bear in mind the UK government's advice can and does change in response to moving events.

Anna-Marie Duthie, travel insurance expert at financial rating firm Defaqto, says that if this happens after you have booked your trip, "you may be covered for cancellation or curtailment".

"You may also be covered for additional travel and accommodation costs should your trip be disrupted due to a catastrophic event, if your insurer offers this cover or you've paid to include it," she adds.

To know if this applies to you, check your policy.

News.title: NHS 'will collapse' without social care reform, PM tells BBC
News.content:
Andy Burnham has told the BBC "the NHS will collapse" if social care is not reformed but said he could not put a timeline on changes.

In his first major interview since becoming prime minister, Burnham said he would not want to leave office without bringing in "substantial change" to the social care system.

The prime minister also suggested making it harder to claim benefits, saying the country had to get serious about getting the welfare bill down.

Conservative leader Kemi Badenoch has meanwhile written to the prime minister, saying he should rule out tax rises or increased borrowing to fund social care reform.

Burnham told the BBC that if the government did not reform social care, the NHS would "collapse under the weight of trying to care for people who've really not needed to end up in the NHS system".

But pressed on whether he would create a new system before the next election, he said he "couldn't put a timeline on it right here, right now", though he would put "whatever political capital I have into fixing broken social care".

Burnham first proposed a universal system of social care in England in 2009 when he was health secretary under Gordon Brown, and a year later pursued the idea of a compulsory levy to fund it.

One of the options floated by that Labour government was allowing people to defer the payment until after they died, which led to the Tories branding it a "death tax".

Burnham is due to make a speech on adult social care on Wednesday.

The BBC understands the PM will stop short of unveiling plans for a new system in this speech, instead announcing he is speeding up the Casey Commission, an independent review that has been considering possible solutions for social care.

Baroness Louise Casey is not expected to give her final recommendations until 2028, but Burnham wants to bring her schedule forward.

He told the BBC: "Social care was on a longer path and I have brought it straight forward."

Adult social care provides state support to help people live more independently, including assistance at home with tasks like washing and cleaning.

Unlike the NHS, social care is not free at the point of use. In England and Northern Ireland, people with savings worth more than Â£23,250 are not entitled to help with care costs from their council.

In Wales and Scotland, different rules apply in terms of eligibility.

Sarah Woolnough, chief executive of healthcare think tank the King's Fund, said the current "punitive system" meant that "quite a lot of people go without care that they need", with one in seven paying in excess of Â£100,000 for social care.

While Burnham has not yet outlined any plans, Woolnough told the BBC Radio 4's Today programme that reforms could range from making social care free at the point of need to placing a cap on the amount people spend.

"The PM has for a long time mooted the idea of a social care system similar to NHS," she said.

"It would be expensive but on the scale of what we spend on other public services - around Â£200bn on the NHS - we are talking for some of these options low billions per year."

Adult social care has proved a complex issue to tackle for successive governments.

Two years ago Sir Keir Starmer was criticised when Labour scrapped plans for an Â£86,000 cap on the amount people in England would spend on social care in their lifetime.

Badenoch wrote in her letter to Burnham that "any solution to the issues around social care must also be fair to those who have made provisions and saved up over the course of their lives".

Layla Moran, the Liberal Democrat MP who chairs the Health and Social Committee, warned against the issue becoming a "political football".

"We do need to discuss where the money is going to come from but also we need to all be putting our political capital into this," she told the Today programme.

Lib Dem leader Sir Ed Davey said he was ready to do "whatever I can to find a real and lasting consensus on social care".

He said: "Family carers must be at the heart of any new system, everyone must get the care they need and no one should lose their home as a result."

Reform Treasury spokesman Robert Jenrick said social care needed fixing but warned the party would fight any proposal for a "universal death tax".

He said: "It's not fair to raid people's life savings and drags hundreds of thousands more families into paying tax when their loved ones pass away."

News.title: UK's iconic Jodrell Bank telescope faces axe in science cuts
News.content:
The Jodrell Bank Observatory, which has housed the UK's largest telescope for nearly 70 years, has lost its funding and could now close, the BBC understands.

The observatory and its network of telescopes have been pivotal to the country's study of distant galaxies and training future astronomers. Scientists have described the decision as "heartbreaking" and "scientifically misguided".

All scientific observations at Jodrell are expected to cease on the 1 April 2028 unless alternative funding can be found.

The funding body, the UK Research and Innovation (UKRI) agency, said it had to focus investment on projects that deliver "the greatest long-term impact".

The site was first established in 1945 and pioneered radio astronomy and the study of galaxies beyond our own.

It was also pivotal during the Cold War, when it was used to monitor Soviet missiles during the height of nuclear tensions between the USSR and Nato powers.

Its contribution to global scientific efforts earned it Unesco World Heritage status in 2019.

But the UKRI, which has an annual budget of just under Â£10bn, says it has had to cut the observatory's annual Â£2.8m budget because planned research costs for physics and the running of its labs had escalated.

The announcement is part of a broader 2.7% cut to astronomy, nuclear and particle physics research over the next four years which will also impact on other projects.

The UK will no longer participate in research at the James Clark Maxwell Telescope in Hawaii, which scientists are using to image supermassive black holes at the centre of galaxies.

UKRI has also cut funding for the UK's involvement in two instruments on the Extremely Large Telescope which is being built in Chile to search for signs of life on other Earth-like worlds.

And there will be a 20% cut in funding that supports UK participation in the Vera Rubin Telescope in Chile, which is creating the first movie of the Universe - the project was only launched last year.

Prof Michele Dougherty, executive chair of the science and technology branch of UKRI, said: "After listening to our community we have protected core discovery research. However, the situation does require some tough, but necessary, decisions.

"These are never easy choices, but we have made what we feel are the right decisions to bring... a sustainable financial position by 2029/30."

News.title: TV presenter and comedian Bill Oddie dies at 85
News.content:
Paying tribute, Oddie's former Springwatch co-host Kate Humble told BBC Radio 4's The World At One: "No-one could tell a story like Bill. No-one could make me laugh like Bill. No-one could enthuse anyone, whoever they were, to go outside and get excited about a robin.

"He just had that way of just making the natural world everybody's world, and I think that's what we all loved about him."

Oddie had many other interests and talents, she said. "He was so interested in so many things. He wasn't just the nerdy birder, or the funny, slightly irascible comedian, or the brilliant musician. He was all of those things. And he was always interested in everything."

She added: "Sometimes he'd be fantastically grumpy and would be the last person I'd want to see first thing in the morning, and other times he would just be the best company in the world, and he talked very openly about his struggles with mental health."

Jo Rowland, chief executive of the RSPCA, said: "I know many of our wildlife rescuers were inspired into animal welfare by Bill's groundbreaking broadcasting work and incredible knowledge of British birds, which brought the wonders of nature into millions of homes across the country.

"Nature has lost one of its best friends, fiercest champions and most iconic defenders. Our thoughts are with his family, friends, and the countless people he inspired to spend time birdwatching, to cherish nature, and to build a kinder world for animals."

News.title: Girlguiding unveils first major redesign of uniform range since 1990
News.content:
Girlguiding has unveiled the first major redesign of its uniform range in more than 30 years, with the aim of allowing its members the "freedom to express themselves".

Under the new, pared-back approach, members will only be required to wear a top from the new range to be considered "in uniform".

The new range has been inspired by feedback from thousands of Guides, Rainbows, Brownies and Rangers that suggested they valued choice and the ability to express their own style.

Girlguiding chief executive Felicity Oswald said "practicality, comfort and sustainability" were at the centre of the redesign, which is the first overhaul of all sections' uniforms since 1990.

The organisation said the uniform combines the charity's heritage with modern colours and prints.

The range is made up of 30 items of clothing, 15 accessories and neckerchiefs - with prices starting at Â£12 for a T-shirt.

Design features include hidden pockets in waist bands, thumb holes and badge sashes which double as cross-body bags.

"It's really comfortable," Isy, 12, who is in the Guides, told BBC Breakfast. "It doesn't feel like the old ones and it's practical to move in."

Poppy, a seven-year-old Brownie, said she wanted "loads of pockets, because I always lose badges, so I wanted somewhere to put them".

She also showed off the new Brownies gilet, which doubles as a pillow. "It has another secret pocket," Poppy added.

News.title: Man and woman die after being pulled from sea off Cornish beach
News.content:
A man and a woman have died after getting into trouble in the sea off a popular beach.

The two people were pulled from the water off Fistral Beach in Newquay, Cornwall, at about 21:45 BST on Sunday, about 15 minutes after HM Coastguard said rescue personnel were called.

Devon and Cornwall Police said both the man who was in his 60s and a woman in her 30s were confirmed dead at the scene.

Search and rescue teams from Newquay, Padstow and St Agnes took part in the operation, along with lifeboats from Newquay RNLI and a coastguard helicopter.

News.title: Amber heat health alerts for parts of UK ahead of next heatwave
News.content:
Amber heat health alerts have been issued for much of eastern England for later this week as temperatures rise again.

The East Midlands, East of England, London, and the South East are all under the amber alerts from 9am on Wednesday until 9am Thursday.

With the temperature forecast to peak in the mid-30s Celsius on Wednesday, the UK Health Security Agency (UKHSA), which issues the alerts, warns that significant impacts are likely across health and social care services due to the high temperatures.

Yorkshire and the Humber, the West Midlands, and the South West are all under less severe yellow alerts for the same period.

This latest heatwave comes after some of the driest regions of the UK missed their chance of rain over the weekend.

Parts of the northern and western UK saw some rainfall on Saturday and Sunday, with further showers and unsettled conditions expected over the next few days.

But southern parts of the country - where the least amount of rain has fallen - are set to see temperatures climb once again, with more dry and sunny weather in the forecast.

It comes as parts of Wales have officially entered drought status, while parts of southern, central and eastern England remain in "prolonged dry weather", the final stage before drought is declared.

The coming days will only exacerbate dry conditions as another heatwave is expected to be declared, with temperatures peaking around 34-35C (93-95F) in south-east England or the East of England.

News.title: Rapper Yung Filly tells trial 'vibes were good' with woman who accuses him of rape
News.content:
UK rapper Yung Filly has told a court that the "vibes were good" between him and a woman he is accused of raping after performing at a nightclub in Australia in 2024.

The rapper, whose real name is Andres Felipe Valencia Barrientos, took the witness stand at the District Court of Western Australia on Monday - a week after the start of his trial.

He is accused of sexually assaulting the woman, then 20 years old, in his hotel room after he performed in Hillarys, a coastal suburb of Perth.

Barrientos, 30, has pleaded not guilty to six counts of sexual penetration without consent, three counts of assault occasioning bodily harm, and one count of strangulation.

Barrientos told the court he had "fancied" the woman when they met at the concert venue. He had been in the VIP area while she leaned over the barrier from the general area.

He denied touching her inappropriately.

"I recall putting my hand on her waist," he told the court. But he said he had not put his hands down her pants or touched her breast.

The "vibes were good" between them later when they arrived at his hotel, Barrientos said.

His security guard took the woman's phone away - a "standard practice" to protect their privacy, according to Barrientos.

The court heard previously that the pair had engaged in consensual sex before Barrientos turned violent and she told him to stop.

Barrientos, who had been touring Australia at the time of the alleged offences, is also known for his work with the YouTube collective Beta Squad, and has appeared in the celebrity version of Bake Off on Channel 4 and presented BBC Three shows.

He has been on bail since being charged and was allowed to fly home to the UK in September for four months, before returning to Western Australia ahead of his trial.

In addition to his 1.8 million YouTube subscribers, he has three million followers on TikTok and and 2.4 million on Instagram.

News.title: Laura Kuenssberg: Our exclusive behind-the-scenes access at No 10 as Andy Burnham became PM
News.content:
Listening carefully during our interview, it seemed Burnham had distinct gears. He was fluent and passionate on his familiar ground: his desire to sort out social care, his track record in Manchester, his desire to run a government that feels relevant and effective where you live, local leaders eager to make many more decisions and able to spend taxpayers' money more freely without permission from Whitehall.

Those are his core beliefs, arguments he's made hundreds, if not thousands of times.

But when it comes to how he'll apply what he thinks in principle to what he does in practice, that was not always so clear. On social care for example, he's long believed there ought to be a National Care Service, like the NHS. But in a speech on Wednesday, that's not likely to be what he unveils.

Instead, he told me he'd "brought it straight forward", understood to mean speeding up the government review by Baroness Louise Casey of what ought to be done, not saying, "here's the plan".

When it came to questions that are on his desk for the first time, there was a contradiction. Burnham told us all many times that he will stick to the manifesto the country voted for in 2024.

But he's also vowed his arrival in office will usher in the biggest change in four decades. You don't have to be a student of political history to find a mismatch there - he's going to stick broadly to Sir Keir's plan, yet shift the government more fundamentally than leaving the EU, or the financial crash? Really?

And beyond the rhetorical tension in several areas, Burnham gave clear indications that he will apply "new eyes". Will he stick to the home secretary's plans to make migrants wait 10 years or more before they can permanently stay in the UK? He's looking at that again he told me, and hinted that care workers could possibly be exempt.

News.title: Funeral boss who lied about burying dad has shown no remorse, daughter says
News.content:
A woman whose dead father was discovered at an undertaker's three months after his funeral says her hellish ordeal has "crucified" her.

The body of Peter Moody, 65, was found by police alongside 34 others and more than 100 sets of ashes at Legacy Independent Funeral Directors in Hull in March 2024. One of the bodies had been there for a year.

Former funeral director Robert Bush, 48, of Otley, West Yorkshire, will appear at Hull Crown Court later for sentencing. He previously admitted 67 offences, including 30 counts of preventing a lawful and decent burial.

Peter Moody's daughter Joanne Moody, 48, who is expected to join other families wronged by Bush in the court's public gallery, said: "It's broke me, it's crucified me."

News.title: 'Antisemitism felt relentless' - Jewish students on life at UK universities
News.content:
Like many campuses across the UK, Cardiff University has seen pro-Palestine protests in recent years and Oliver said he believed some behaviour he witnessed crossed the line from criticism of Israel into antisemitism.

Holding Jewish people responsible for the actions of the Israeli government is a form of antisemitism, according to the International Holocaust Remembrance Alliance.

"That first year was absolutely terrifying," he said.

"You go home and think, 'do I carry on? Do I try to go to the next day?'"

Oliver said he stopped speaking Hebrew outside his home, and hid his Star of David pendant when on campus.

Over the following three years, Oliver said the antisemitic abuse he experienced at university became "relentless".

"I've been in clubs [or] just wandering around the uni and you hear these conversations and you see pamphlets being handed around where it's literally saying that your belief and your history is fake," he said.

"I've been at house parties where, when someone's found out I'm Jewish they started calling me Netanyahu behind my back.

"Like you found out my religion and you've decided I'm a bad person."

Oliver said when he had reported antisemitic incidents that had happened to him and others, he had felt they had been often "swept under the rug" by the university.

Although he said some positive action had been taken, he feels more needs to be done.

Cardiff University said it was sorry that "any student felt unsafe" on campus and that it adopts a "zero-tolerance approach to harassment and discrimination of all kinds".

It said there was no place for antisemitism or hatred at the university and they have "robust procedures" in place for investigating allegations of antisemitism. Where it is found, the university said appropriate action would be taken.

It said it had reached out to the university's Jewish Society and reminded students to report incidents to them.

News.title: Two women dead after diving trip at Scottish loch
News.content:
Two women in their 20s have died after a diving trip at a Scottish loch.

Police Scotland said the alarm was raised at Loch Fyne in Argyll and Bute, at about 15:30 on Sunday.

The force said a 26-year-old woman was pronounced dead at the scene at St Catherines, Cairndow.

The body of the second diver, who was 24, was found after further searches in the water.

Coastguard Rescue Teams from Crinan, Dunoon, Kames and Inveraray and lifeboats from Tignabruich, Campbeltown and Largs joined the search.

A Coastguard helicopter was also sent the scene.

Police Scotland said it responded to a "report of concern" for two female divers.

A spokesperson said: "The deaths are being treated as unexplained and a post mortem examination will take place in due course."

Loch Fyne It extends 40 miles (65km) from the Sound of Bute and is the longest sea loch in Scotland.

It is a popular diving location and known for its oysters and seafood.

News.title: Carer who took 'demeaning' videos of dementia patients sentenced
News.content:
Families have said their grieving process was made more difficult after a senior nursing assistant took and shared videos of patients with advanced dementia.

Ciara Corvan was sentenced to two years probation and 100 hours community service.

The 28-year-old from Cathedral View in Armagh, was working at the Bluestone Unit of Craigavon Area Hospital in 2023 when she took the videos, which included comments deemed offensive.

Colleagues who received the videos reported the behaviour.

In May of this year Corvan pleaded guilty to seven charges against four victims.

The court heard these included a video of a patient in the bath, another of a patient in bed and another with her nose almost touching one of the patients.

On Monday, Judge Patrick McGurgan said that, although the offending was not physical in nature, it was a "serious breach of trust".

"Each family who placed a love one in care as a last resort expects them to be treated with respect and dignity," he said.

Handing down a sentence of two years probation and 100 hours community service for seven counts of ill treatments of patients under the Mental Health Order (NI) 1986.

"It was demeaning to those you owed a duty of care to. I do not expect you were naive in this matter. The public must have confidence in those who provide care," he said.

News.title: Charli XCX photo purchased by National Portrait Gallery
News.content:
A portrait of the pop star Charli XCX has been added to the National Portrait Gallery's collection - the same week she is aiming for her second number one album of the year.

The picture, which shows the singer leaning against a wall in a white crop top and unbuttoned black jeans, was taken in 2024 by British photographer Harley Weir.

It became one of the key images in the promotion of her Brat album, matching the the music's debauched swagger and emotional candour.

Announcing the acquisition, the National Portrait Gallery called Charli "one of the defining artists of our time".

The photo will be displayed in the gallery's History Makers Now space, which celebrates figures who have shaped contemporary culture. The purchase was funded by a gift from the Bukhman Foundation.

Praising the portrait, the gallery's senior curator Brandei Estes said: "Harley Weir has developed a distinctive photographic language that combines intimacy with a powerful sense of presence.

"We are delighted to acquire this striking portrait of Charli XCX, which captures one of the defining cultural figures of her generation."

News.title: Businessman and philanthropist Sir Ian Wood dies aged 84
News.content:
The Aberdeen-based businessman and philanthropist Sir Ian Wood has died aged 84, his family has announced.

Sir Ian was one of the UK oil and gas industry's most respected leaders, who turned his family's fishing boat repair yard into a global engineering player in the North Sea and internationally.

He retired as chief executive in 2006 and a year later began concentrating on his charitable work, creating The Wood Foundation, which works on social and economic inequality, especially in Scotland and sub-Saharan Africa

His family said he died peacefully at home and they would remember his "kindness, generosity, determination and unwavering commitment to his family."

Sir Ian was one of Scotland's wealthiest people, with a personal worth estimated at Â£1.8bn.

Wood Group started as a family fishing business before Sir Ian took over in 1967.

Over the next decades, he formed a separate engineering company servicing the rapidly-growing North Sea oil business.

At its height, the Wood Group was valued at more than Â£5bn, carrying out work in the energy industry around the world. It went public in 2002 and was sold to a Dubai company last year.

Sir Ian, who retired as chairman of the group in 2012, was knighted in 1994 for services to the oil and gas industry and was later made a member of the Order of the Thistle, Scotland's highest order of chivalry.

News.title: Police hunt darts match attacker in lobster suit
News.content:
Detectives are hunting a man who seriously injured another man, punching and knocking him unconscious following a World Darts Championship match in north London.

The victim, who is in his twenties, was assaulted outside Alexandra Palace on 13 December and is still suffering from "significant injuries" seven months later, police said.

The suspect is believed to have been among a group of men who attended the darts tournament dressed in lobster costumes.

The Met Police has released a CCTV image taken at the venue in the hope of tracing the man and jogging the memory of any witnesses.

The victim was leaving Alexandra Palace at about 16:30 GMT when he encountered the group of men in costume.

He became involved in an argument with them and they were separated by security staff.

Soon afterwards, the victim ran into the group again on the venue's concourse and one of the men punched him, knocking him out.

He later reported the incident to the Met.

Det Con Lizzie Coster, who is leading the investigation, said: "Our thoughts are with the victim in this case, and we hope the best for his recovery.

"This assault occurred outside at a major sporting event, and the suspect was wearing a distinctive costume.

"We are releasing a CCTV image of the suspect in the hope that it will jog the memory of attendees, or anyone else who was in the area at the time."

Ronnie Le Drew, the TV presenter and puppeteer behind classic Rainbow character Zippy, has died, aged 78.

Candian-British star Le Drew was one of the squawking voices that brought the divisive Zippy to life in the beloved ITV series, alongside Roy Skelton, who died in 2011. Rainbow was the UK’s answer to the American educational series Sesame Street.

The British Puppet Guild announced the death of Le Drew – the organisation’s president – on Monday (27 July), writing: “We are saddened to announce the death of our President and friend Ronnie Le Drew, following a short illness.

open image in gallery James Le Drew was the man behind ‘Rainbow’ character Zippy ( Ken McKay/ITV/Shutterstock )

“Ronnie has been our president for 10 years, possibly the most active and supportive president we have ever had or will have.

The statement continued: “Attending nearly every event, whether it be online or in person, often performing when asked and always willing to chat, tell stories and entertain in whatever way he could.

It added that, while he was known for Zippy, “his legacy in the puppetry world stretches far more than that, and there will be countless puppeteers mourning the loss of our dear friend”.

“He meant so much to so many, and the legacy of his life will live on,” they said.

Le Drew’s TV career began in 1964, when he appeared on A Touch of Don Juan, and his Rainbow tenure commenced in 1973, lasting for 20 years.

He also appeared on an array of other children’s series, including Playdays, Utterly Brilliant with Timmy Mallett, and The Sooty Show, mainly playing Sooty’s sidekick, Sweep.

open image in gallery Ronnie Le Drew had an illustrious career as a puppeteer ( PA )

Le Drew had puppeteering roles in fantasy musical films Labyrinth, starring David Bowie, and The Little Shop of Horrors, both released in 1986, as well as The Muppet Christmas Carol (1992). He noted he was particularly proud of his work in Little Shop as his puppeteering work – a plant dialling a phone – received a close-up in the finished edit.

Le Drew taught at London’s Little Angel theatre, which specialises in productions for children and their families, for 30 years. His association with the theatre, founded by John and Lyndie Wright, led to him appearing in their director son Joe’s film Pan in 2015.

More recently, he played several background characters in 2019 Netflix series The Dark Crystal: Age of Resistance.

Speaking about the enduring appeal of Zippy, Le Drew told The Guardian in 2015: “We got so much more money than a puppeteer could ever have dreamed of.”

He also credited shows like War Horse and Avenue Q with “helping people understand” that puppetry “is sophisticated, and perhaps not only for children”.

Le Drew released an autobiography, titled Zippy and Me: My Life Inside Britain’s Most Infamous Puppet, in 2019, and would often tour live shows where he spoke about his career and brought some of his most memorable puppets to life.

Gabriel Langton has admitted he feared for his gymnastics future after his horrific fall at the Commonwealth Games.

The 19-year-old fell headfirst from three metres to the floor after missing his catch on the horizontal bar during the men’s team event, spending the night in hospital.

He confirmed he had not suffered a concussion as he returned to the Team England base wearing the silver medal he had still helped win.

open image in gallery Gabriel Langton avoided serious injury after a horror fall at the Commonwealth Games ( PA )

“I knew that I could still talk, I could move a lot of things. I was just hoping I could do gym again,” he said.

“Neck injuries are there to be taken seriously. I was just hoping that it wasn’t anything too bad. When I got the scans back, it was a big relief. My thought process switched quite quickly to being, ‘I should be back in the gym quite soon.’

“I’ve spoken to Team England doctors and physios, and hopefully it won’t be too long. It’ll be a gentle reintroduction, but hopefully not too long.

“I’m doing a lot better now. Slightly sore, but a lot better than I was a couple of days ago, knowing that it’s nothing too serious.”

open image in gallery Gabriel Langton fell while working on the horizontal bars ( PA )

Langton – who found out he had won a silver medal while in the medical room at the Glasgow International Arena – claimed the fall was just a fluke and said he cannot wait to get back in the gym.

“I’ve done that skill so many times, and this has happened once,” he added.

“I have performed it safely ten thousand times. If you look at those stats, this was just kind of a freak accident. I think I’ll be pretty confident that I can just put that to the side and trust in my gymnastics again.

“If I am to be in the headlines, then I’d rather be in it for winning medals. It’s more motivation to get back in the gym. I want to get back out there and prove that I’m here to win medals.

“I can’t wait to get back on the big stage again and be talked about for different reasons.”

open image in gallery Gabriel Langton can’t wait to return to competition ( PA Wire )

Langton revealed he remembers every moment of the fall, recalling how his first instinct was to climb back onto the horizontal bar and finish his routine despite landing headfirst.

“I remember pretty much all of it,” he said.

“We were slightly behind in the competition, so I was trying to go as close to perfection as I could. I really attacked that first go and, obviously, it went slightly wrong.

“I was in quite a lot of pain when I fell, but initially I thought I needed to get back on the bar and finish my routine. Then more medical staff came over, and I realised I probably wasn't going to get back on the bar.

“I was just really frustrated that it had happened at that moment. The team were behind and I felt I could have contributed to the team score, so I was disappointed in myself. Then, when the adrenaline wore off, I started to feel the pain.”

Carly Simon has revealed she was diagnosed with Parkinson’s disease and skin cancer.

The iconic singer, 83, has been absent from the spotlight for years, and revealed July 27 in a statement that her privacy was partly prompted by her health complications.

“So many people have written to me, kindly wondering about my relative silence, asking how I am and what I have been doing,” Simon said in a statement obtained by People. “The truth is, I’ve been learning how to live with Parkinson’s disease.”

She continued: “It has taken me some time to understand the diagnosis, to adjust to it, and to decide how much I wanted to say about it publicly. Parkinson’s is different for everyone, and it can be unpredictable. Some days I’m so tired I can’t get the day moving at all. On others, it gives me a little more room to move, think, work, and feel like myself.”

Simon went on to say that her health problems first started with arthritis in both of her knees and one hip, explaining, “I eventually had all three joints replaced, out with the old and in with delicate bouquets of metal and plastic. After three replacement surgeries, I assumed my difficulty walking was simply an unfortunate and rather ironic part of the recovery process.”

Carly Simon has revealed her Parkinson’s and skin cancer diagnoses ( Getty )

However, the “You’re So Vain” hitmaker’s mobility only worsened, and she found it increasingly difficult to stand up from chairs and had trouble walking.

She was then evaluated at the Mayo Clinic and diagnosed with Parkinson’s, prompting her to start treatment including medication.

“There is no tidy or predictable schedule to the illness. It does not consult my calendar before deciding what kind of day I am going to have,” she said.

Simon said that Parkinson’s has brought on mental symptoms as well as physical ones.

“It can bring anxiety, depression, exhaustion, and apathy,” she explained. “The apathy is particularly strange. You can find yourself lying there like a starfish drying in the sun, arms pointing in all directions, while nothing inside is telling you to get up, read, watch, write, sing, call someone, or do much of anything at all.”

She continued: “That has been one of the hardest things to explain. It is not simply sadness or laziness. It is as though the part of the brain that sends out invitations to participate in life has temporarily misplaced the guest list.”

No, Anthony Joshua’s win over Kristian Prenga was not fixed. But his fight with Tyson Fury might be broken beyond repair.

When Joshua cascaded to the canvas inside 20 seconds on Saturday, there was a brief feeling that his super-fight with Fury was collapsing him with. But barely five minutes later, Joshua was laughing off this scare as Prenga’s head snapped against the bottom ropes, leaving the helpless heavyweight to fade back into boxing obscurity as his consciousness faded, too.

Suggestions that the outcome was fixed (and there are a strange number of them) should not be entertained for a second. Every measurement of pain and damage in those chaotic few minutes were real. That should not need explaining.

open image in gallery Anthony Joshua (left) and Tyson Fury in their fights on the last weekend of July ( Getty )

Yet the narrative of the fight flipped almost as quickly as the narrative around Joshua vs Fury, which was being touted 24 hours earlier as a bout that was destined to go “AJ”’s way – such was the lacklustre nature of Fury’s win over Mariusz Wach. Fury was victorious after seven rounds in Thailand (although the fight was broadcast nowhere), but a 46-year-old Wach was no litmus test for the abilities of the “Gypsy King”.

Just as he did against Arslanbek Makhmudov in April, Fury looked comfortable but nothing more. Still, in fairness, comfortable is better than what Joshua experienced in Saudi Arabia.

So the relevant pages will read “Fury def. Wach via seventh-round TKO (3:00); Joshua def. Prenga via second-round KO (2:43)” – a removal of the final hurdles between the British heavyweights. However, the issue is that Fury and Joshua are certainly not speeding down the track to a November showdown at Wembley.

The 2am GMT ring walks proposed by Saudi matchmaker Turki Alalshikh were already farcical, but now there is talk that Joshua’s contract dictates a showdown on British soil. In contrast, Fury’s contract allows for a meeting in the US.

Furthermore, there must be conversations behind closed doors about whether Joshua is in the right state mentally to return to the ring in November.

In other words, two hurdles were dismantled at the weekend (laboriously, rather than being battered down), but two more might have arisen.

Do not be surprised if Joshua vs Fury is delayed until 2027. Do not be surprised if more warm-up fights are suggested. Do not be surprised if we never see the big one, even if those involved with the contracts might bristle at that suggestion.

open image in gallery Joshua climbs off the canvas after one of two first-round knockdowns ( Getty )

Do not forget: Joshua vs Fury has been signed before, and it still fell through.

Against Prenga, Joshua was already making a remarkably quick comeback after surviving a car crash in December, a tragic accident in Nigeria that killed two of his teammates. For all of Joshua’s admirable determination, for all of the soul searching, for all of the time spent training with his old rival Oleksandr Usyk in Ukraine, the blunt truth is that he was dropped by the first meaningful shot Prenga threw.

Whether Joshua’s mind or chin is not right, either is cause for concern against Fury. Then again, the weekend’s fights led one boxer to tell The Independent: Joshua vs Fury could be a case of “chin is gone” versus “legs are gone”.

There was already a consensus that Fury vs Joshua, should it take place in November, would be occurring several years too late. But at various points in the last few years, this writer would have told you that each boxer might have diminished to a similar degree, and not to an excessive one, making the match-up an alluring prospect still. Of course it would have been best to see them clash at the heights of their powers, but all you really needed was to believe that both had a realistic chance of winning – and the odds have shifted time and again over the years.

But now, Joshua vs Fury really might come down to who has declined more severely, to the point that it is no longer an enticing proposition.

open image in gallery Fury eased past Mariusz Wach, one day before Joshua beat Kristian Prenga ( Getty )

It’s not unusual for heavyweights to box into their 40s, but some of the all-time greats have looked closer to their primes at that age than Joshua and Fury do at 36 and 37.

So, it’s not just that the former champions aren’t speeding down the track to their long-awaited fight, as mentioned above; either man might run out of road before it arrives.

Each time a step towards Joshua vs Fury is taken, the fight inches further out of reach, like some sort of Sisyphean punishment. The fight, as a concept rather than an actual sporting contest, has become an endless, hellish loop. I can’t be the only one who wants out.

Three women - one reportedly pregnant - were attacked on the streets of Paris on Monday by a man armed with two kitchen knives.

The incident took place at about 9.30am near Porte de Clichy in Paris. Interior Minister Laurent Nunez told reporters the man attacked the three women, who were aged 19, 24 and 36, severely wounding two of them.

According to a witness speaking to Le Figaro, one of the victims was pregnant.

Two of the victims who were taken to hospital remain in critical condition. Local media reports one woman was hit in the lower back and the other in the abdomen.

Le Figaro reported the ⁠man declared: "It is Allah who ordered me" while he was being arrested.

open image in gallery Police officers work at the site of a knife attack near the Porte de Clichy in Paris ( Reuters )

The motive of the attack remains unknown, Nunez said, adding police could not verify the identity of the attacker, whose declarations were "incoherent" when he was being arrested.

Footage from the scene posted on social media shows a man holding a knife while crossing traffic.

The minister said the man was detained by an off-duty police officer. "I pay tribute to him, it was a courageous act," Nunez added.

This is a developing story. More to follow...

I make these Black Sesame-Brown Butter Rice Krispies Treats, excerpted from my book “108 Asian Cookies,” with my mother in mind.

Growing up, I ate my fair share of Rice Krispie Treats because they were one of the few Western sweets my mom made over and over again. Maybe it was because they were so easy to make and helped her feel a little closer to the typical mothers we saw on American sitcoms and primetime TV. Or maybe she just liked their chewiness.

But for whatever reason, my mom never gave her Rice Krispies Treats an Asian spin. She always followed the recipe directions on the cereal box to a T.

But she loves black sesame desserts, especially sweet black sesame soup. As a child, I remember her telling me how black sesame would keep our Chinese hair black and long. We both have short hair peppered with gray now, but we still have a thing for desserts that sport a lovely shade of gray or black.

Black Sesame and Brown Butter Rice Krispie Treats

Makes 12 to 16 Rice Krispie Treats

Start to Finish 55 minutes

Ingredients

6 tablespoons unsalted butter

One 12-ounce bag mini marshmallows

1/4 cup black sesame seeds

2 1/2 tablespoons black sesame paste

1 teaspoon red miso

6 cups Rice Krispies cereal

1/3 cup freeze-dried strawberry slices or haw flakes (optional)

Directions

1. Crumple, then uncrumple a large sheet of parchment paper and use it to line a 9-inch-square cake pan with some overhang. Smooth and press down the parchment paper with your hands. Alternatively, generously grease the baking dish with butter or toasted sesame oil.

2. To make the brown butter, melt the butter in a heavy saucepan or pot over medium heat while whisking continuously until the butter foams, the foam subsides, the butter is golden, and brown (not black) bits form on the bottom, at least 5 minutes. You’re looking for a nutty aroma and not a burnt smell. Reduce the heat to low and add the marshmallows. Stir until the marshmallows have melted into one thick fluff, like foamy, melty mozzarella cheese, a few minutes. There should be no lumps of marshmallow. Add the black sesame seeds, black sesame paste, and miso and mix to combine. Turn off the heat and dump in the cereal, about 2 cups at a time, while stirring; if you like, add the freeze-dried strawberries or haw flakes as well. Stir and mix with a spatula or wooden spoon until all the ingredients are thoroughly coated with gray-black melted marshmallows.

3. Transfer the mixture to the prepared pan and flatten into a leveled square. I find it easier to do this with a layer of parchment paper on top and pressing down with a fondant smoother. You can also use a greased spatula or your clean hands when the mixture is cool enough to touch.

4. Cover and let it rest on the counter at room temperature for about 30 minutes to let the mixture set. Then, use a sharp knife to cut into 12 to 16 equal pieces.

___

Kat Lieu is a food writer, recipe developer, content creator, and founder of the popular online group Subtle Asian Baking, which aims to spread the love of Asian baking and fundraises for Asian American and Native Hawaiian-Pacific Islander communities. She lives in Renton, Washington.

George Groves has said Anthony Joshua and Tyson Fury’s wins at the weekend combined to make the “worst  in history” for their planned fight.

On Saturday, Joshua survived two first-round knockdowns to stop relative unknown Kristian Prenga in round two, one day after Fury beat a 46-year-old Mariusz Wach in seven rounds – with the latter fight not broadcast anywhere.

Those bouts were seen as the final hurdles for a long-awaited, all-British clash between Fury and Joshua, a pair of former world heavyweight champions.

open image in gallery Anthony Joshua climbing off the canvas after one of two first-round knockdowns ( Getty )

But after Joshua’s concerning performance, and amid fresh talks about whether a fight with Fury will take place in the UK or US, hype for the “mega-fight” is not where it should be, per Groves.

The former super-middleweight champion, speaking to the Independent via Betselect.co.uk, said:“Fury is a clever man in terms of the opponents he’ll pick, to make sure that he wins, but him against Wach looked like two grandads having a punch-up in a Thailand sort of dojo.

“[It was as if] they’ve had a midlife crisis, they’ve sold up, they’ve moved to Thailand, and they fancy having a fight. When people are telling you [Fury] is about to be involved in the biggest fight in the history of boxing, I’m left scratching my head.

“Up until about Saturday night, I thought: ‘If he fights Joshua... Fury just looks so old now, his career’s catching up with him, the lifestyle is catching up with him, Joshua’s probably gonna weather the distance better.’

“But [Joshua] walks into Jeddah, fights someone that none of us have really heard of, who’s got a good record – but it doesn’t mean anything – and he gets dropped with the first punch. He’s away with the fairies, he’s almost out for the count. He gets up, gets dropped again, and then surprisingly Prenga in the second round decides not to throw a punch and gets stopped himself.

“So, the show goes on, but it’s got to be the worst  to sell a mega-fight in history. I can’t think of anything that would get close to this.

“And I know we’re doing interviews now talking about Fury and Joshua, that’s why it’s stayed this relevant, because these guys are famous enough to get a headline and engage with people, but when it comes around... I’ll be interested, but I’m not on the edge of my seat; I don’t think anyone truly can be.

“You needed something that was a statement. I mean, the Jake Paul fight was more exciting than the Joshua fight at the weekend, in terms of: ‘What’s next for Joshua?’”

open image in gallery Tyson Fury (left) failed to impress against Mariusz Wach ( Reuters )

Groves, 38, was referring to his fellow Briton’s fight with Paul in December, when Joshua, 36, stopped the YouTuber-turned-boxer in six rounds.

Ten days later, “AJ” survived a car crash in Nigeria that killed two of his teammates, and in the subsequent months, Joshua began training with his former opponent Oleksandr Usyk in Ukraine. A relieved-looking Usyk was ringside in Jeddah as Joshua beat Prenga.

“I applaud that [comeback] to a certain degree, if there’s something left to deliver,” Groves said, “but you’re finished. He’s finished, and Tyson Fury’s finished.”

Fury’s win over Wach came three months after he outpointed Arslanbek Makhmudov at Tottenham Hotspur Stadium, as Fury emerged from retirement for the fifth time. That comeback followed two consecutive points losses to Usyk in 2024.

Joshua, 36, versus Fury, 37, has been mooted for London’s Wembley Stadium in November, but Saudi matchmaker Turki Alalshikh has said ring walks would need to begin at 2am GMT. However, since Joshua beat Prenga, it has emerged that the US is back on the table as a possible location for the all-British showdown.
