World.title: Mango factura 1.852 millones en el primer semestre, el 7,2% más
World.content:
Mango cerró el primer semestre del año con una facturación de 1.852 millones de euros, un 7,2% más respecto al año pasado, según ha comunicado la compañía esta mañana a través de un comunicado. El crecimiento, que a tipo constante fue del 10,7%, indica la capacidad de la compañía para no verse afectada por la imputación de Jonathan Andic, ex vicepresidente la empresa e investigado por la muerte de su padre, el fundador de la firma. La empresa ha asegurado que estos resultados “evidencian la fortaleza de su propuesta de valor y reafirman la trayectoria de crecimiento sostenido” de los últimos años.

Mango ha operado este primer semestre de año en un entorno muy complejo. Para acabar de blindarse ante el caso Andic, el heredero del fundador dejó el pasado mes de mayo el puesto que ocupaba dentro de la compañía. Los resultados apuntan a que el grupo, por ahora, está logrando esquivar todo el ruido mediático alrededor de la familia Andic y enfila el final de su plan estratégico para el periodo de entre 2024 y 2026. El presidente y consejero delegado, Toni Ruiz, ha recordado en la nota difundida a los medios que ese programa tiene el objetivo de cerrar este año con una facturación de 4.000 millones. “Los resultados del primer semestre reflejan una evolución positiva, con un crecimiento por encima de la media del mercado, y refuerzan nuestro posicionamiento como referente internacional en moda”, ha dicho.

La empresa ha seguido, además, invirtiendo para mpliar y mejorar sus tiendas. En concreto, dedicó 90 millones a esas obras, a fortalecer operaciones y capacidades tecnológicas y expandir el Campus Mango, la sede corporativa ubicada en Palau-solità i Plegamans (Barcelona) donde el grupo tiene a más de 2.000 trabajadores. En concreto, la empresa ha realizado 127 aperturas y 37 reformas durante el primer semestre, y cerró junio con una red de más de 2.960 puntos de venta en más de 120 países.

Mango ha explicado que el negocio internacional “continuó mostrando una sólida evolución” durante el periodo y alcanzó el 77% del total de la facturación, y que los principales mercados fueron España, Francia, Turquía, Alemania y Estados Unidos. Además, ha recordado que sigue en marcha su plan para abrir 45 tiendas en Francia hasta 2028 (de las cuales, este año 15) con un presupuesto de 66 millones; su alianza estratégica con Coin para abrir 27 establecimientos en Italia hasta 2028, y la voluntad de inaugurar 10 tiendas en Reino Unido y otras 10 en Turquía este año. El negocio online también registró un incremento de doble dígito y representó el 32% de la facturación total.

World.title: A San Andrés de Teixido, por el Camiño Vello
World.content:
Una ruta a pie por la salvaje Costa Ártabra, en el extremo septentrional de España, buscando el segundo santuario más visitado de Galicia, que se alza desde tiempos remotos al pie de los acantilados más altos de Europa

Dicen que “a Santo André de Teixido vai de morto quen non foi de vivo”. ¿Y eso es malo? Respondamos gallegamente: depende. Si para ir allí, uno se reencarna en una babosa y se arrastra a cámara lenta por un camino abarrotado de peregrinos, corriendo el serio peligro de acabar espachurrado bajo una suela Vibram, no es bueno. En cambio, si se reencarna en una bolboreta, en una mariposa macaón o en una blanca esbelta ­–por citar dos especies habituales en el extremo norte de la Península–, y se va parando en cada flor a libar y copular, no está mal.

Probablemente Dios y san Pedro no pensaron en esta posibilidad cuando hallaron a san Andrés triste y solo en su santuario coruñés, pues no recibía ni la milésima parte de visitas que el de Santiago, y le prometieron que a su templo vendrían todos los mortales y que aquel que no lo hiciera en vida, lo haría reencarnado en un animal. O no lo pensaron bien o no sabían de mariposas.

Más información 13 razones por las que queremos viajar

Tras los pasos del Padre Sarmiento

Al santuario de San Andrés de Teixido, como al de Santiago, llevan todos los caminos. Hay casi tantos como peregrinos, que son legión –unos 70.000 al año– desde que se enteraron de que Dios y san Pedro habían prometido lo que prometieron a san Andrés. Todos valen, pero el original, el primero del que hay noticia fidedigna, es el que siguió el ilustrado Padre Sarmiento en 1755. Este escritor y erudito benedictino, que había pasado su niñez y parte de su juventud en Pontevedra, se interesó como ningún otro en su tiempo por todo lo gallego, en especial por la lengua y la geografía, a tal punto que iba anotando en un cuaderno los nombres exactos de los lugares por los que andaba. Gracias a eso, hoy puede seguirse sin dificultad el camino que hizo. Bueno, y gracias también a la Diputación de A Coruña, que lo señalizó en 2001 con monolitos de granito en los que un pescado rojo indica la dirección correcta. Para más facilidad, en Wikiloc están la descripción, el mapa y el track de este camino de 39 kilómetros, que suele hacerse dividiéndolo en dos etapas de unas seis horas de duración cada una.

El santuario de San Andrés de Teixido, destino final del histórico Camiño Vello y uno de los principales centros de peregrinación de Galicia. Andrés Campos

El Camiño Vello, que así se llama –aunque también podría llamarse Bello, con be, porque lo es– arranca en el monasterio de San Martiño de Xuvia, en la parroquia de O Couto, en Narón, junto a la ría de Ferrol. Bordeando ésta se sube hasta el molino de mareas de As Aceas –de mediados del siglo XVIII, que llegó a ser una de las mayores fábricas de harina de Galicia­­­–, donde el camino se desvía tierra adentro para ir en busca del Pazo Libunca, un palacete modernista de 1922 cuyo primer dueño y constructor, el indiano Francisco Montenegro, dicen que se encendía los puros con billetes de mil pesetas. Ahora es un hotel muy majo pero carillo, donde se necesitan al menos 24 de aquellos billetes –unos 145 euros– para dormir una noche de verano. Pasando después por la necrópolis prehistórica del Monte dos Nenos y por el Marco de Portonovo de Valverde –pedrusco milenario donde confluyen los términos de Narón, Valdoviño y San Sadurniño– se llega, ya casi al final de la primera etapa, a la ermita de Liñeiro, más conocida como la Capela da Fame, la Capilla del Hambre, nombre popular que suena fuerte y claro, como las tripas del peregrino después de caminar 22 kilómetros.

Las caldupeiras de Porto do Cabo

En Porto do Cabo –pueblo chico pero de hermosos y extensos dominios, divididos entre los municipios de Valdoviño, Cedeira y Cerdido–, se acaba la primera etapa del Camiño Vello y también la fame, el hambre que cualquiera arrastra tras andar seis horas por el monte. Aquí, alrededor del puente medieval, se ponían antaño las caldupeiras, mujeres que por poco dinero –un patacón de cobre– daban a los peregrinos una cunca rebosante, no de aguachirle, sino de guiso sustancioso: un caldo gallego, vaya. Y aquí se siguen poniendo, con pañoletas, mandiles, zuecos de cuero y ollas humeantes, las mujeres de la Asociación Veciñal Porto de Cabo, cuando se celebra la romería más importante a San Andrés de Teixido, el primer fin de semana de septiembre.

Vecinas de Porto do Cabo caracterizadas como caldupeiras durante la romería de San Andrés de Teixido, una tradición que recuerda a las mujeres que alimentaban a los peregrinos. Andrés Campos

Una de estas caldupeiras, Antonia Martínez, y su marido y presidente de la asociación vecinal, José Picallo, son los propietarios de Casa do Morcego, bautizada así en recuerdo de los muchos murciélagos que la habitaban antes de ser transformada en un hotelito rural encantador, el mejor de la ruta. Murciélagos ahora se ven pocos. En cambio, hay bolboretas a patadas: mariposas de los muros, vanesas pintadas, mantos oscuros, colias, níspolas… El huerto está lleno de ellas y también de verduras que acaban en la cocina de la casa y en las tripas cada vez más silenciosas del caminante.

Casa do Morcego es un lugar que envicia, donde uno se estaría, no una noche, sino una semana explorando los contornos de la mano de Antonia Martínez y José Picallo. En el mismo Porto do Cabo se conservan la histórica hospedería Casa da Bastona y el puente medieval sobre el río das Mestas, el cual desagua en la ría de Cedeira cerca de un lugar donde se acaba la poca fame que el caminante pueda aún tener: Taberna do Puntal. Tampoco se come mal en el restaurante O Castro, con vistas a la playa de Pantín, la catedral gallega del surf. Ni en Badulaque, en el puerto de Cedeira, a tiro de caña de la lonja. Más frescos, los rapes y las almejas no pueden llegar. Luego lo suyo es dar un largo paseo digestivo viendo el casco viejo de Cedeira, el castro Sarridal, el Castelo da Concepción y el atardecer desde el mirador de San Antonio de Corveiro.

Bichos y bestas de la Serra da Capelada

Tras desayunar y sellar el pasaporte de peregrino en Casa do Morcego, comienza la segunda etapa del Camiño Vello subiendo por espesos y fragantes montes de eucaliptos para, a los cinco kilómetros –una hora y media a paso regular– pararse a desayunar otra vez en Panadería Prados (981 48 24 58), en A Venta, en la parroquia cedeiresa de San Román de Montoxo. En este horno de leña, además de un pan irresistible –lo habitual en Galicia–, hacen ricas cocadas, bollas de manzana, bizcochadas y empanadas de raya. Conviene llevar una mochila XXL porque todo, dentro del cuerpo, no cabe.

La ermita de San Roque de Reboredo marca la entrada a la Serra da Capelada en la segunda etapa del Camiño Vello. Andrés Campos

Siguiente parada, en la capilla de San Roque de Reboredo, ermita del siglo XVII que señala la entrada a la Serra da Capelada. Quienes peregrinan a Teixido han de mirar siempre bien dónde pisan, por si alguien que no fue allá en vida está haciendo el camino transmutado en insecto, anfibio o reptil, pero aquí deben extremar las precauciones porque el prado de la ermita está plagado de ranas galaicas y de luciones, lagartos ápodos, sin patas, también conocidos como culebrillas de cristal. A los que pasen sin despanzurrar ninguno, san Andrés se lo agradecerá. Y san Roque, patrón de los peregrinos y amigo de los animales, no digamos. Esta era una de las muchas capelas habitadas por ermitaños que dieron nombre a la Serra da Capelada, orónimo que el Padre Sarmiento explicó en 1755, cuando peregrinó anotando todo en su cuaderno de viaje.

A partir de aquí, el paisaje se vuelve más agreste. Se puebla de bestas, los caballejos semisalvajes que cada primavera rapan y marcan con festiva algazara los ganaderos de la comarca. Y se puebla también de amilladoiros, montones de piedras en los que el peregrino previsor arroja la que ha transportado en la mochila desde su lugar de origen para que el día del Juicio Final demuestre que ha estado aquí en vida y no tenga que volver desde el más allá, convertido en un bicho. Eso, si es que es capaz de encontrarla, sepultada como está bajo hogazas de pan, dulces varios y empanadas de raya.

Un artesano elabora y vende sanandresiños, los tradicionales amuletos de pan asociados a la romería de San Andrés de Teixido. Andrés Campos

En el mirador Chao do Monte, a un kilómetro justo del final, se obtiene la primera vista del santuario de San Andrés de Teixido. Si el caminante no supiera que está en la esquina más norteña de Galicia, diría que aquella iglesia de allá abajo y aquellas casitas de piedra casi negra con llagas blancas, rodeadas de acantilados y de verdores tan intensos que hacen daño a la retina, son un pueblecito de la isla canaria de La Gomera. Y si no supiera que san Andrés no pisó nunca España y que terminó atado a una cruz en forma de aspa en la ciudad griega de Patras, diría lo que dice la leyenda: que aquella peña oronda que aflora del mar al pie del blanco caserío, cual navío panza arriba, es la barca de piedra en la que vino a Galicia, emulando a Santiago, y con la que naufragó al llegar, demostrando que estos acantilados no son un buen lugar para atracar.

“A San Andrés van dos y vuelven tres”

Una vez en San Andrés de Teixido, la tradición manda acercarse a los puestos de productos típicos –exvotos, licores, herba de namorar, rosquillas, juncos del bien parir, pines con forma de percebe…– para comprar los sanandresiños, amuletos hechos con masa de pan sin fermentar, endurecidos al horno y pintados de vivos colores, que tienen diferentes formas, adecuadas al uso que se les va a dar: la flor, para conseguir el amor; la mano, para formular un deseo; la sardina que pescó san Andrés, para conjurar las envidias… Son muy bonitos y prometedores, pero para comer no valen. Para eso, están los percebes y todo lo que sirven, sin florituras, en la Taberna Hermanos Bouza.

Lo segundo que hay que hacer en San Andrés de Teixido es entrar en la iglesia, erigida sobre la roca viva, y pedir la bendición del titular, a cuyos pies suele haber gran variedad de ofrendas: fotos de carné, extremidades de cera, barquitos de madera… Por haber, hay hasta ataúdes de personas que, gracias al santo, no llegaron a necesitarlo. Y lo tercero, dirigirse a la fuente de los Tres Caños, de los cuales tres hay que beber para que se cumpla un deseo. Si se arroja una miga de pan y flota, también es buena señal. Y si se tiene una verruga y se lava con esta agua, puede que se caiga o puede que no. En el peor de los casos, se tendrá una verruga lustrosa. Las que tienen una piel preciosa, verde brillante con reticulado en negro y ocelos axiales azules, son las lagartijas serranas (Iberolacerta monticola) que pululan en el merendero aledaño.

Una lagartija serrana junto a la fuente de los Tres Caños, donde la tradición invita a beber tres sorbos para pedir un deseo. Andrés Campos

Antiguamente, también era tradición bajar hasta la rompiente en busca de la hierba de enamorar, hacer un ramito con ella y depositarla en el santuario como ofrenda. Ahora, que hay más conciencia ambiental, se recomienda comprar la que venden en los tenderetes, procedente de cultivos. A la Armeria pubigera se le atribuyen propiedades enamoradoras –una pizca en el bolsillo del otro obra el milagro–, afrodisiacas y empreñadoras. Y no falla, según lo que dicen: “A San Andrés van dos y vuelven tres”.

Acantilados gigantes y playas salvajes

En San Andrés de Teixido termina el Camiño Vello, pero el viaje a pie se puede alargar una jornada más –tres en total– bordeando los acantilados situados al noreste del santuario, que hay quienes dicen que son los más altos de Europa continental, aunque otros, más cautos, añaden que están a la par con los de Irlanda y Noruega. En el filo más elevado, a 620 metros sobre el océano, descuella la Vixía de Herbeira, un puesto de vigilancia costera del siglo XVIII desde el que los barcos enemigos debían de verse, si es que se veían, como microbios. El mar sí se ve, pero tan lejos que no se oye. Aquí, incluso en verano, sopla un viento recio, fresco, de jersey obligado. En ir y volver desde San Andrés de Teixido se tarda cuatro horas, siguiendo esta ruta de Wikiloc.

La playa de Fornos, en el municipio coruñés de Cariño, destaca por sus aguas transparentes y su entorno prácticamente virgen. Andrés Campos

El cabo Ortegal, ya en el vecino concejo de Cariño, es el segundo más norteño de la Península después del de Estaca de Bares. Y el más afilado, con el sitio justo para la carretera y un faro como de juguete. Le acompañan tres temibles islotes, Os Aguillóns, como si él solo no diera ya bastante miedo. Los que saben de percebes dicen que aquí se cogen los mejores de Galicia. Y los que saben de rocas, que estas son las más antiguas de la península Ibérica, de hace 1.156 millones de años. De la Vixía de Herbeira al cabo Ortegal hay 11,5 kilómetros de camino, unas tres horas sin parar apenas.

A la Vixía de Herbeira y al cabo Ortegal también se puede ir en coche, si es que uno no tiene las fuerzas o las ganas suficientes para prolongar a pie el Camiño Vello. Pero a donde solo se puede ir andando es la playa de Teixidelo. Escondida al pie de los tremendos acantilados de la Serra da Capelada, es la única playa del mundo de arena negra no volcánica. Su misterioso color es producto de la erosión de rocas ricas en peridotita y olivino. Para descubrirla, se ha de caminar desde el mirador de Teixidelo, muy cerca de San Andrés de Teixido, siguiendo una ruta de circular breve pero muy abrupta y empinada, de seis kilómetros y casi tres horas de duración, solo para senderistas expertos. Los que no lo sean se moverán mucho mejor por estos vertiginosos vericuetos de la Serra da Capelada acompañados por los guías de Portal Norte.

Otras playas salvajes alucinantes, con acceso más sencillo, son las que rodean la península de Figueiroa, en el vecino concejo de Cariño. A un lado de la península está la de Fornos, de 400 metros de largo por 60 de anchura, cuyas aguas verdes nada tienen que envidiar a las del Caribe. Salvo la temperatura, lógicamente. Al otro, la de Figueiras, más pequeña –260x15 metros– y recogida, frecuentada por las mariscadoras que siembran y luego recogen, rodilla en tierra, su cosecha berberechil. Y en medio, la más seductora, la de Os Cabalos o de A Postiña –350x30 metros–, solo accesible a pie desde las otras dos cuando la marea baja. Las fuertes corrientes de la ría y las violentas mareas hacen casi imposible bañarse en ella. Si nos gusta bajar a la playa cinco minutos, a deshora y sin gente, es perfecta.

World.title: Aging population puts pressure on dental care
World.content:
New research by Rabobank shows that the country’s aging population will put pressure on dental care providers.

A report published on Monday warns that there are not enough dentists too keep up with the specialsed needs of the elderly.

“The increasing aging of the population also brings with it changing challenges in terms of knowledge and the way of working in dental practices,” the report says.

In 2045, more than one in seven residents of the Netherlands will be older than 75, compared to one in ten now.

The proportion of people over 75 without their own teeth has fallen considerably in the last two decades, thanks to technological advancements and the improved financial situation for many later in life. As such, older people often need more frequent and specialised care including the maintenance of crowns, bridges and implants.

On average, a person over 75 contacted the dentist 3.2 times a year in 2025, compared to 1.6 times in 2014, the report says.

The professional association KNMT warned the House of Representatives in 2021 that a shortage of service providers was loom and called for more capacity to train dentists.

Currently, there are 259 dental training places at three universities. Last year, the education ministry decided to gradually expand the number of dentistry study places to 290 by 2027.

The gaps are already being filled by dentists from other countries. Some 25 percent of the dentists working in the Netherlands were trained abroad and that number continues to rise.

World.title: ICC’s chief prosecutor dismissed over sexual misconduct claims
World.content:
The chief prosecutor of the International Criminal Court, Karim Khan, has been dismissed after a member states voted to remove him over allegations of sexual misconduct.

The 56-year-old British lawyer was relieved of his duties more than a year ago at his own request after members of his team, including a 39-year-old Malaysian lawyer, came forward with detailed claims of harassment.

Khan vigorously denied the allegations, but an internal investigation at the court, based in The Hague, concluded in June that he had committed a “serious breach of duty” by having a sexual relationship with a junior member of staff. He subsequently tried to pressure her into dropping her complaint, the inquiry found.

Supporters of Khan claimed he had been the victim of a smear campaign linked to his decision to issue arrest warrants for Israel’s prime minister Benjamin Netanyahu and former defence minister Yoav Gallant as part of an investigation into war crimes in Gaza.

It is the first time a prosecutor has been dismissed by the ICC in connection with a disciplinary investigation. Khan’s lawyer said he would challenge “the lawfulness and fairness of the decision”, but it is not clear what legal avenues are available.

“Brick by brick”

The vote by a two-thirds majority of the ICC’s 125 members comes at a time when the court is coming under renewed pressure from the United States government.

US Secretary of State Marco Rubio claimed the court was a threat to American sovereignty and vowed to dismantle the institution “brick by brick”.

In an op-ed in the Wall Street Journal, Rubio claimed US border officials and elected leaders could be “dragged before an international court” and tried by foreign judges for the “so-called ‘crime’ of defending their own country.”

In fact, the ICC has no jurisdiction on US soil because the United States is not a member state.

In 2002 Congress passed the American Service-Members’ Protection Act (ASPA), nicknamed the Hague Invasion Act, which authorises the president to use “all means necessary and appropriate”, including military intervention, to release any American services personnel detained or imprisoned by the ICC.

World.title: Drive to recruit more teachers sparks 13.5% rise in applications
World.content:

More university students are opting for teacher training courses, raising hopes of an end to the shortage of staff in schools, latest figures show.

The number of new registrations increased by 13.5% last year, according to figures from Universiteiten van Nederland (UNL) reported by Trouw.

UNL chairman Caspar van den Berg said the development was “very good news” for efforts to tackle a nationwide shortage of 13,000 teachers in primary, secondary and vocational college education.

Some schools in the major cities have had to cut their timetable to a four-day week because of staff shortages.

“In the last few years universities have started more courses and put a lot of effort into promoting university teaching courses, ” Van den Berg said. “We are now reaping the benefits.”

Universities have introduced accelerated courses to get trainee teachers into work faster and concentrated on subjects with the most acute shortages, such as maths and science.

One-year masters

Matriculations for the latter category were up by 14% last year, while languages, which are also struggling with a lack of qualified staff, grew by a more modest 6.8%.

The biggest rise in applications was for the one-year masters course, which grew by 21.5% in the last year.

But the colleges’ association Vereniging Hogescholen said in February that applications for regular teacher training courses had also increased for the second year in a row.

High summer temperatures are set to return later this week after a cloudy start with showers in many places around the Netherlands.

By Monday afternoon, the sun will increasingly break through the clouds and temperatures will eventually reach between 19 to 23 degrees, according to Weeronline.

Tuesday afternoon will see the temperature rise, and by the afternoon it will already be a summery 25 degrees or more.

Wednesday and Thursday will be hot, with temperatures topping 35 degrees in some places. Wednesday night promises to be a truly sticky one, as temperatures stay about 20 degrees.

By Friday, we are likely to see cloud cover and a few showers, dropping the temperature to 25 to 28 degrees and as low as 21 degrees on the coast.

The weekend will be similar. There will also be patches of clouds and showers, with some sun. The temperature will range between 21 and 28 degrees.

World.title: Earthquake of 1.6 recorded in Groningen: “The whole house shook”
World.content:
Add as a favourite source on Google Add DutchNews as a favourite source on Google

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

An earthquake measuring 1.6 on the Richter scale has been recorded in Sappermeer, a village in the former Groningen gas field.

The quake struck at a depth of 3km below the surface and triggered dozens of messages to local broadcaster RTV Noord.

One woman living in Froombosch, a neighbouring village, said “everything in the house shook”, while another heard a loud bang and saw her dining table move.

The meteorological agency KNMI classed the incident as an “induced earthquake”, meaning it was caused by human activity such as gas drilling.

The number of earthquakes in Groningen has diminished since the Slochteren gas field was shut down two years ago, but the KNMI has warned that the effects will continue to be felt for years.

Last November a quake measuring 3.4 hit the village of Zeerijip, the second largest ever recorded in the province. A dozen residents were told their homes may no longer be safe to live in.

World.title: Van der Poel digs in for dramatic win in final Tour stage
World.content:
Mathieu van der Poel won a dramatic closing stage of the Tour de France as his late breakaway in Paris proved to be just enough to hold off the peloton.

The 31-year-old Dutch rider made his move with 10km to go as the riders climbed the hill towards Montmartre for the third and final time.

He was joined by overall race leader Tadej Pogacar, who was already assured of a record-equalling fifth Tour de France win and determined to sign off in style.

The pair opened up a gap of a handful of seconds over the rest of the field, but as the finish line neared it looked as it they were destined to pipped on the line as the pack closed in fast.

Pogacar gave up the effort in the final stretch, but Van der Poel pressed on and crossed the line a few centimetres ahead of his Alpecin team-mate Jasper Philipsen.

Philipsen was closing fast in the final 500m and just edged out Mads Pedersen, winner of the green jersey for the best sprinter in the Tour, for second place.

”From your toes”

An exhausted Van der Poel admitted in his post-race interview that he expected to be passed before the line.

He said: “I just went as hard as I could, and I was just waiting until a wheel was coming past, and it didn’t happen.

“If there was one race I still wanted to win in my career – I have a few, of course, but this was one of them.

“We have a saying in Dutch that it has to come from your toes. I don’t know where this came from, but not from my toes!”

The body of a Dutch man who dived into Lake Como to save his son was recovered on Sunday, Italian press agency ANSA reports.

The family had taken a rental boat out onto the Italian lake when the man’s 16-year old son dove into the water and had trouble returning to the craft.

The 45-year-old father went into the water to help him but disappeared. The boy was later rescued by someone on a paddle board.

The Italian coast guard spent more than a day searching for the man using sonar and under water cameras. They recovered his body lying 25 metres deep. The body was taken to a nearby hospital for an investigation.

World.title: Blood on Her Tongue: A modern vampire tale not for the squeamish
World.content:
Johanna van Veen’s gothic horror Blood on Her Tongue offers up a classic vampire tale with some modern contemplations.

The book follows Lucy Goedhart as she is called to the ominously named Zwartwater (black water) estate, where her sister has taken ill. In 1887, there isn’t much in the way of medical treatment, but Lucy’s sister Sarah isn’t fighting off a regular illness.

Sarah has become obsessed with a body found in the bog of the vast estate and since interacting with the 300-year-old corpse she has become increasingly incoherent, struggles with taking care of herself and has developed an insatiable hunger.

As Lucy tries desperately to save her sister, she finds that her sister’s husband, her sister’s doctor and childhood friend, and several other characters who are present at the remote manor house all have their own interests and motivations – some as dangerous as whatever condition is plaguing Sarah.

The book is not for those easily bothered by gore. The title – Blood on Her Tongue – is a pretty good indication of what is to come. Van Veen does not shy away from the horror elements, including two separate scenes of eyeball gouging.

Like any good horror novel, the macabre monster is not the scariest part. The threats Lucy faces are from the men surrounding her sister. Her brother-in-law attempts to seduce Lucy while badgering her to send Sarah away to an asylum.

Sarah’s doctor expresses his own interest in Lucy, pushing his vision of the future while supposedly devoting himself to his patient. The mores of 19th-century upper-class society may be the biggest piece of villainy of all.

In the tradition of Dracula, Blood on Her Tongue tells its story through letters, journal entries and newspaper clippings. The personal correspondence adds to the claustrophobia of the work, with everyone limited to an isolated house, but the media reports remind the reader that the world outside does exist.

The work is the second book from Dutch author Johanna van Veen. It was published in 2025 in English and became a USA Today bestseller. Her first book, My Darling Dreadful Thing, was nominated for the Bram Stoker Award for best horror novel. Van Veen grew up in the Netherlands as a triplet, something that influenced her writing about the sisters Lucy and Sarah.

If horror is your thing, Blood on Her Tongue will creep you out and keep you turning the pages.

You can get your copy at the American Book Center.

UNESCO has added the modernist city centre of the Polish port city of Gdynia to its World Heritage List, recognising its interwar urban planning and architecture. The designation, approved during the World Heritage Committee’s 48th session in Busan, South Korea, is Poland’s 18th World Heritage site and comes as Gdynia marks the centenary of gaining city rights. In its justification, UNESCO referred to “an urban organism that harnesses a building-block-based planning approach to develop a characteristic, compact complex of modernist architecture, with robust individual architectural expressions”. Gdynia’s city centre “illustrates a critical break with historicism in the progression of turning the village of Gdynia into a new major sea gateway of the first Polish Republic between the First and Second World Wars”, it added. Granted city status in 1926, Gdynia was rapidly developed by the newly independent Polish state from a small fishing village into a major Baltic seaport, growing to more than 100,000 residents in under 20 years and providing Poland with a modern maritime gateway. It is now Poland’s 13th largest city by population, with just under 210,000 residents, and the third largest by area when including its maritime territory. Nowy tydzień zaczynamy od dobrych wieści! Komitet Światowego Dziedzictwa UNESCO oficjalnie uznał modernistyczne centrum Gdyni za dobro o wyjątkowym znaczeniu dla całego świata. Nie ma lepszego momentu niż 100-lecie Gdyni na to wyjątkowe wyróżnienie!https://t.co/L3WZZCJCAz — Gdynia (@MiastoGdynia) July 27, 2026 Oktawia Gorzeńska, Gdynia’s deputy mayor, who represented the city in Busan, celebrated the decision of the committee as “a wonderful gift for our anniversary and a tribute to the vision and determination of the people who created one of Europe’s great modernist cities”. The city’s mayor, Aleksandra Kosiorek, added that the decision “confirms that the vision which launched the history of modern Gdynia over a century ago has retained its power and universal significance.” Gdynia’s central district of Śródmieście was built largely between 1926 and 1939. Its rapid development at the time drew international attention, with a National Geographic reporter writing that “Poland dreams of building her New York”. Unlike Warsaw and nearby Gdańsk, it escaped extensive destruction during World War Two, preserving much of its original street layout and interwar architecture. According to the city authorities, UNESCO experts have recognised the Gdynia’s centre as one of the world’s most outstanding examples of early modernism in urban planning. The nomination also highlighted Gdynia’s distinctive model of modernist urban planning, setting it apart from contemporaneous developments such as Germany’s Bauhaus, Berlin’s housing estates, Kaunas in Lithuania and Tel Aviv. Gdynia’s modernist architecture is characterised by white façades and maritime-inspired details, including round windows and building forms resembling ship hulls. Gdańsk in Poland has been named a global City of Literature by @UNESCO. It is now one of only 63 such cities in the world, and the third in Poland to obtain the distinction https://t.co/QdMxlT65V4 — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) November 3, 2025 Notable examples include the so-called “bank building”, a modernist tenement block, and the Museum of Emigration, housed in the former Maritime Station, which from the 1930s until 1979 was a transit building from which thousands of Polish emigrants left for their new homelands. According to the city, the road to recognition took over 20 years, beginning in 2007, when the historic urban layout was entered into the regional register of monuments. It was designated a Monument of History in 2015, and Poland submitted the site to UNESCO’s Tentative List in 2019. Two sites in Poland were included in the inaugural World Heritage List in 1978: the Historic Centre of Kraków and the nearby Wieliczka and Bochnia Royal Salt Mines. Gdynia’s inscription is the 18th for Poland overall and the first for a Polish modernist urban complex. The most recent Polish additions before Gdynia were the Krzemionki Prehistoric Striped Flint Mining Region in 2019 and, in 2021, the beech forests in the Bieszczady Mountains. World.title: Polish president obstructs windfall tax on fuel firms’ excess profits, prompting government criticism
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support. Prime Minister Donald Tusk has condemned opposition-aligned President Karol Nawrocki’s “shocking decision” not to sign into law the government’s planned windfall tax on excess profits by fuel companies amid a sharp surge in fuel prices caused by the war in Iran. While Nawrocki did not veto the bill, he exercised his right to refuse to sign it and instead send it to the Constitutional Tribunal (TK) for assessment, a process that can take years. The president argued that the retroactive nature of the tax “raises serious constitutional concerns”. Nowy podatek nie obniża cen paliwa. Ma przede wszystkim dostarczyć pieniędzy do budżetu. Nie mogę zaakceptować sytuacji, w której próbę łatania finansów państwa przedstawia się obywatelom jako ochronę ich interesów, podczas gdy skutkiem będzie kolejna fala podwyżek – Prezydent… pic.twitter.com/LqI7Cojdrr — Kancelaria Prezydenta RP (@prezydentpl) July 24, 2026 In mid-June, the government approved a 60% tax on excess profits from liquid fuel sales, calculated as the amount that would have been generated using a company’s average 2025 fuel sales margin, increased by 20%. The measure was expected to raise around 4 billion zloty (€927 million). When announcing the plans, the finance ministry said the levy was justified by this year’s “exceptional economic and geopolitical conditions that have led to above-average financial results in a specific segment of the fuel sector, not resulting from improved operational efficiency…but from a supply shock”. The tax was intended to offset the roughly 4.7 billion zloty the government spent on keeping fuel prices lower for consumers amid the crisis in the Middle East by, among others, cutting VAT and introducing a maximum daily price. The bill was approved by parliament on 3 July. It received support from Tusk’s ruling coalition, which ranges from left to centre right, but was opposed by the right-wing and far-right opposition. According to a regulatory impact assessment, state energy giant Orlen is expected to account for about 60% of the tax base for the windfall tax, with the remaining 40% generated by other market participants. Poland’s government has approved a windfall tax on fuel companies' excess profits after the surge in energy prices due to the war in Iran. It expects the measure, which still requires parliamentary and presidential approval, to raise 4bn zloty (€940m) https://t.co/DpXa8VJDjf — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) June 17, 2026 The legislation then passed to Nawrocki, who has vetoed a record number of bills since becoming president last year. However, this time he instead exercised his right to refer the bill to the TK without either signing or vetoing it. In a speech announcing his decision on Friday, Nawrocki said that the proposed measures “raise serious constitutional concerns”. In particular, he criticised the fact that tax would be retroactive: it would go into force in August but would apply to revenue earned from the beginning of March. “In a democratic state governed by the rule of law, citizens and businesses must know what regulations apply at the time decisions are made,” said Nawrocki. “The state cannot change the rules a few months later and send a bill for actions taken in accordance with applicable law.” The president also argued that, ultimately, the costs of the tax would be passed on to consumers, who have already been paying much higher fuel costs since the government’s protective measures expired at the end of June. “Unfortunately, it appears that the government first lowered fuel prices for propaganda purposes, and now has decided to impose a hefty bill on Poles,” declared Nawrocki. Once a bill is sent to the TK for assessment, there is generally no time limit on how long the tribunal can take to consider it. In practice, this means that some cases can can remain unresolved for years. If the TK does find a bill to be constitutional, the president must sign it into law. Currently, a majority of judges on the TK, including its chief justice, were appointed by and are regarded as aligned with the national-conservative Law and Justice (PiS) party that ruled Poland until 2023 and which supported Nawrocki’s presidential candidacy last year. The chief justice of the constitutional court has refused to accept four new judges appointed by parliament but whom the opposition-aligned president has refused to swear in. The decision deepens an unprecedented standoff over Poland's top court https://t.co/B02DKA3uBL — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) April 9, 2026 Nawrocki’s decision not to approve the windfall tax was condemned by government figures, including finance minister Andrzej Domański, who accused the president of “once again striking against Poland’s public finances”. In December, Nawrocki vetoed an increased tax on alcoholic and sweet drinks. “Instead of standing on the side of Poles, he sided with fuel corporations reaping huge profits from the current situation on the fuel market,” wrote Domański on social media. Tusk, meanwhile, wrote that the president had “blocked a bill that would have allowed taxing the gigantic profits of fuel conglomerates, making it possible to fund cheaper fuel at our stations”. He told consumers to “remember this [when you are] at the fuel pumps”. In response, the head of Nawrocki’s cabinet, Paweł Szefernaker, called Tusk an “economic dilettante” for thinking that imposing a tax would somehow lower costs rather than cause prices to rise. He instead called on the government to again lower VAT and excise duty on fuels. Od dawna wiadomo, że obecny premier jest gospodarczym dyletantem. Teraz próbuje przekonać Polaków, że nałożenie nowego podatku na paliwa sprawi, iż ceny na stacjach spadną. Zamiast nakładać kolejne podatki, proszę obniżyć VAT i akcyzę, tak jak robił to rząd Prawa i… https://t.co/3xvav6Dieu — Paweł Szefernaker 🇵🇱 (@szefernaker) July 25, 2026 The dispute over the tax comes as Poland faces an increasingly difficult fiscal situation. It had the second-largest budget deficit in the European Union last year, at 7.3% of GDP. That was far higher than the 5.5% the Polish government had pledged in 2024 when it was placed under the EU’s excessive deficit procedure. Data released last week by Eurostat showed that, in the first quarter of 2026, Poland had the EU’s third-largest annual increase in debt-to-GDP ratio, at 4.5 percentage points. In March, credit rating agency Fitch, which last year switched Poland’s credit outlook to negative, warned that the “political gridlock” between the president and the government will continue to hinder policymaking, including tackling “large fiscal deficits and rapidly rising debt”. Poland’s public debt has passed 60% of GDP for the first time, thereby exceeding the limit enshrined in EU law. World.title: Poland identifies remains of legendary anti-communist resistance fighter
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support. Poland’s state Institute of National Remembrance (IPN) has identified the remains of Mieczysław Dziemieszkiewicz (pictured above on the right), a prominent figure in the underground resistance that fought against the Soviet-installed communist authorities in the years after World War Two. Dziemieszkiewicz, who was killed by the communist security services in 1951 and dumped in an unmarked mass grave, was identified through a combination of historical detective work and genetic testing, including exhuming the remains of his deceased mother and sister to obtain DNA samples. “Once again, we can say that the communist authorities did not win. Heroes prevail,” declared Krzysztof Szwagrzyk, deputy head of the IPN. “Even in the most difficult situations, we must seek the truth, find those of whom no trace was supposed to remain, and restore their names.” While World War Two officially came to an end in 1945, tens of thousands of Poles, known as the “cursed soldiers” (żolnierze wyklęci), continued to fight against the Soviets and the communist regime they installed in Poland. While most had laid down arms by 1947, some continued fighting well beyond then, including Dziemieszkiewicz, who operated under the nom de guerre “Rój” (meaning “swarm”). Dziemieszkiewicz, who was 20 years old when the war ended, came from a family that had been part of Poland’s wartime resistance. His anti-communist views were hardened when his elder brother, Roman, was killed by Red Army soldiers in 1945. After being conscripted that year into the Soviet-backed Polish People’s Army, Dziemieszkiewicz defected and joined the underground resistance forces, where he rose to command a unit tasked with eliminating regime officials and members of the communist Polish Workers Party (PPR). Dziemieszkiewicz’s group killed around two dozen members of the communist security services and more than 20 informants, according to the IPN. In 1950, the communist authorities intensified efforts to dismantle Dziemieszkiewicz’s unit, using threats and blackmail to recruit hundreds of agents and informants in an effort to locate the resistance fighters. Eventually, one such informant gave up Dziemieszkiewicz’s location in exchange for a promise to release her parents from captivity. Dziemieszkiewicz found himself surrounded by several hundred soldiers and was killed while trying to escape. After his body had been identified by his family, Dziemieszkiewicz was buried in a section of Powązki Cemetery in Warsaw where the remains of those killed by the communist security services were placed en masse in unmarked graves. Exhumations by the IPN, which was established after the fall of communism to investigate communist and Nazi crimes in Poland, have located over 200 complete bodies at that site as well as several thousand bone fragments. During that work, one set of remains was found buried with an eagle symbol and remnants of a black cloth. IPN researchers realised that the item was similar to a beret that appeared in posthumous photographs of Dziemieszkiewicz’s body taken by the communist security services. That prompted them to carry out genetic testing on the remains and compare them to samples taken from Dziemieszkiewicz’s mother and sister, who were buried in a cemetery in the town of Maków Mazowiecki. “We have found ‘Rój’, commander of one of the longest-fighting units of the independence underground,” declared the IPN on Friday, announcing the confirmation of his identity. They described Dziemieszkiewicz as “legend in life and a symbol of the fight against communist oppression”. The identification was announced today during a press conference at @PrzystanekH. The identification is the result of many years of work carried out by the IPN. It was preceded by extensive archival and investigative research, the analysis of forensic evidence, archaeological… https://t.co/Rcf4wemJFc pic.twitter.com/XgMUAgSQc6 — Institute of National Remembrance (@ipngovpl_eng) July 24, 2026 At a conference announcing the findings, the IPN noted that Dziemieszkiewicz’s remains had been located right next to those of another prominent anti-communist resistance fighter, Zygmunt Szendzielarz, who fought under the nom de guerre “Łupaszko”. “It is an incredible situation that two great and distinguished soldiers of the Polish underground lie next to each other in this part of the Powązki Cemetery,” said Szwagrzyk. However, Szendzielarz, who was executed by the communist authorities in 1951, has a contested legacy, given evidence that his unit was involved in the massacre of dozens of Lithuanian civilians. Some other “cursed soldiers” have faced similar accusations of war crimes. While it was often IPN historians who uncovered evidence of such actions, the institution has more recently begun to honour those figures, particularly under the rule of the national-conservative Law and Justice government between 2015 and 2023. Opposition MPs walked out of parliament yesterday as the chamber commemorated an underground officer who fought against Nazi-German occupation and the imposition of communism in Poland, but has also been accused of a war crime against civilians https://t.co/MIY7krOxTw — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) February 9, 2022 Dziemieszkiewicz himself, however, like most of the cursed soldiers, has not faced such accusations. In 2007, President Lech Kaczyński posthumously awarded Dziemieszkiewicz the Commander’s Cross with Star of the Order of Polonia Restituta, one of Poland’s highest honours. In 2020, his image was featured on a commemorative silver coin issued by the National Bank of Poland. Through a combination of brutal repression and offering amnesties, the communist authorities managed to end most resistance efforts by 1947. However, the last “cursed soldier” to die in combat, Józef Franczak, was killed in 1963, 18 years after the end of the war. World.title: Three quarters of Poles support cooperation with Ukraine against Russia despite historical dispute
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support. A new study shows that, while most Poles were angered by President Volodymyr Zelensky’s recent decision to name a military unit after a group that massacred Poles in World War Two, they still overwhelmingly support cooperation with Ukraine and believe that Russia benefits from the dispute. The study, carried out by Polish state research agency CBOS, also finds that a large majority of Poles believe good relations with Ukraine will only be possible once historical issues are resolved. The polling was carried out this month in response to the ongoing diplomatic crisis that began in May, when Zelensky named a military unit after the “heroes of the Ukrainian Insurgent Army (UPA)”. The UPA is widely revered in Ukraine for its role in fighting against Moscow-backed Soviet rule. However, in Poland it is associated with the Volhynia massacres, in which around 100,000 Polish civilians – mostly women and children – were slaughtered during World War Two, often with great brutality. Zelensky’s decision sparked anger in Poland, where the massacres are regarded as a genocide (though Ukraine strongly rejects that label). In June, Polish President Karol Nawrocki stripped Zelensky of the Order of the White Eagle, Poland’s highest honour, which he had received in 2023. In its new survey, CBOS found that 59% of Poles support Nawrocki’s decision, while only 28% oppose it. However, they were divided over the consequences, with 41% saying it would bring Poland more losses than benefits and the exact same proportion saying the benefits would outweigh the costs. More broadly, 84% said the Polish state should react when another country glorifies historical figures responsible for crimes against Poles. However, when asked if Ukrainians have the right to honour their own historical heroes, even if those figures left a negative mark on Polish history, 44% agreed and 42% disagreed. At the same time, over three quarters of respondents (77%) said that good Polish-Ukrainian relations could not be built without addressing the past, but a similar proportion (73%) also believe that politicians on both sides “fuel conflicts between Poles and Ukrainians for their own political gain”. Poland has cautiously welcomed President @ZelenskyyUa's announcement of a five-point plan to alleviate the diplomatic crisis triggered by his earlier decision to name a military unit after a group that led massacres of Poles during WWII https://t.co/M3GXD9vtAr — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) July 18, 2026 Yet the survey also showed that, for Poles, historical disputes have not displaced security concerns, and in particular the view that, for Poland and Ukraine, Russia is a shared enemy. Some 75% of respondents agreed with the statement that “Poland and Ukraine should, above all, cooperate in the face of the threat from Russia, rather than focus on the issues that divide them”. The most frequently cited priorities in relations with Kyiv were security cooperation (61%), building good neighbourly relations (46%), commemorating victims of the Volhynia massacres (43%), strengthening Poland’s regional leadership (41%), and ensuring Polish companies participate in Ukraine’s reconstruction (40%). Just over half of Poles (52%) agree that “Poland and Ukraine have more common aims and interests than conflicting ones”, while 32% disagreed. A huge majority (80%) agreed that “Russia benefits from the Polish-Ukrainian dispute”. W ocenie społecznej zdecydowanym priorytetem w relacjach z Ukrainą powinna być współpraca na rzecz bezpieczeństwa – wskazało ją 61% badanych.📊 ➡️Więcej w komunikacie #CBOS "Wokół polsko-ukraińskiego sporu o imponderabilia i nie tylko":https://t.co/pIvYbu8gyz#Ukraina #relacje pic.twitter.com/LOpmAKNnXn — CBOS (@CBOS_Info) July 23, 2026 Based on the answers in the survey, CBOS identified three broad groups of respondents classified by their views of the dispute. The largest, described as “moralists”, accounted for 46% and placed greater emphasis on historical grievances. Among this group, 99% supported Nawrocki’s decision and said good Polish-Ukrainian relations could not be built without addressing the past. “Pragmatists”, who made up 34% of respondents, placed greater emphasis on future cooperation. Some 96% said Poland and Ukraine should cooperate against the Russian threat rather than focus on historical disputes. The smallest group, labelled by CBOS as “withdrawn”, represented 20% of respondents who were more likely to lack a clear view on Polish-Ukrainian relations. Long-simmering tensions between Poland and Ukraine over WWII massacres have finally boiled over, prompting a diplomatic crisis.@danieltilles1 looks at how we got here and what it may mean for the two countries and Europe more broadly https://t.co/a8tiYJJHRr — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) June 22, 2026 Recent weeks have seen moves from Ukraine towards finding a diplomatic solution to the crisis. In early July, foreign minister Andrii Sybiha visited Warsaw to propose an “anti-crisis package” of measures. Last week, Zelensky himself outlined a five-point plan to alleviate the dispute, including opening up Ukrainian historical archives and permitting more exhumations of victims of the massacres, most of whom remain buried in mass graves in Ukraine. The Polish authorities have cautiously welcomed Zelensky’s announcement, though also emphasise that they are waiting to see concrete action. Meanwhile, there is no indication that Zelensky will change his decision to name a unit after the heroes of the UPA. World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! We cannot do what we do without your support. Keeping dogs and cats chained up at home will be banned in Poland from next year, after President Karol Nawrocki signed into law a bill prohibiting the practice. His decision ends a long-running dispute over the issue, after Nawrocki last year vetoed a previous proposal to ban chaining because it also included what he argued were excessive and unrealistic additional measures on minimum kennel sizes for dogs. Zawetowana w listopadzie 2025 r. ustawa łańcuchowa była źle przygotowana i przeregulowana, ponieważ nakładała na obywateli obowiązki, których wielu nie byłoby w stanie spełnić. Dzisiaj otrzymujemy ustawę lepszą, z pozytywnym głosem takich podmiotów jak rolniczy samorząd.… pic.twitter.com/h7kIAI77KR — Kancelaria Prezydenta RP (@prezydentpl) July 24, 2026 The new law bans owners from tethering dogs and cats at home. Animals must be kept either inside the house, in a fenced garden or, if that is not possible, in a kennel “large enough for the animal to move freely and satisfy its natural needs”. Dogs kept in kennels must be provided with daily exercise outside of it. Dogs and cats can still be put on leashes in certain situations, such as when they are being walked, but also during transport, while participating in shows, performances or training, if they are at vets or groomers, or if they represent a danger to humans or other animals. Those who are found to have violated the new law can be fined between 1,000 and 100,000 zloty (€232-23,166). If they are deemed to have acted with “extreme cruelty”, they can also face a prison sentence of up to five years, reports the Forsal news service. Now that the bill has been signed by Nawrocki, it will be published in the official Journal of Laws (Dziennik Ustaw), after which it goes into force 12 months later. The new measures represent a successful second attempt to introduce a leashing ban. A previous bill was approved by parliament last September. However, in December, Nawrocki, who is aligned with the right-wing opposition, announced that he was vetoing it. The president argued that, “although the intention – protecting animals – is just and noble, the law itself was poorly drafted”. In particular, he said that elements introducing minimum sizes for dog kennels were unrealistic and would “harm farmers, breeders and ordinary rural households”. After an attempt by parliament to overturn the veto failed, legislators went back to the drawing board and, following discussions with the president’s chancellery and animal rights groups, drafted a compromise bill that was approved by parliament earlier this month. The bill received support from the current ruling coalition, which ranges from left to centre right, as well as most MPs from the national-conservative Law and Justice (PiS), the main opposition party. The far-right Confederation (Konfederacja) and Confederation of the Polish Crown (KKP) voted against it. Thousands of people have protested in Warsaw against President @NawrockiKn's veto of a law that would have banned the chaining up of dogs Parliament will vote on Wednesday on whether to overturn Nawrocki's veto, which would require a three-fifths majority https://t.co/0GRup2sppb — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) December 15, 2025 “We now have a better law, with positive feedback from entities such as the agricultural chamber,” said Nawrocki today. “It demonstrates that the pressure of the presidential veto makes sense. My previous decision to refuse to sign this bill forced the government and parliament to work harder.” However, although Nawrocki said the new law would no longer entail “rigid and costly requirements” for kennels, his office noted in a separate statement that the legislation requires the agriculture minister to issue a regulation establishing “minimum kennel area, taking into account the dog’s size”. It remains unclear if and how that would differ from the requirements Nawrocki previously vetoed. The presidential chancellery also noted that the law itself already outlines that kennels must be made of “wood or wood-like material with thermal insulation”, must be insulated from the ground, and must have openings on at least two sides to allow light and air to enter. A dog who throws a ball to passers-by from a balcony above one of Poland’s most famous streets and waits for them to throw it back has become a star. Police officers and rangers have stepped up joint patrols in Poland’s mountainous Tatra National Park during the peak summer season, following a spate of rule-breaking including swimming in the park’s lakes and ponds, driving cars and going off marked trails. Meanwhile, national park authorities have repeated warnings that bathing, littering and breaking other rules can damage the park’s fragile ecosystem. Local police officers have joined Tatra National Park rangers on patrols on popular tourist routes. On one such patrol last week, officers focused on education and prevention, reminding visitors not to leave marked trails or litter and explaining how to behave safely and responsibly in the mountains. They also checked that organised groups were accompanied by qualified mountain guides, as required by law. Fines for such offences range from 50 zloty (€11.55) to as much as 1,000 zloty (€231) in the event of environmental damage or multiple offences. Police said that all visitors encountered during the patrol were complying with the park’s regulations. However, they added that similar patrols would continue on a regular basis. The Tatra National Park, home to Poland’s highest peaks, and the nearby mountain resort of Zakopane are among the country’s most popular holiday destinations, with crowds taking to park trails in the summer season. The park, the most visited of Poland’s 23 national parks, welcomed a record 5.3 million visitors in 2025 and offers 275 km of marked hiking trails, including high-altitude routes that connect at several points with the adjacent national park in Slovakia. 🚨 Ukraiński Influencer wjechał nielegalnie samochodem na Morskie oko 🗣️: Jesteśmy pierwszymi ludźmi w historii, którzy wjechali samochodem nad Morskie Oko. To było jedno z miejsc, do których chcieliśmy dotrzeć podczas tej podróży i wszyscy znajomi oraz przyjaciele mówili, że… pic.twitter.com/tA9shZ6Rqk — Pigułka 💊 (@informacyjnie) May 23, 2026 This season has already seen a number of high-profile cases of transgressions of the park’s strict rules. In May, a Ukrainian social media influencer sparked outrage after driving a sports car along a road closed to traffic to Morskie Oko, a picturesque lake nestled between the mountains. As a result, he was banned from entering Poland and other Schengen Area countries for five years. Tourists have also been filmed entering Morskie Oko and other protected lakes and ponds, which is not permitted in the national park. This month, a group of young Dutch tourists were filmed bathing in Przedni Staw Polski in the Valley of the Five Lakes, one of the Tatras’ best-known hiking destinations. Witnesses repeatedly warned the group that entering the lake was prohibited, but they ignored the warnings, reports Gazeta Wyborcza. Park authorities have responded to such incidents by reminding visitors of the reasons for the strict rules. “Tatra ponds are incredibly delicate ecosystems. Cosmetics, UV filters, insect repellents, and bacteria entering the water can have a long-lasting impact on its chemical composition and the organisms living in the lakes,” they warned. A national park in Poland’s southern mountains has completed testing of an electric bus that could replace horse-drawn carriages carrying tourists to a famous lake. World.title: Polish opposition PiS party set to split, with over 30 MPs being expelled
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support. More than 30 MPs from the national-conservative Law and Justice (PiS), Poland’s main opposition party, have effectively resigned after refusing to sign a loyalty pledge, party leader Jarosław Kaczyński has announced. The dispute centres around a more moderate faction in the party aligned with former prime minister and deputy PiS leader Mateusz Morawiecki, who is one of those now set to be expelled from the party. They have for months been unhappy with PiS’s move in a hard-right direction. 💬 Prezes PiS Jarosław Kaczyński @OficjalnyJK. 👉 Udostępnij pic.twitter.com/bycjE0Yq0f — Prawo i Sprawiedliwość (@pisorgpl) July 24, 2026 “Around 30-something…of our group’s MPs have resigned,” revealed Kaczyński at a press conference on Friday. He added that their departures would be formalised at a meeting of the party’s political committee scheduled for Tuesday next week. Kaczyński’s announcement came after a deadline expired at midnight on Thursday for its MPs to sign a pledge of loyalty to the party that included a commitment not to be members of any external political associations. That measure was aimed in particular at an association called Development Plus (Rozwój Plus) founded by Morawiecki in April. The former prime minister had always insisted that his organisation was intended as complementary to PiS, rather than a rival to it. However, many figures in the party saw it as an attempt by Morawiecki to create a separate centre of power, and potentially to use the association as a launchpad for creating his own party ahead of the autumn 2027 parliamentary elections. The right-wing opposition PiS party has threatened disciplinary action, including exclusion from electoral lists, against dozens of its MPs who have joined a new internal group led by former PM @MorawieckiM and intended to appeal to more moderate voters https://t.co/y62Cm361U2 — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) April 17, 2026 After PiS issued a resolution on Wednesday last week requiring that its parliamentarians pledge to withdraw from any such associations, most of its 186 MPs quickly complied. However, a group of between 30 and 40 who are part of Development Plus refused to do so. “Everyone knew what they were supposed to sign, and knew the consequences of not signing,” said Kaczyński on Friday. “And so they made the decision they did.” “In this situation, we cannot view the [Development Plus] association as anything other than a component of a plan…to split our party,” he added. However, although its supporters will now leave PiS, “we want to part ways without any animosity”, said Kaczyński. After Kaczyński’s announcement, senior figures from Development Plus made clear that no one from their association had resigned from PiS. They had simply not signed the declaration of loyalty demanded by the party. Later, Morawiecki himself held a press conference in parliament surrounded by his supporters. He claimed that an unnamed “small group of schemers” within PiS had been seeking to turn Kaczyński against him and push him out of the party. “We fought for the unity of Law and Justice until the very end,” declared Morawiecki, who said that his group included 40 MPs, one senator and three MEPs. However, three of the MPs are not members of PiS, and therefore were not expected to sign the loyalty declaration. Szanowni Państwo! 🟦Do ostatniej chwili walczyłem o jedność Prawa i Sprawiedliwości. Nie o stanowiska. Nie o osobiste ambicje. Nie o wpływy. 🟦Walczyłem o jedność obozu, który przez osiem lat zmieniał Polskę – budował jej bezpieczeństwo, rozwijał gospodarkę i przywracał godność… pic.twitter.com/PP7sOkzMHp — Mateusz Morawiecki (@MorawieckiM) July 24, 2026 If the expulsion of Morawiecki’s supporters is confirmed, it will mark a major shake-up of Poland’s political landscape. PiS has for the last two decades been the dominant force on the Polish right, including periods leading governments in 2005-2007 and 2015-2023. However, since losing power at elections in 2023, when the party won 35% of the vote, PiS has seen its average support in polls fall to around 23-24%, the lowest level in 14 years. Meanwhile, it has been challenged by the rise of the far right, where two parties, Confederation (Konfederacja) and Confederation of the Polish Crown (KKP), now together poll a similar combined level of support to PiS. In response, Kaczyński in March named a hardline figure, Przemyszław Czarnek, as PiS’s candidate for prime minister in next year’s elections. Czarnek was seen as someone who could appeal to far-right voters, while also potentially working with the far right if a coalition was needed after the elections. Support for PiS has fallen to its lowest in 14 years, as the party grapples with internal division, the rise of far-right challengers, living in President Nawrocki's shadow, and the unpopularity in Poland of PiS ally Donald Trump, writes @danieltilles1 https://t.co/QRScBpEQQG — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) March 2, 2026 However, there has been no rise in support for PiS since Czarnek was named, prompting growing concern from more moderate figures within the party, led by Morawiecki. They argue that PiS has wrongly disowned many of the successes of its time in office before 2023, and they fear that its rightward shift damages its chances of winning over more centrist voters. Morawiecki, who was an international banker before joining PiS to become finance minister and then prime minister, wants the party to focus on more technocratic issues, such as economic development, rather than Euroscepticism and culture wars. That has led to frequent public sparring between his supporters and others in the party. In April, PiS threatened disciplinary action against members of Development Plus. Kaczyński and Morawiecki then reached an agreement that allowed the association to continue. But that uneasy truce has now fallen apart. World.title: Polish president renews bid for referendum on EU climate policy
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support. President Karol Nawrocki has submitted a second request to parliament for a nationwide referendum on whether Poland should continue implementing the European Union’s climate policies, which he argues are too costly. Nawrocki, who is aligned with the right-wing opposition, first proposed a referendum in May. But it was rejected by the Senate, the upper house of parliament, where the more liberal government has a majority. Senators argued that the proposed referendum question was “absurd”. The president has now submitted a revised proposal featuring a simplified question and again proposed holding the referendum on 27 September this year. Nawrocki’s originally proposed question was: “Are you in favour of implementing EU climate policy, which has led to an increase in citizens’ cost of living, energy prices and the cost of running business and agricultural activity?” However, following criticism in the Senate that the question was clearly intended to elicit a specific answer, this time he has proposed a more neutral one: “Are you in favour of Poland implementing the European Union’s climate policy?” “I’m looking for compromises, looking for solutions,” said Nawrocki on Thursday while announcing the new referendum bid. “The Senate wasn’t satisfied with the [previous] question”, so “we prepared a different one…[that] does not suggest anything”. However, the president has also proposed that the ballot paper would include information on what answering “yes” or “no” would mean in practice. Voters would be told, for example, that maintaining EU climate policy would result in, among other things, “Poland bearing costs estimated at 3.5 trillion zloty by 2040”, “burdens on agriculture”, “increasing costs for industry” and “obligations for owners of buildings”. By contrast, voting “no” would mean “negotiating exceptions and exemptions for Poland with the relevant EU bodies that will protect Polish industry and citizens from the burdens of climate policy”. The ruling coalition of Prime Minister Donald Tusk controls 63 seats in the Senate, making approval of proposals brought forward by Nawrocki, who often clashes with the government and regularly vetoes its bills, unlikely. While the government is generally pro-EU, it has also been critical of Brussels’ green policies, arguing that they place too great a burden on Poland.
