World.title: Sally McManus and Michele O'Neil resign from top ACTU jobs
World.content:
The powerful heads of the Australian Council of Trade Unions (ACTU), Sally McManus and Michele O'Neil, have announced their resignations to ''make way for a new generation''.

Ms McManus has been the peak body's secretary since 2017 and Ms O'Neil its president since 2018.

Ms McManus will finish in the role at the end of August and Ms O'Neil will depart before the end of the year, in order to ''assist with the leadership transition''.

Michele O'Neil will step down by the end of the year. (ABC News: Tom Hancock)

Their replacements are yet to be decided on, according to a statement from the ACTU.

''The ACTU's union affiliates will decide on the next leadership team, initially with the ACTU Executive filling the casual vacancies and then through an election at next year's Congress, which will coincide with the ACTU's 100th Anniversary," the statement said.

Ms McManus said it was "the right time" for new leaders "to take our movement forward".

''I am proud of our movement's achievements, and it has been an honour to serve the union movement and working people as the secretary of the ACTU for nearly a decade,'' she said.

The Transport Workers' Union was among the first to thank the outgoing leaders, noting their work fighting for the COVID-era JobKeeper scheme and pushing Labor to establish a Fair Work Court, which it announced plans for at the party conference last week.

In 2024 Ms McManus denied she knew about the alleged infiltration of criminals into the Victorian branch of the Construction, Forestry and Maritime Employees Union (CMFEU).

She also oversaw the ACTU's suspension divisions of the CFMEU while it cleaned up its act.

Prime Minister Anthony Albanese also thanked the pair for their "tireless advocacy" for workers, but also for their support to him personally.

"It is fitting that Sally and Michele announce they're stepping down from their respective positions at a time when there have been significant wage increases in critical and long-undervalued sectors, the gender pay gap is at a record low and union membership is growing for the first time in decades" he said in a statement.

"Personally, I will miss the friendship and support these two giants of the labour movement have offered me over many years, but especially since I became Labor Leader in 2019 and then Prime Minister is 2022."

World.title: SA's first industrial manslaughter charges laid against Adelaide company
World.content:
An Adelaide manufacturer has been charged with South Australia's first case of industrial manslaughter two years after the death of a 28-year-old worker, a workplace safety watchdog says.

Lachlan Carslake died after he was allegedly "struck in the head by a metal object" while operating a milling machine at the Nylastex's Edwardstown plant on July 24, 2024, according to court documents.

The Director of Public Prosecutions (DPP) filed charges in Adelaide Magistrates Court against Nylastex Tooling Pty Ltd, Nylastex Holdings Pty Ltd and the directors last week.

The charges followed what SafeWork SA described as an "extensive" investigation.

Court documents alleged the companies used a number of milling machines, each fitted with an interlock guarding switch designed to prevent the machine operating at a hazardous speed with the guard open.

According to the documents, this switch was allegedly "in a disabled state" on the machine Mr Carslake was operating on July 24, 2024.

SafeWork SA says the case is the first time the state has filed industrial manslaughter charges. (YouTube: SafeWork SA)

The documents also alleged Mr Carslake "died as a result of" being hit by a metal object ejected from the machine while the switch was disabled and a moveable guard was opened.

SafeWork SA said two days prior to Mr Carslake's death, an external technician engaged by Nylastex Tooling Pty Ltd had allegedly advised the company of "safety concerns" regarding the guarding switch.

SafeWork SA said the companies and its two directors had allegedly "breached" their health and safety duty "by engaging in conduct with gross negligence that caused the death of the worker or were reckless as to the risk of death or serious injury".

A project manager of the company has also been charged for allegedly engaging in gross negligence or reckless conduct under the Work Health and Safety Act 2012.

They were all expected to appear in court in August.

Industrial manslaughter became a criminal offence in South Australia on July 1, 2024, and carries a maximum penalty of 20 years imprisonment while the maximum fine for a corporate is $18 million.

The company has been contacted for comment.

World.title: Police investigating punch during country footy game
World.content:
An on-field punch during a country football game that left a player in hospital has sparked a police investigation.

The incident occurred on Sunday in Kojonup, about 260 kilometres south of Perth, during a clash between the hometown Cougars and Bridgetown Bulldogs in WA's Lower South West Football League.

Footage of the game shows a Bridgetown player running up behind a Kojonup player before punching them in the side of the head.

The Kojonup player falls to the ground and the Bridgetown player runs off to continue play.

A WA Police spokesperson said the victim, aged in his 20s, was threatened and assaulted while taking part in the game.

"The victim lost consciousness during the incident and sustained facial injuries," the spokesperson said.

Police said the man was taken to Kojonup Hospital, where his injuries were treated.

A spokesperson from the Lower South West Football League told the ABC it was aware of the incident.

"The matter has been referred to the Country Football WA tribunal process and will be dealt with in accordance with the applicable rules and procedures," the spokesperson said.

The league would not comment further, in order to "preserve the integrity and fairness of the tribunal process".

The Bridgetown Football Club said it would not comment until the league and Country Football WA finalised their investigations.

The Kojonup Football Club has been contacted for comment.

The police spokesperson said the investigation was ongoing and that anyone with footage or other information around the incident should make contact with police.

World.title: Protesters mount High Court challenge over Queensland hate speech laws
World.content:
A group of pro-Palestinian protesters have launched a High Court challenge against Queensland laws that banned the phrases "from the river to the sea" and "globalise the intifada".

The two phrases have been deemed antisemitic by the government and many Jewish organisations and have been outlawed when used to menace or offend someone.

Both of the contested phrases have been commonly used by pro-Palestinian protesters.

More than 20 people have been charged under the laws since they took effect in March.

Hate speech laws passed in Queensland Parliament Sweeping new hate speech laws banning certain expressions in a way that makes a member of the public feel menaced, harassed or offended have passed in Queensland Parliament.

The laws carry a maximum jail term of two years.

According to filings lodged with the High Court last week, the activists allege the legislation is invalid because it infringes on the right to political communication.

The Queensland government has been contacted for comment.

It has previously defended the laws and argued in favour of their validity.

In April Deputy Premier Jarrod Bleijie said the laws defended against "venomous, poisonous rhetoric".

Seven protesters have signed the filings, including Remah Naji, a spokesperson for the Justice for Palestine group.

Four of the signatories Stephen Werner Heydet, Edward Joel Matthew Carroll, Katherine Mary Dennehy and Samuel Woripa Watson — were arrested and charged under the laws, according to the documents.

Each are accused of displaying or saying the banned phrase.

The High Court challenge was filed by activist Remah Naji and six other protesters. (ABC News: Lucy Loram)

One of the other applicants, James Frances Hillier, alleges he was told to withdraw some of his artwork that contained the banned phrase after being contacted by police in March.

The group claims neither of the banned phrases have a "fixed meaning", an "inherently antisemitic or racist meaning" or an "inherently violent meaning".

The filing lays out 12 alternative meanings of "from the river to the sea".

The filing alleges the ban causes inequality or discrimination because it seeks to criminalise one perspective on a "political controversy".

The group also argues it imposes a burden on the implied freedom of political communication in the constitution.

Jewish Board of Deputies president Jason Steinberg said he and other Jews felt unsafe when hearing the banned slogans chanted at rallies and protests.

"We have people who will not come into a central business district when there is protests on, when they know that there is going to be this kind of antisemitism on our streets," he said.

A 'chance of succeeding'

Constitutional law expert Anthony Gray believes a High Court challenge to the state's hate speech legislation has a "chance of succeeding".

He said the High Court had already recognised Australians have an implied freedom to communicate about political matters.

"On one view, the two phrases that have been banned are communications about something that is broadly political in nature," Professor Gray, who was not involved with preparing the challenge in any way, told the ABC.

The Bond University expert characterised the state government's legislation as "unusual" because it criminalised specific phrases and sought to outlaw one particular viewpoint.

He added that the nature of the phrases also added to the difficulty of banning them, as some people who used them may not have any "bad intentions".

The court could also consider whether the state government could demonstrate the legislation was necessary to protect some groups from suffering harm, Professor Gray explained.

World.title: Doctors' union concerned by nurses' behaviour at SA health service
World.content:
A patient's clinical care plan was allegedly blocked by a health service manager against the advice of specialists at a facility north of Adelaide, a report by the South Australian doctors' union claims.

The report by the SA Salaried Medical Officers Association (SASMOA) documents a litany of concerns about workplace culture at Gawler Health Service, including alleged "bullying, harassment and disrespectful behaviours from various nursing staff".

The report stressed that not all nursing staff were accused of such behaviour, but said doctors had been left feeling "anxious, distressed, and very concerned about their professional liability and that patient care is being jeopardised".

One incident detailed in the report involved a nurse who allegedly "snatched a mobile computer station from a doctor during a patient admission".

In another incident, the potential demotion of a senior doctor was "openly discussed" with colleagues without that doctor's knowledge or consent, the report stated.

The report, which alleges such behaviour was in breach of workplace safety requirements, has been submitted to watchdog SafeWork SA.

The report also claimed that the behaviour had implications for patient care.

"Workers described as terrible an incident of a manager overriding the clinical judgement of three specialist doctors and blocking a clinical care plan for a patient," the report stated.

The Barossa Hills Fleurieu Local Health Network (BHFLHN) — the SA Health division that covers the Gawler Health Service — said SafeWork SA representatives had visited the site on July 2, several weeks after SASMOA's inspection, and found no breaches of work health and safety laws.

The Australian Nursing and Midwifery Federation (ANMF) said it took all such allegations seriously, but its representatives had not identified any evidence "indicating systemic bullying by nursing staff".

But SASMOA chief industrial officer Bernadette Mulholland said the concerns at the Gawler Health Service had been ongoing for "about 18 months", and that doctors felt local administrators "did not step in quickly enough".

"That made them feel angry, it made them feel a sense of anxiety," she said.

"What it does do is make people feel like they just don't want to come to work anymore.

"They were feeling not heard, not listened to, there were concerns in relation to anxiety — some people knew that their health was suffering because of the conflicts."

Bernadette Mulholland says the issues have been going on for 18 months. (ABC News: Marco Catalano)

In a statement, ANMF SA branch secretary Elizabeth Dabars said it was important that such allegations be "properly investigated through appropriate workplace processes".

"Staff who are the subject of concerns must be given an opportunity to respond, and findings should be based on evidence," she said.

"Based on the information currently available to ANMF, some of the issues raised appear to extend beyond allegations of bullying and include broader matters such as staffing, workload, communication, leadership and clinical governance.

"These issues require constructive engagement and resolution by management in consultation with all professional groups."

BHFLHN chief executive Bronwyn Masters said SA Health was investing in steps to support employees and strengthen workplace culture.

"BHFLHN is committed to providing a safe and secure working environment for all of our staff and we work with them every day to ensure we are providing one," she said.

Ms Mulholland said Gawler Health Service was working to bring the doctors' and nurses' unions together to discuss solutions.

"We know that currently there's a review being done," she said.

"My understanding is it's happening now — they've got an external reviewer coming in to review and make recommendations about how improvements to that particular hospital site can be done."

World.title: Man fined $31k after botched smuggling attempt kills 55 reptiles
World.content:
A New South Wales man has been fined more than $30,000 for a bid to smuggle reptiles out of Western Australia that killed almost all of the animals.

Northam Magistrates Court heard Nicholas Thomas Havet, 28, travelled to Western Australia twice in 2023, where he captured reptiles and attempted to mail them home to NSW.

Two parcels intercepted by Australia Post at Perth Airport contained 65 animals, including bobtail lizards, ornate crevice dragons, thorny devils, western blue tongue lizards, geckos and variegated dtella.

Four of the reptiles were deceased, and a further 51 were euthanised due to their poor condition.

The haul of lizards Havet was trying to smuggle included blue tongues, like the one pictured here. (ABC Wimmera: Andrew Kelso/ File)

The remaining 10 reptiles were rehomed.

Prosecutors said Havet's motive was financial gain, with the lizards' value on the black market estimated to be between $65,000 and $1.3 million.

The 28-year-old did not appear in court for either his sentencing or a hearing in July where he was found guilty in absentia of six charges of exporting fauna without lawful authority.

Havet had travelled to WA on two occasions, collecting reptiles to smuggle to NSW. (Supplied: DBCA)

Smuggler travelled around WA

Prosecutors told that hearing Havet had travelled to WA on two occasions between March and April in 2023, renting a vehicle in Perth before travelling to the state's north west.

He was captured on CCTV purchasing two parcels from a post office in Narembeen, 290 kilometres east of Perth, before lodging the parcels containing the lizards in Merredin, 70km away.

Prosecutors say Havet's motive was profit, with the lizards worth significant amounts on the black market. (Supplied: Parks and Wildlife/ File)

The court heard Mr Havet was in WA for four days before he was apprehended at the Port Hedland Post Office, an additional 1,500km north, while waiting for a delivery.

A search of his vehicle located plastic containers with holes drilled in them, an endoscope camera and two mobile phones.

The court heard Havet had previously lodged five parcels suspected to contain lizards that were successfully delivered.

Havet was found guilty of sending fauna without legal authority. (ABC Midwest & Wheatbelt: Eliza Bidstrup)

During sentencing, Magistrate Sarah Wisbey told the court Havet exposed the reptiles to "cruel and inhumane treatment" and was running an "illegal operation for profit".

Havet was fined a total of $31,000, with each of the six charges carrying a maximum penalty of $50,000.

World.title: ‘Really devastated’: Saints coach Lyon reveals King’s anguish after another injury woe
World.content:
In today’s AFL Briefing, your wrap of footy news: Max King suffered a season-ending hamstring strain on Sunday.

Brisbane’s Ty Gallop will face a serious misconduct charge.

St Kilda’s Darcy Wilson has re-committed on a new two-year deal. St Kilda coach Ross Lyon maintains the club is committed to Max King at Moorabbin, revealing the injury-prone forward was “really devastated” and asked if the club had had enough of him. The 26-year-old has been put in cotton wool for the rest season but St Kilda stresses the 84-gamer is “incredibly important” to the Saints and they’re determined to get him back playing senior footy. King will not play again until at least next year after it was confirmed on Monday he suffered a season-ending left hamstring strain in his return AFL game against North Melbourne on Sunday. Lyon spoke about the extent of King’s frustration and disappointment, with the Saint seeking assurances that they would still back him as an AFL player.



Max King during his comeback game. Getty Images Tied to the Saints until the end of 2032 after signing a six-year contract extension two years ago, King faces a huge challenge to overcome his injury woes. “His concern was he’d let the club and a lot of his team down,” Lyon said on Fox Footy. “And shame is too strong a word, but [he was] probably embarrassed. “Like [he was] saying, ‘Have you guys had enough of me?’ And I said, ‘Hang on here. We’re in.’”



King’s season-ending left hamstring strain is a devastating blow for the Saints and King, who had not played at AFL level for 757 days before his latest setback, and has now suffered hamstring injuries twice this year. Lyon is adamant the Saints did everything in their power to ensure King was fit enough to return to senior football. Loading “Every parameter … was really strong. I mean he got to half-time [on Sunday] healthy. Anyone who thinks it’s fatigue [is off the mark],” he said. “There’s nothing on the parameters [we look at] or the demand of the game that caused this.”



Lyon had already defended the club’s decision to play King in the senior side and bypass the VFL this time, but the star forward will now have played just once in three seasons after a torturous run that includes injuries to both knees and calf issues. Max King gets a kick away against the Kangaroos. AFL Photos King left Sunday’s 31-point win over North Melbourne midway through the third quarter and did not return. He started each term on the bench and played in six-minute stints, but managed just one kick and one handball while playing at different times on Charlie Comben and Aidan Corr. Saints football boss Lenny Hayes said the club would “wrap our arms” around King.



“It’s an incredibly disappointing outcome for Max, who has done everything possible throughout his rehabilitation to put himself in the best position to return,” said Hayes. “He’s an incredibly important part of our football club. We’ll continue to wrap our arms around him and provide all the support he needs as he works through this latest setback. “Our focus now turns to ensuring Max undertakes a full pre-season to allow him to get back and play consistent senior football in 2027.” King signed a six-year contract extension in October 2024 that ties him to the Saints until the end of the 2032 season. His horror injury run started about three months before he inked that deal, when he sustained a season-ending posterior cruciate ligament tear in his left knee in a two-point loss to Port Adelaide.



King also hurt his right knee in a pre-season game mere months later that ultimately required three separate surgeries and wiped out his 2025 season. After a delayed start to the past off-season, a new calf problem sidelined him again. King made it back from that setback, only to suffer a hamstring strain in his second VFL game in May. The 26-year-old went into an extended rehabilitation period after that, including spending time on the Gold Coast with his twin, Suns focal point Ben, who is expected to sign as a restricted free agent with Hawthorn. Lyon said St Kilda’s high-performance team was satisfied that King had proven he was ready with a significant volume of running, including at high speeds and game-like intensity.



“We stand by our decision to play him,” Lyon said on Sunday. There are still six seasons left on King’s deal, and he will be desperate to repay the Saints’ faith in him to avoid becoming the poster child for how long-term contracts can go wrong. King won’t play again until the 2027 season. AFL Photos The No.4 pick from the 2018 AFL draft displayed his immense potential in a career-best 52-goal season in 2022. St Kilda are clinging to a wildcard berth with a month to go in the home-and-away season, with matches to come against Sydney, Carlton, Richmond and Gold Coast, all of which will be played in Melbourne.



In positive news for the Saints faithful, it was confirmed on Monday evening that Darcy Wilson has committed to the club on a new two-year deal. The hard-running midfielder had attracted plenty of rival interest after a breakthrough season. The 20-year-old, who was drafted at pick 18 in the 2023 draft, will remain at the club until the end of the 2028 season. The Saints made a splash in last year’s player movement period, recruiting Tom De Koning, Jack Silvagni, Sam Flanders and Liam Ryan, after making Nasiah Wanganeen-Milera the league’s first $2 million-a-season man. St Kilda’s big spending has so far delivered only a mediocre return, worsened by Flanders suffering a season-ending Achilles injury. De Koning also missed games with broken ribs and a punctured lung, but demonstrated what he could bring in a strong performance against the Roos on Sunday.



Lion straight to tribunal on misconduct charge Brisbane youngster Ty Gallop has been sent straight to the AFL tribunal for shoving Port Adelaide’s Mitch Georgiades’ head into the turf. Gallop has been charged with serious misconduct for the incident in the second quarter of Brisbane’s win over Port at the Gabba on Sunday. The 20-year-old rolled Georgiades in a heavy tackle but has come under scrutiny for his actions off the ball immediately after. As the Lions swept downfield, Gallop lifted Georgiades by the jumper before slamming him back into the turf head first.



Depending on how the tribunal sees the incident, Gallop could face multiple weeks on the sidelines. “It wasn’t a great look, but I’m on the other side of it,” Port Adelaide coach Josh Carr said. “They’re a team that plays tough and pushes the limits. We got the free kick, so we got rewarded. There’s not much more to say.” Carr said Georgiades was unaffected by the incident after the game.



Gallop’s choice to hit out at Georgiades was described as “a stupid action” by former Brisbane great Alastair Lynch. “We’ve been singing the praises of Ty Gallop over the last half a dozen weeks particularly,” Lynch said on Fox Footy. “But that’s just a stupid action. We don’t want to see that. Mitch has had some problems with concussion. AAP and Scott Spits Keep up to date with the best AFL coverage in the country.

World.title: Same source, different names: The allegations rocking Four Corners
World.content:
BusinessCompaniesMedia & marketing Same source, different names: The allegations rocking Four Corners Calum Jaspan July 27, 2026 — 8:54pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

The Four Corners boss who oversaw two episodes led by reporter Mahmood Fazal that were removed by the ABC over accuracy concerns says he was shocked to learn the program had allegedly misrepresented the identity of an anonymous source. In a statement to this masthead on Monday evening, Matthew Carney, who was executive producer of Four Corners from 2022 until earlier this year, says he referred both investigations – Cocaine Nation and Meth Highway – to more senior editorial managers before they were aired. “Brendan” was presented as a meth dealer in the 2024 Four Corners episode Meth Highway, and also featured under a different name in an earlier investigation. ABC “[The programs] went through a rigorous fact check, verification and legal process,” Carney said in response to a series of questions from this masthead. “More than two years after broadcast [in 2023 and 2024] rumours emerged that a source could be compromised in one of these stories and I started an investigation. “Late last year I received a confidential email outlining there was an allegation of misrepresentation of an anonymous interviewee,” he said. “I was shocked by the contents and did my own inquiries, and the ABC investigated the matter after I had retired.”



The episodes were removed by the ABC on Friday, with the broadcaster citing concerns about the “veracity of certain sources used in both programs”. But ABC sources now suspect that Fazal featured the same person in both episodes under different identities. In one, the person, who this masthead has chosen not to name, was presented as a drug dealer under one identity and the second time as an anonymous meth dealer named “Brendan”, but behind a mask. Mahmood Fazal reporting for the ABC’s Four Corners program. The ABC said it had no further comments beyond the statement it issued on Friday. Fazal, who the ABC sacked in May, did not respond to a request for comment. He has previously said he had not been told the nature of the ABC’s concerns with his reporting and branded the broadcaster’s decision a “worrying precedent”.



“Brendan”, the man who was in both broadcasts, did not respond to a request for comment. While the ABC’s independent ombudsman is still preparing its investigation into the programs that were retracted last week, the ABC’s internal editorial standards department has also spent months investigating all the work produced by Fazal during his time on the show. The ABC decision to remove the programs preceded a lengthy piece published by The Monthly on former ABC news director Justin Stevens’ tenure, which focused on the Fazal saga and included the sourcing issue. The piece was written by Carney’s predecessor as executive producer of Four Corners, Sally Neighbour, who left the ABC in 2022 after seven years running the show. Almost everyone involved in the chain of command during Fazal’s reporting of the two episodes has left the ABC, aside from ABC head of investigations Jo Puccini and supervising producer Alice Brennan. Fazal, Carney and Puccini’s boss Stevens have departed, as have managing director David Anderson and chair Ita Buttrose. This masthead does not suggest any of the exits were related to Fazal or the investigation.



The ABC previously stood by Fazal following allegations published by this masthead in 2024, including that Fazal passed on threats from the Alameddine crime organisation to YouTuber FriendlyJordies, real name Jordan Shanks, and his producer, Kristo Langker, in 2024. But the broadcaster then suspended him after the launch of an independent podcast Fazal hosted with underworld media personality Ryan Naumenko. Related Article ABC Sacked Four Corners reporter lashes ABC move to pull episodes Fazal’s public fallout with Naumenko over the financial terms of the podcast led to the public feud. The ABC said the podcast appearances did not receive final sign-off approval. They were published featuring advertising for an online crypto casino. Fazal has previously denied any wrongdoing relating to the podcast and has lodged an unfair dismissal case in the Fair Work Commission. Since Fazal’s exit from the show, the ABC has installed a new executive producer for Four Corners, Joel Tozer. Last month, this masthead reported that one of Tozer’s first acts as Four Corners boss was to overhaul the show’s commissioning and standards processes. Part of the overhaul included the newly created commissioning and standards editor position, appointing former 7.30 producer Patricia Drum. World.title: TV presenter and comedian Bill Oddie dies at 85
World.content:
CultureCelebrityVale TV presenter and comedian Bill Oddie dies at 85 India McTaggart July 27, 2026 — 8:48pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Bill Oddie, the comedian and wildlife presenter, has died aged 85. The TV personality’s agent paid tribute to the “intelligence and wit” of “Britain’s best-loved birder”. TV presenter and comedian Bill Oddie, pictured here in 2020, has died at the age of 85. Getty Images Oddie, who found fame in the 1970s as a member of comic trio The Goodies alongside Tim Brooke-Taylor and Graeme Garden, died on Saturday (London time). Announcing his death, David Foster, his agent, said: “Bill was a multi-talented celebrity – wildlife presenter, broadcaster, comedian, writer, songwriter, musician and conservationist. Yet it was never fame that he valued.



“Instead he encouraged us to respect and protect the environment. He taught us the wonder of it. He protested, lobbied and campaigned for it.” He added that his thoughts were with Bill’s wife, Laura, and his daughters Bonnie, Kate and Rosie. Oddie, Brooke-Taylor and Garden formed The Goodies after meeting at the University of Cambridge in the early 60s. The Goodies wearing Brooke-Taylor's trademark Union Jack waistcoat. Getty Images They were flatmates and members of the Footlights Club, which also previously included the members of Monty Python – John Cleese, Graham Chapman and Eric Idle.



The Goodies performed in the same student venue – Cambridge Circus – and performed on Broadway before the trio starred together in a BBC sketch show titled Broaden Your Mind. Brooke-Taylor, who became president of Footlights in 1963, died at the age of 79 with coronavirus in April 2020. The Goodies hamming it up in London in 2003. AP Oddie later turned his lifelong passion for birds from a hobby into a job. He wrote several books on the subject, including Bill Oddie’s Little Black Bird Book and Birdwatching with Bill Oddie, which were illustrated with his own photographs and drawings.



Oddie also fronted an array of wildlife programmes, including The Bird Business and The Big Bird Race for Channel 4 as well as The Great Kenyan Bird Safari and two series of Bird In The Nest for the BBC. Related Article Review ‘I am, I suppose, a TV personality’: the many lives of Bill Oddie He spoke openly about suffering from crippling depression and was admitted to a psychiatric hospital in 2009 after being dropped from the BBC’s Springwatch, of which he was one of the original presenters. He was finally diagnosed with bipolar disorder. Speaking in 2014, he said he still felt sad that his days on Springwatch were cut short, adding that he had rarely watched the programme since. He said: “I very much miss it, but when I do see it, it brings back many happy memories and I like to think I contributed to its success.



“It’s still so well loved and helps encourage people to enjoy the natural world. That’s all to the good because I fear so many people wear earphones for their phones and music players that increasingly they miss out on everyday joys like birdsong. “My plea to people would be to ‘go naked’ occasionally – take off those earpieces so you hear nature and, of course, birdsong. You may not realise how precious it is until it’s gone.” The Telegraph, UK Get the day’s breaking news, entertainment ideas and a long read to enjoy. World.title: Brisbane man’s defence of ‘aggressive’ magpies nabs him $15,000 prize
World.content:
NationalQueenslandCity life Brisbane man’s defence of ‘aggressive’ magpies nabs him $15,000 prize Nick Dent July 27, 2026 — 8:39pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Nearly 5000 magpie attacks are logged in Australia each year, but Kailum Graves has good reason to feel warmly towards the swooping birds. The Coorparoo author has just won a $15,000 literary prize for his story about the tense relations between magpies and humans. The Magpies Have Unionised nabbed Graves the 2026 Furphy Literary Prize in a ceremony at the Shepparton Art Gallery in northern Victoria on Saturday. Kailum Graves visiting Swoop the Big Barrwarrang – the big magpie in Euroa, Victoria. Kailum Graves In the 4669-word story, magpies who are tired of being maligned as “aggressive” and “sky bastards” demand an apology from a local council and begin a targeted swooping campaign.



“We reject these characterisations. We are not aggressive. We are parents,” the birds write in an email. Among their demands are the replacement of the phrase “magpie attack season” with “heightened interspecies boundary awareness period”. Furphy Literary Award winner 2026 Kailum Graves on receiving his prize. Amina Barolli Furphy Literary Awards judge John Harms said the story was brilliantly written, fanciful and familiar. “Kailum Graves’ allegorical masterpiece introduces magpies that will bring a tear to your eye in a way that magpies never have before,” he said.



Graves, 41, said he had a grudging respect for magpies, who were a part of life in Coorparoo. Related Article Good Weekend ‘It’s a bit gamified, almost like Pokemon Go’: The tracking app preventing magpie attacks “I feel bad for them because we’ve invaded their space, but we’re painting them as the aggressor,” he said. “The signs should be more aimed at us looking after the magpies as opposed to us being the victims of the swooping because they’re really just protecting their young.” According to Magpie Alert, Queensland had over 1000 reported swooping attacks in 2025, out of nearly 5000 nationwide.



Graves’ ultimately moving story takes the point of view of a council worker and mother who becomes an interspecies mediator and whose young daughter is terrified of the birds. Satirising local government, the story was inspired by Graves’ recent stay in Germany, where he was struck both by the absence of birdsong and the prevalence of government bureaucracy. One of the council’s swooping warning signs. Reddit “I missed birds, I didn’t realise how much I loved them – even just bird songs in the morning and butcher birds in Brisbane singing,” Graves said. “In Germany, they’re the experts of pointless bureaucracy. Once I went to get a parcel at the post office, and I took my Australian passport and then they refused to give me my parcel, saying ‘it’s not real ID’.”



Graves studied philosophy and art history at the University of Queensland and has carved out a practice as a conceptual media artist concerned with the internet. Editor's pick Review Which new books are worth your time? Our critics decide He has been shortlisted for the Brisbane Portrait Prize several times. Pivoting to literature, he has written a time-travel novel, currently with his American agent seeking a publisher. The Furphy Literary Prize is named after Australian author Joseph Furphy, who wrote the novel Such Is Life (1903) and whose family name has become synonymous with tall tales.



The Magpies Have Unionised, which beat 880 other submissions to win the award, took more than 60 drafts to write. It will be published in a 2026 anthology and is available to read online. Graves has also been invited to a residency program in Shepparton. Start the day with a summary of the day’s most important and interesting stories, analysis and insights.

World.title: Three storeys everywhere: The radical plan to drive down house prices
World.content:
PoliticsFederalProperty prices Three storeys everywhere: The radical plan to drive down house prices Shane Wright July 27, 2026 — 10:30pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

The nation’s sprawling suburbs of single-storey homes would be transformed under a plan from the Productivity Commission to make the property market affordable, with three-storey developments allowed everywhere and high-rise apartment blocks built near train, tram and bus stations. Declaring state and local government planning regulations a key reason for Australia having some of the most expensive homes in the world, the commission also wants the minimum size of home lots to be reduced while allowing more European-style mixed commercial and residential developments. Single-block homes would be replaced by three-storey townhouses under a plan to reduce the cost of housing across Australia. Getty Images Commission chair Danielle Wood said regulation was the handbrake on new homes, with the time needed to save for a deposit climbing by almost 30 per cent over the past 20 years. “When people can’t live near work or family the economy and the community suffers. We cannot solve our housing affordability problem unless we build more homes where people want to live,” she said.



The commission has been charged by Treasurer Jim Chalmers to examine the nation’s building approval process, land use, access to infrastructure and construction methods. Related Article Opinion

Property prices A generations-long belief about house prices has just been shattered Shane Wright Senior economics correspondent The government, which in the budget committed $2 billion towards states and councils for housing-related infrastructure, is more than 100,000 properties behind its own target of building 1.25 million homes between mid-2024 and mid-2029. Despite a slowdown in the nation’s property market since February, house prices are still at record levels of unaffordability. Median house prices in some cities are still climbing, with Perth up 87 per cent since 2020 and in Brisbane up by 92 per cent. In its interim report, the commission said state and territory governments should allow three-storey developments on all residential land, with exceptions only for environmental factors, particular hazards or heritage listings where benefits of protection outweighed the costs.



State and council planning schemes would allow four- to nine-storey and high-rise apartments in high-demand areas with existing transport infrastructure, or where it could be quickly upgraded. Minimum lot sizes on new developments should be cut, especially in designated high-demand areas. Commercial zones that effectively prohibit residential development should also be overhauled to enable mixed-use areas. Productivity Commission chair Danielle Wood says the country has to build more homes where people want to live. Eamon Gallagher Commissioner Alison Roberts said there were far too many regulations that had driven up the cost of building or reduced supply. “Regulation is essential – particularly where it ensures buildings are safe and built to a high standard. But too often, other rules are making it illegal or unviable to build the kinds of homes people need in the places they want to live,” she said.



“The kind of rules that stop you adding a granny flat in your garden or replacing a single home with townhouses are at the core of our housing challenge.” The commission said the surge in the cost of housing had led to an almost 18-percentage-point drop in the number of people between 25 and 34 with their own home between 1981 and 2021. Australian mortgage debt is among the highest per person in the developed world. In a bid to reduce construction costs, the commission recommends car parking requirements be reduced or axed completely, especially in areas where there is evidence that off-street parking is not being used or there are high levels of public transport. Loading Broad heritage listings would be replaced by more specific protections that had gone through a cost-benefit analysis. Instead of blanket heritage protections, specific buildings or small areas would attract heritage listings, with more options to delist buildings.



A constant complaint from the housing sector is the imposition of developer contributions for new projects. The Urban Development Institute of Australia estimates developer fees can make up to 20 per cent of the cost of bringing a new lot to market. Related Article Analysis

Property market Saying there’s an upside to falling house prices is sacrilege. But Labor needs to admit it The commission found developer contributions should be used where there is a “close nexus” to the proposed development and local infrastructure needs. Estimates of developer fees should be made before the release or rezoning of land, with proponents given the option to make the payments over a period of time or later in the development process. Under the commission’s proposals, current restrictions in areas such as minimum dwelling and balcony sizes and storage requirements for apartments would be axed. Current dwelling and bedroom size requirements differ between states and territories.



The commission said “state, territory and local governments should avoid regulating observable characteristics that do not negatively affect the wider community”. Restrictions on housing types would also be ditched. Another area targeted by the commission is the time many authorities take to approve new housing. Wood said in one case, a developer spent an extra three years on reports and waiting for approvals for a 1600-lot development on Melbourne’s urban fringe. The commission’s final report is due by March next year. Cut through the noise of federal politics with news, views and expert analysis. Lyon had already defended the club’s decision to play King in the senior side and bypass the VFL this time, but the star forward will now have played just once in three seasons after a torturous run that includes injuries to both knees and calf issues. Max King gets a kick away against the Kangaroos. AFL Photos King left Sunday’s 31-point win over North Melbourne midway through the third quarter and did not return. He started each term on the bench and played in six-minute stints, but managed just one kick and one handball while playing at different times on Charlie Comben and Aidan Corr. Saints football boss Lenny Hayes said the club would “wrap our arms” around King.



“It’s an incredibly disappointing outcome for Max, who has done everything possible throughout his rehabilitation to put himself in the best position to return,” said Hayes. “He’s an incredibly important part of our football club. We’ll continue to wrap our arms around him and provide all the support he needs as he works through this latest setback. “Our focus now turns to ensuring Max undertakes a full pre-season to allow him to get back and play consistent senior football in 2027.” King signed a six-year contract extension in October 2024 that ties him to the Saints until the end of the 2032 season. His horror injury run started about three months before he inked that deal, when he sustained a season-ending posterior cruciate ligament tear in his left knee in a two-point loss to Port Adelaide.



King also hurt his right knee in a pre-season game mere months later that ultimately required three separate surgeries and wiped out his 2025 season. After a delayed start to the past off-season, a new calf problem sidelined him again. King made it back from that setback, only to suffer a hamstring strain in his second VFL game in May. The 26-year-old went into an extended rehabilitation period after that, including spending time on the Gold Coast with his twin, Suns focal point Ben, who is expected to sign as a restricted free agent with Hawthorn. Lyon said St Kilda’s high-performance team was satisfied that King had proven he was ready with a significant volume of running, including at high speeds and game-like intensity.



“We stand by our decision to play him,” Lyon said on Sunday. There are still six seasons left on King’s deal, and he will be desperate to repay the Saints’ faith in him to avoid becoming the poster child for how long-term contracts can go wrong. King won’t play again until the 2027 season. AFL Photos The No.4 pick from the 2018 AFL draft displayed his immense potential in a career-best 52-goal season in 2022. St Kilda are clinging to a wildcard berth with a month to go in the home-and-away season, with matches to come against Sydney, Carlton, Richmond and Gold Coast, all of which will be played in Melbourne.



In positive news for the Saints faithful, it was confirmed on Monday evening that Darcy Wilson has committed to the club on a new two-year deal. The hard-running midfielder had attracted plenty of rival interest after a breakthrough season. The 20-year-old, who was drafted at pick 18 in the 2023 draft, will remain at the club until the end of the 2028 season. The Saints made a splash in last year’s player movement period, recruiting Tom De Koning, Jack Silvagni, Sam Flanders and Liam Ryan, after making Nasiah Wanganeen-Milera the league’s first $2 million-a-season man. St Kilda’s big spending has so far delivered only a mediocre return, worsened by Flanders suffering a season-ending Achilles injury. De Koning also missed games with broken ribs and a punctured lung, but demonstrated what he could bring in a strong performance against the Roos on Sunday.



Lion straight to tribunal on misconduct charge Brisbane youngster Ty Gallop has been sent straight to the AFL tribunal for shoving Port Adelaide’s Mitch Georgiades’ head into the turf. Gallop has been charged with serious misconduct for the incident in the second quarter of Brisbane’s win over Port at the Gabba on Sunday. The 20-year-old rolled Georgiades in a heavy tackle but has come under scrutiny for his actions off the ball immediately after. As the Lions swept downfield, Gallop lifted Georgiades by the jumper before slamming him back into the turf head first.



Depending on how the tribunal sees the incident, Gallop could face multiple weeks on the sidelines. “It wasn’t a great look, but I’m on the other side of it,” Port Adelaide coach Josh Carr said. “They’re a team that plays tough and pushes the limits. We got the free kick, so we got rewarded. There’s not much more to say.” Carr said Georgiades was unaffected by the incident after the game.



Gallop’s choice to hit out at Georgiades was described as “a stupid action” by former Brisbane great Alastair Lynch. “We’ve been singing the praises of Ty Gallop over the last half a dozen weeks particularly,” Lynch said on Fox Footy. “But that’s just a stupid action. We don’t want to see that. Mitch has had some problems with concussion. AAP and Scott Spits Keep up to date with the best AFL coverage in the country.

World.title: Same source, different names: The allegations rocking Four Corners
World.content:
BusinessCompaniesMedia & marketing Same source, different names: The allegations rocking Four Corners Calum Jaspan July 27, 2026 — 8:54pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

The Four Corners boss who oversaw two episodes led by reporter Mahmood Fazal that were removed by the ABC over accuracy concerns says he was shocked to learn the program had allegedly misrepresented the identity of an anonymous source. In a statement to this masthead on Monday evening, Matthew Carney, who was executive producer of Four Corners from 2022 until earlier this year, says he referred both investigations – Cocaine Nation and Meth Highway – to more senior editorial managers before they were aired. “Brendan” was presented as a meth dealer in the 2024 Four Corners episode Meth Highway, and also featured under a different name in an earlier investigation. ABC “[The programs] went through a rigorous fact check, verification and legal process,” Carney said in response to a series of questions from this masthead. “More than two years after broadcast [in 2023 and 2024] rumours emerged that a source could be compromised in one of these stories and I started an investigation. “Late last year I received a confidential email outlining there was an allegation of misrepresentation of an anonymous interviewee,” he said. “I was shocked by the contents and did my own inquiries, and the ABC investigated the matter after I had retired.”



The episodes were removed by the ABC on Friday, with the broadcaster citing concerns about the “veracity of certain sources used in both programs”. But ABC sources now suspect that Fazal featured the same person in both episodes under different identities. In one, the person, who this masthead has chosen not to name, was presented as a drug dealer under one identity and the second time as an anonymous meth dealer named “Brendan”, but behind a mask. Mahmood Fazal reporting for the ABC’s Four Corners program. The ABC said it had no further comments beyond the statement it issued on Friday. Fazal, who the ABC sacked in May, did not respond to a request for comment. He has previously said he had not been told the nature of the ABC’s concerns with his reporting and branded the broadcaster’s decision a “worrying precedent”.



“Brendan”, the man who was in both broadcasts, did not respond to a request for comment. While the ABC’s independent ombudsman is still preparing its investigation into the programs that were retracted last week, the ABC’s internal editorial standards department has also spent months investigating all the work produced by Fazal during his time on the show. The ABC decision to remove the programs preceded a lengthy piece published by The Monthly on former ABC news director Justin Stevens’ tenure, which focused on the Fazal saga and included the sourcing issue. The piece was written by Carney’s predecessor as executive producer of Four Corners, Sally Neighbour, who left the ABC in 2022 after seven years running the show. Almost everyone involved in the chain of command during Fazal’s reporting of the two episodes has left the ABC, aside from ABC head of investigations Jo Puccini and supervising producer Alice Brennan. Fazal, Carney and Puccini’s boss Stevens have departed, as have managing director David Anderson and chair Ita Buttrose. This masthead does not suggest any of the exits were related to Fazal or the investigation.



The ABC previously stood by Fazal following allegations published by this masthead in 2024, including that Fazal passed on threats from the Alameddine crime organisation to YouTuber FriendlyJordies, real name Jordan Shanks, and his producer, Kristo Langker, in 2024. But the broadcaster then suspended him after the launch of an independent podcast Fazal hosted with underworld media personality Ryan Naumenko. Related Article ABC Sacked Four Corners reporter lashes ABC move to pull episodes Fazal’s public fallout with Naumenko over the financial terms of the podcast led to the public feud. The ABC said the podcast appearances did not receive final sign-off approval. They were published featuring advertising for an online crypto casino. Fazal has previously denied any wrongdoing relating to the podcast and has lodged an unfair dismissal case in the Fair Work Commission. Since Fazal’s exit from the show, the ABC has installed a new executive producer for Four Corners, Joel Tozer. Last month, this masthead reported that one of Tozer’s first acts as Four Corners boss was to overhaul the show’s commissioning and standards processes. Part of the overhaul included the newly created commissioning and standards editor position, appointing former 7.30 producer Patricia Drum. World.title: TV presenter and comedian Bill Oddie dies at 85
World.content:
CultureCelebrityVale TV presenter and comedian Bill Oddie dies at 85 India McTaggart July 27, 2026 — 8:48pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Bill Oddie, the comedian and wildlife presenter, has died aged 85. The TV personality’s agent paid tribute to the “intelligence and wit” of “Britain’s best-loved birder”. TV presenter and comedian Bill Oddie, pictured here in 2020, has died at the age of 85. Getty Images Oddie, who found fame in the 1970s as a member of comic trio The Goodies alongside Tim Brooke-Taylor and Graeme Garden, died on Saturday (London time). Announcing his death, David Foster, his agent, said: “Bill was a multi-talented celebrity – wildlife presenter, broadcaster, comedian, writer, songwriter, musician and conservationist. Yet it was never fame that he valued.



“Instead he encouraged us to respect and protect the environment. He taught us the wonder of it. He protested, lobbied and campaigned for it.” He added that his thoughts were with Bill’s wife, Laura, and his daughters Bonnie, Kate and Rosie. Oddie, Brooke-Taylor and Garden formed The Goodies after meeting at the University of Cambridge in the early 60s. The Goodies wearing Brooke-Taylor's trademark Union Jack waistcoat. Getty Images They were flatmates and members of the Footlights Club, which also previously included the members of Monty Python – John Cleese, Graham Chapman and Eric Idle.



The Goodies performed in the same student venue – Cambridge Circus – and performed on Broadway before the trio starred together in a BBC sketch show titled Broaden Your Mind. Brooke-Taylor, who became president of Footlights in 1963, died at the age of 79 with coronavirus in April 2020. The Goodies hamming it up in London in 2003. AP Oddie later turned his lifelong passion for birds from a hobby into a job. He wrote several books on the subject, including Bill Oddie’s Little Black Bird Book and Birdwatching with Bill Oddie, which were illustrated with his own photographs and drawings.



Oddie also fronted an array of wildlife programmes, including The Bird Business and The Big Bird Race for Channel 4 as well as The Great Kenyan Bird Safari and two series of Bird In The Nest for the BBC. Related Article Review ‘I am, I suppose, a TV personality’: the many lives of Bill Oddie He spoke openly about suffering from crippling depression and was admitted to a psychiatric hospital in 2009 after being dropped from the BBC’s Springwatch, of which he was one of the original presenters. He was finally diagnosed with bipolar disorder. Speaking in 2014, he said he still felt sad that his days on Springwatch were cut short, adding that he had rarely watched the programme since. He said: “I very much miss it, but when I do see it, it brings back many happy memories and I like to think I contributed to its success.



“It’s still so well loved and helps encourage people to enjoy the natural world. That’s all to the good because I fear so many people wear earphones for their phones and music players that increasingly they miss out on everyday joys like birdsong. “My plea to people would be to ‘go naked’ occasionally – take off those earpieces so you hear nature and, of course, birdsong. You may not realise how precious it is until it’s gone.” The Telegraph, UK Get the day’s breaking news, entertainment ideas and a long read to enjoy. World.title: Brisbane man’s defence of ‘aggressive’ magpies nabs him $15,000 prize
World.content:
NationalQueenslandCity life Brisbane man’s defence of ‘aggressive’ magpies nabs him $15,000 prize Nick Dent July 27, 2026 — 8:39pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Nearly 5000 magpie attacks are logged in Australia each year, but Kailum Graves has good reason to feel warmly towards the swooping birds. The Coorparoo author has just won a $15,000 literary prize for his story about the tense relations between magpies and humans. The Magpies Have Unionised nabbed Graves the 2026 Furphy Literary Prize in a ceremony at the Shepparton Art Gallery in northern Victoria on Saturday. Kailum Graves visiting Swoop the Big Barrwarrang – the big magpie in Euroa, Victoria. Kailum Graves In the 4669-word story, magpies who are tired of being maligned as “aggressive” and “sky bastards” demand an apology from a local council and begin a targeted swooping campaign.



“We reject these characterisations. We are not aggressive. We are parents,” the birds write in an email. Among their demands are the replacement of the phrase “magpie attack season” with “heightened interspecies boundary awareness period”. Furphy Literary Award winner 2026 Kailum Graves on receiving his prize. Amina Barolli Furphy Literary Awards judge John Harms said the story was brilliantly written, fanciful and familiar. “Kailum Graves’ allegorical masterpiece introduces magpies that will bring a tear to your eye in a way that magpies never have before,” he said.



Graves, 41, said he had a grudging respect for magpies, who were a part of life in Coorparoo. Related Article Good Weekend ‘It’s a bit gamified, almost like Pokemon Go’: The tracking app preventing magpie attacks “I feel bad for them because we’ve invaded their space, but we’re painting them as the aggressor,” he said. “The signs should be more aimed at us looking after the magpies as opposed to us being the victims of the swooping because they’re really just protecting their young.” According to Magpie Alert, Queensland had over 1000 reported swooping attacks in 2025, out of nearly 5000 nationwide.



Graves’ ultimately moving story takes the point of view of a council worker and mother who becomes an interspecies mediator and whose young daughter is terrified of the birds. Satirising local government, the story was inspired by Graves’ recent stay in Germany, where he was struck both by the absence of birdsong and the prevalence of government bureaucracy. One of the council’s swooping warning signs. Reddit “I missed birds, I didn’t realise how much I loved them – even just bird songs in the morning and butcher birds in Brisbane singing,” Graves said. “In Germany, they’re the experts of pointless bureaucracy. Once I went to get a parcel at the post office, and I took my Australian passport and then they refused to give me my parcel, saying ‘it’s not real ID’.”



Graves studied philosophy and art history at the University of Queensland and has carved out a practice as a conceptual media artist concerned with the internet. Editor's pick Review Which new books are worth your time? Our critics decide He has been shortlisted for the Brisbane Portrait Prize several times. Pivoting to literature, he has written a time-travel novel, currently with his American agent seeking a publisher. The Furphy Literary Prize is named after Australian author Joseph Furphy, who wrote the novel Such Is Life (1903) and whose family name has become synonymous with tall tales.



The Magpies Have Unionised, which beat 880 other submissions to win the award, took more than 60 drafts to write. It will be published in a 2026 anthology and is available to read online. Graves has also been invited to a residency program in Shepparton. Start the day with a summary of the day’s most important and interesting stories, analysis and insights.

World.title: Veteran broadcaster Jim Hopkins dies aged 80
World.content:
Veteran broadcaster and Waitaki District councillor Jim Hopkins has died at the age of 80.

Hopkins was a regular on New Zealand screens before first being elected to the council in the Oamaru Ward in 2007.

He was the deputy mayor for three years from 2010.

But for decades before his move into politics, Hopkins worked both behind and in front of the camera on New Zealand television - switching between comedy and serious reporting.

He was a writer for the classic soap opera Close to Home in the 1970s and later for the satirical comedy series Public Eye.

He was a reporter and presenter for both news current affairs and light documentary, and wrote a best-selling book Blokes and Sheds, which became a TV series.

Known for his wit, Hopkins was a regular on radio and TV panel shows and was a popular public speaker.

His switch to local body politics suited him well.

Jim Hopkins. Supplied / Waitaki District Council.

The Waitaki District Council said he was a "beloved" councillor who will be remembered with respect and gratitude.

In a posting on its website, Mayor Mel Tavendale said he would be deeply missed.

"He was a fierce advocate for the people of Waitaki, both within and beyond council, and he scrutinised every detail. He kept us all honest," she said.

"The council chamber will not be the same without him, his passionate arguments, attention to detail and incredible wit.

World.title: Data centre opponents welcome Greens policy, warn of 'potential crisis'
World.content:
Opponents of a $3.5 billion data centre near Invercargill have welcomed a Green Party policy that would halt further centres from being consented and want other political parties to consider tighter controls.

The Greens are calling for a one-year pause on new AI data centres until stronger rules and regulations are put in place.

Singapore-based company Datagrid has been given resource consent to develop the 78,000 square-metre factory in Makarewa.

The centre would use 280 megawatts of power, making it the country's second-largest electricity user, behind the Tiwai Point aluminium smelter.

The consents would include the ability to draw more than 600,000 litres of groundwater every day, although Datagrid has been adamant it will not use any groundwater, preferring Invercargill's naturally cool air temperatures and rainwater when needed.

Hundreds of people packed into the Invercargill Workingmen's Club at a 22 July meeting organised by the Southland Sustainable Resource Coalition to voice their concerns about the data centre.

Organiser Kelly Blomfield said people were worried about the environmental impact, water use and noise pollution.

"We don't want something that is taking massive resources out of our community without putting anything back in, and it's just the non-notified consent process where everybody finds out after the paperwork's signed and sealed, it's just not good enough," she said.

Construction of the Datagrid centre in Makarewa is expected to start in the next month. Supplied / Datagrid

Blomfield said she supported the Greens' policy and hoped it would be considered by other parties.

"It is a fantastic policy and it's one that I hope all parties will adopt, that all parties will be looking at - this as a humongous potential crisis," she said.

"I understand that New Zealand wants to be part of a race to have data centres and to be forward-thinking, but why can't we be known as the country that said no? Like the country that said, 'you know what, we're actually going to put our people first'."

The centre is expected to create more than 1200 jobs during construction and between 50 to 80 permanent jobs, while a Boston Consulting Group report estimates that scaling up data centre infrastructure in New Zealand could unlock up to $70 billion in economic activity over the next decade.

Tech expert Dr Karaitiana Taiuru believed it was worth slowing down to consider alternative solutions to address some of the environmental risks posed by data centres.

Solutions could include treating seawater or wastewater so it could be used like fresh water if necessary, instead of using groundwater for cooling.

"This is a really good time for us to re-evaluate and say, 'look, there are alternatives'," he said.

Taiuru said the government needed to lead a cross-industry discussion, otherwise the country risked being left behind in the new age of AI.

The government was already paying overseas tech companies millions of dollars to store data, Taiuru said.

"If we bring these data centres back to New Zealand or create them in New Zealand then we lower the environmental impact on a global scale, we increase our own security and decrease taxpayer funding to pay for current infrastructure," he said.

Southland mayor Rob Scott said the $3.5 billion project would bring investment and jobs to the region in the short term, but questioned the long-term benefits and who profited from data the centre produced.

While there had been much criticism of the centre's non-notified resource consent process and people felt like they had no say, Scott said the process had been robust.

"What was very clear at that meeting last week was people care deeply about the environment and their backyard out here, and we need to make sure that it's not progress at all costs," he said.

A balance between enabling investment in data centres, and regulation, was important, Scott said.

"Everyone moans about the likes of councils and government having too much red tape and getting in the way of development until something comes through that they don't like, and then all of a sudden it's the opposite and council gets blamed for not stopping things," he said.

"Everyone's got the right to ask the questions and be curious, but we've got to be careful that we don't create uncertainty for anyone trying to invest in New Zealand as well, so it's a delicate line around how these things are done."

Prime Minister Christopher Luxon told Morning Report officials did not expect the data centre to put pressure on power prices.

"Data centres can be a net positive for the economy, they will create jobs, will create opportunities for us, and we do need some sensible rules," he said.

"That does mean things like making sure additional electricity generation happens, investments in grid stability, and that they pay for transmission upgrades and those kinds of things."

Luxon discusses new parental leave policy, tariffs, polling Morning Report Download MP3 6m

He said the government would have common-sense rules in place ahead of increased investment in data centres.

"We are an attractive place [for data centres] because we have some competitive advantages with high renewables, cooler climates, and political stability - that makes those investments attractive."

Luxon said New Zealand was "last cab off the rank" and must not get left behind.

Electricity company Mercury has spent $53 million to acquire a 12.7 per cent stake in Datagrid NZ.

Mercury chief executive Stew Hamilton said New Zealand had the capability to build data centres powered by renewable energy to support the country's economic growth.

He said the concerns raised around the use of water, power and jobs were legitimate.

"[They] are three things that absolutely should be addressed, and we think with this project that we have with Datagrid, we think they're well looked after and we're keen to be a part of that solution," Hamilton said.

"We absolutely believe that data centres should be building or should be coming on stream with additional power to make sure that it's contributing to New Zealand's grid."

World.title: National rules out working with Opportunity Party
World.content:
National has ruled out working with the Opportunity Party, with leader Christopher Luxon saying National would not do business with a party that wants to raise taxes.

Opportunity's leader says New Zealanders are tired of that way of thinking, and suspected Luxon would change his tune if National needed Opportunity come November.

Opportunity was on 4.7 percent in the latest RNZ-Reid Research poll, just shy of the 5 percent needed to enter Parliament.

The party has been open to working with both National and Labour, should either need its support to form a government after the election.

Opportunity's flagship policies include establishing a universal basic income of up to $370 a week, and a 1.75 percent annual tax on the value or urban land and 0.5 percent on rural land.

At his weekly post-Cabinet media conference, Luxon was asked whether National could work with Opportunity.

"We wouldn't be in business with people who want to increase taxes," Luxon responded.

He added that it was his "very, very strong position" that National would not work with Opportunity.

"It's a vote for Labour and the Greens because essentially, at the moment, and I look at their policies, you've got a universal basic income that wants to make every New Zealander a beneficiary. You've got a land tax sitting there that actually is going to be massive."

Pressed on whether that meant National would not go into a governing arrangement with Opportunity in any form, Luxon said it would not be a surprise that National did not want to "do business" with Opportunity.

Afterwards, Luxon's office confirmed to RNZ this amounted to a formal rule-out.

Opportunity was on 4.7 percent in July's RNZ-Reid Research poll. Supplied / Facebook/ Opportunity Party

Opportunity leader Qiulae Wong said the rule-in, rule-out game was "the old school way" of doing politics, which New Zealanders were tiring of.

"The tribalism is not taking us anywhere, and it's not solving our big issues. So we've really got to start leaving ideology at the door, and looking at the policies and the ideas that are going to take New Zealand forward."

Wong said Opportunity's door would remain open for National, but she encouraged the party to engage with its policies constructively.

"Our tax policy overall actually would be a tax cut for 70 percent of New Zealanders. They would be better off under our full tax policy. 20 percent would be about neutral, and then only 10 percent would be paying slightly more," she said.

"The fact that we are offering a tax cut to hardworking New Zealanders, many people who rent, that is something that the National Party has campaigned on in the past, and I would think would be open to. So I would encourage them to look a bit deeper and come and have a conversation with us about it."

Labour's campaign chair Kieran McAnulty suspected Luxon had ruled Opportunity out by accident.

"I think they themselves are surprised by the decision that the prime minister has announced today," he said.

McAnulty said Labour would announce who it would and would not work with "very shortly".

Labour is yet to make a call on New Zealand First, despite New Zealand First ruling Labour out.
