World.title: Let him roam, owner says: Chase the Christchurch celebrity cat
World.content:
Christchurch cat explorer gains thousands of online fans Checkpoint Download MP3 4m

Wanted posters have sprung up around Christchurch for an explorer named Chase. But unlike your traditional 'wanted' poster, this one is to tell people that it is ok for Chase to roam.

Chase is a cat.

With Chase attracting regular attention - and occasionally going missing - his owner Nick White resorted to posting the messages about town and starting a Facebook group for Chase, hoping to teach people how to look after the wandering cat's best interests, with messages such as: "If I tell you I am hungry, do not believe me. If you meet me, please pat me and tell me to go home."

The Facebook page Has Anybody Seen Chase? now attracts regular updates with paparazzi-like shots of the celebrity cat on his latest exploits. Sometimes in quite unexpected places.

The central city is Chase's favourite destination. Supplied/ Nick White

White told Checkpoint: "About six months ago he all of a sudden hit his teenage years, and just left. And now he comes home exhausted and doesn't really have any time for us anymore."

"He disappeared about 10 o'clock this morning and we haven't seen him all day. He comes and goes."

Chase's visits include a Mexican restaurant, Te Pae Christchurch Convention Centre, he has been seen trying to get into a hotel by Victoria Square, and wandering up and down the Bridge of Remembrance.

Chase loves attention from people he encounters on his adventures. Supplied/ Nick White

"I'm not sure if he's actually aware of his fame," White says. "He's gained weight - he's definitely gained fame weight, because I think his fans - despite the posters mentioned - have been feeding him, and he hangs around a lot of ice-cream shops.

Chase has been a repeat visitor at the Bridge of Remembrance. Supplied/ Nick White

"He sleeps upstairs in a whisky bar, apparently, which has been great - on Regent Street.

"He likes to hit the streets on big rugby weekends or Saturday nights, and wander round getting pats and dropped kebabs, I think."

While Chase "tends to go in one direction, toward the central city", videos of black cats wandering through houses and yards, that do look like Chase, have also been sent in.

"Because he's a pretty generic black cat, it's difficult to tell," White says.

But problems have arisen when about seven or eight times, people have found Chase, thought he was lost and taken him with them.

The cat is now equipped with a distinctive orange high-vis collar, with the url for his Facebook page embroidered on it: "We're just trying to use the Facebook page as a GPS, so we know where he's actually been," White says.

Supplied/ Nick White

"The longest he's been away for is about 13 days, and we thought he'd been kidnapped or something."

Supplied/ Nick White

"[Once] he got stuck between two buildings in Cathedral Square. [He's been] taken as far as Ferrymead out by the beach, and [we've been] having to pick him up from vets."

Local vets know who Chase is, and regularly advise people who call them about the cat to leave him be and just put him back down. But sometimes people still insist on delivering the cat to the vets' care, White says, and he gets another call-out to pick him up.

"Which is terribly annoying - he just wants to go adventuring."

If Chase can be left to own devices - apart from pats and scratches - he'll be fine wandering, and will keep bringing joy to those he meets, White says.

World.title: Teen arrested after doing burnouts holding a machete live on TikTok
World.content:
A teenager has been arrested in Auckland after allegedly livestreaming himself doing burnouts while brandishing a machete.

Police say the 18-year-old came to their attention on Sunday night after a member of the public saw the livestream and reported it.

The man was allegedly doing burnouts in the Titirangi town centre, in west Auckland, and streaming it live on the social media platform TikTok.

Police say his BMW was spotted shortly after and ordered to stop.

Senior Sergeant Jon Winthrop said when officers went to speak with the car's occupants "they were met by the unmistakable smell of cannabis."

He said a search located over 100 grams of cannabis packaged into bags and 18 capsules of cannabis oil.

The machete allegedly shown in the livestream was also found, as well as a 30cm-long knife.

The driver was arrested and taken into custody and found to be holding a "significant" quantity of cash.

He was charged with possessing offensive weapons and possessing cannabis and cannabis oil for supply.

World.title: Kiwi swimmer's lost golden opportunity: 'The judges couldn't make up their mind'
World.content:
A New Zealand school girl was taking on the world's best, and against the odds it seemed like she had won gold.

That school girl was Vivien Boyd - Vivien Haddon as she was then - and the finish in the 1962 Commonwealth Games 100-metre breaststroke swimming final in Perth was as close as it gets.

But what happened next still rankles, even after six decades.

Six decades on swimmer reflects on stolen win Checkpoint Download MP3 5m

A split decision

Perth in 1962 seems like a lifetime ago.

It was a new world for Vivien Boyd - a long way from Palmerston North's Freyberg High School, where she was a student, and the city's outdoor municipal baths, in which she trained.

Vivien Boyd showed off her 1962 games medals at a civic reception in Palmerston North. Manawatū Standard Archive / Manawatū Heritage

Although it was not quite straight out of the classroom into the swimming pool. The swimmers trained in Tauranga ahead of the games, so Boyd did her school studies from there.

She loved the sprint races, as her speed and grit powered her on.

But she was up against quality swimmers, including Olympic medalist Anita Lonsbrough.

In the 200-metre breaststroke, Vivien won bronze.

"And then I swam the 100m against her and was awarded the silver medal, unfortunately, for me," Boyd told RNZ from her Brisbane home. She has lived in Australia for more than 40 years.

"But anyway, that was the way it was. The judges couldn't make up their mind who won. They took half an hour to make up their mind.

"It was a bit of a controversy because everybody thought I had won."

Boyd said footage from the race showed she was home first, not Lonsbrough.

Timekeeping technology was in use, but it was only on trial so could not decide the official result.

"I've read that it gave me four hundredths or two hundredths, whichever, you can pick whichever one you like but, yes, I did win it...

"Two judges awarded me the win. Two judges gave Anita Lonsbrough the win. The final judge couldn't make up his mind.

"He took half an hour to make a decision, so he went with the Olympic champion."

Boyd said Lonsbrough showed her experience too, by celebrating when she hit the end of the pool. Boyd finished the race quietly.

The agonising half-hour wait for the result was spent chatting with Australian swimming legend Dawn Fraser.

"She sat with me because I knew her and was telling me to take a loss.

"I was absolutely fine because I had only just turned 17 and it was my first big international meet.

"I'd only been swimming breaststroke for about 18 months, so I was happy to get anything," Boyd said.

"I think they actually only had a certain amount of gold medals and they didn't have any spares. That's my theory."

Keys to the city

Looking back, Boyd said a shared gold medal would have been fair, and she was disappointed New Zealand officials did not protest on her behalf.

Vivien Boyd moved to Australia more than 40 years ago, but regularly returns to New Zealand. Supplied

On her return to Palmerston North she was feted, although she said she did not like attention and did not deal with it well.

"I never like to be noticed very much. You'd pick up the paper every morning and your name's front page and photo's front page, because it was such a big thing back then. It did attract a lot of attention in Palmerston North," she said.

"I can remember standing there in the middle of The Square, under the new clock tower, and people standing around and the mayor handing me the keys of the city, which I still have."

Boyd regularly returns to New Zealand, and in the late 1990s Palmerston North tried to put right the unfair result from Perth, as former city council public affairs manager Malcolm Hopwood remembers.

"I got the guys at the council to build and design a dinner plate version of the gold medal that she should have won back in 1962," he said.

"She came back for the opening of the covered pool at Freyberg High School. She swam a length and I presented the gold medal to her - our gold medal tour on behalf of the city."

In 1966 in Jamaica Boyd won bronze again in the 200-metre breaststroke, before retiring. She had also competed at the 1964 Olympics.

She made a comeback in the early 1970s and won national titles, but that was it for big competitions.

Limited training to take on the world

Boyd's from a sporty family - one brother Gerald Haddon was a squash champion and first-class cricketer, and other brother Malcolm Haddon a national title-winning sailor.

Boyd's youngest son Sean Boyd continued that tradition, representing Australia at water polo during the Sydney Olympics in 2000. Boyd fondly remembers watching on.

Now, she can look back on her own achievements with fondness too. She's also looking forward to getting back into the pool again after a knee injury.

"I'm pretty happy with what I achieved. I was a very active, sporty person," she said.

The way she trained would be impossible to imagine now.

"I used to swim three months a year and was expected to go to the Olympics on three months of training. The other side of the world - they just swim all year and have competitions in Europe all the time.

"Things have changed and it's so much more competitive and better for the kids today. They just have it all.

"They wouldn't have dived into the water in the morning when it had those little black swimming beetles and things in the pool. And the temperature of the water was probably about 12 or 15 degrees."

Times have changed for the Commonwealth Games too - they are no longer the patriotic celebration of empire seen in Perth.

They were still important though, Boyd said.

"The Commonwealth Games were a wonderful thing.

"A lot of people want to say they're not valid now, but I believe they are because they bring the Commonwealth together.

"They bring all those swimmers that haven't had the chance at big competitions to have that experience. I just think it's an amazing.

"I'd hate to see it not happening."

World.title: Live: Nketia sprints into 100m semis as Browning slams 'weird' qualifying rules
World.content:
(ABC Sport)

Just a day or two before the start of the athletics program we received word that the top eight sprinters in the rankings would be given a free ticket into the semifinals, leaving the rest of the field to duke it out in the heats.

Not only that, but there would be no automatic qualifiers from those heats for finishing in the top two, as is usually the case.

Instead, the entire field is running a huge time trial.

Australia's Rohan Browning, who finished second in his heat in 10.24 said it is an unfair system that was sprung on them at the last moment.

"It's unheard of, it's extremely weird. It's really hard to know, I have no idea what times have been run, I have no idea where I sit in the placings.

(Getty Images)

"It's gusty out there, so when they just make up these rules about eight guys get to go through and the rest of us on a time trial rather than first or second across the line, the reality is some heats will have better conditions than others, so I don't know what's going on.

Browning made the cut in 16th and compatriot Eddie Nketia was fourth fastest with his 10.07, but before he knew that Browning revealed the whole set-up had been sprung on them.

He said he always turns up prepared to run three rounds but the other folks, including countryman Lachie Kennedy, don't have to.

"It's not fair, clearly it's not fair. It's clearly been engineered to try to achieve a desired outcome. Whatever's motivated that decision, I don't know what it is or if it's reasonable or not, but clearly it's not fair. I think everyone would agree on that.

"At the end of the day this sport is meritocracy at its finest; if you're quick enough you go through, so I suppose you could say those guys have earned their place. In all likelihood they were probably the guys paying the best odds to make the final regardless, but you just don't know. Some guys might be injured, some guys might be out of shape. I don't even know when they took the performances from."

World.title: Max King's season is over after first AFL game in two years
World.content:
Luckless St Kilda spearhead Max King's season is over after confirmation the key forward suffered a hamstring injury in his first AFL game in two years.

King left the field in the third quarter of the Saints' 13.15 (93) to 8.14 (62) win over North Melbourne, his first AFL appearance in 757 days, due to hamstring tightness.

Scans confirmed a strain to King's left hamstring, with St Kilda drawing a line through his season on Monday.

"It's an incredibly disappointing outcome for Max, who has done everything possible throughout his rehabilitation to put himself in the best position to return," general manager of football Lenny Hayes said.

"He's an incredibly important part of our football club. We'll continue to wrap our arms around him and provide all the support he needs as he works through this latest setback.

"Our focus now turns to ensuring Max undertakes a full pre-season to allow him to get back and play consistent senior football in 2027."

Saints coach Ross Lyon had defended the decision to play King in his first AFL game since June 30, 2024, having battled knee injuries as well as soft-tissue concerns.

The 26-year-old played two VFL games earlier in the year and suffered a hamstring injury in one of those, pushing his comeback past the two-year mark.

King is on a monster contract until the end of the 2032 season, but has largely been unable to play since signing it.

The 10th-placed Saints remain firmly in the finals wildcard mix, but losing King is a blow to their September hopes.

There was also bad news for GWS dynamo Finn Callaghan, who will require season-ending ankle surgery.

The exciting midfielder sprained his ankle late in the derby loss to Sydney.

"Following scans and a specialist consultation, Callaghan and the club's medical team have opted for surgery to repair the damage," the Giants said.

"Callaghan is expected to be sidelined for approximately 12 weeks."

GWS sit 12th, a win and significant percentage outside the wildcard places.

World.title: Disgruntled Tiger Doueihi expected to return to training
World.content:
Adam Doueihi has smoked the peace pipe with Wests Tigers powerbrokers and is expected to return to training on Tuesday.

Doueihi and his manager Isaac Moses met coach Benji Marshall, chief executive Shaun Mielekamp and football manager Pat Richards at the club's Concord headquarters on Monday morning to thrash out their differences.

Mielekamp emerged from the crisis talks claiming the meeting was "positive" after weekend fears Doueihi had played his last game for the Tigers.

Luai joins Parramatta, Marshall slams relationship breakdown rumours Benji Marshall has slammed "bull**** rumours" claiming a fractured relationship with Jarome Luai contributed to the star five-eighth's early exit from Wests Tigers.

Contracted until the end of the 2029 NRL season, Doueihi was said to have fallen out with Marshall after making himself unavailable for Saturday's 56-10 loss to Canberra.

The playmaker was upset about being asked to move from halfback to lock to make way for rookie debutant Javon Andrews.

But the 27-year-old could now even be rushed back for Sunday's clash with Parramatta following Monday's clear-the-air meeting.

"It was a very positive and productive meeting," Mielekamp read from a brief prepared statement.

"Adam will be at training tomorrow, which is a very good sign."

Asked to elaborate on Monday's talks, Mielekamp was tight-lipped.

"What was said in the room will stay in the room," he said.

"That's important for us as a club. We're all doing what's best for the club."

The Doueihi drama is the latest controversy to hit the embattled club after superstar playmaker Jarome Luai recently signed a one-year deal with the Eels ahead of his arrival at the PNG Chiefs for their 2028 entry to the competition.

After briefly sharing top spot on the table this season, the Tigers have dropped to second-last and out of finals contention for a 15th consecutive season.

AAP

World.title: 'The diggers have arrived': Works begin at Hobart's $1.13b stadium site
World.content:
The Tasmanian government says plans for a new Hobart stadium have reached a significant milestone with the start of preparatory earthworks at Macquarie Point.

The stadium is a key requirement for the entry of the Tasmania Devils into the AFL competition.

Jeremy Rockliff had a go on the tools at the commencement of works at the site. (ABC News: Mitchell Woolnough)

The project, which was approved by parliament last year, has polarised the community because of its $1.13 billion price tag and its location in the heart of Hobart's historic CBD.

While construction of the facility is still a year away, trucks have started shifting huge amounts of soil from the site to local waste facilities.

Aerial view of the earthworks shared on the Instagram account of Liberal Marcus Vermey. (Instagram: Marcus Vermey)

"There's about 100,000 cubic metres to be moved off this site," Hazell Bros managing director Geoffrey Hazell said.

" So, there should be a truck leaving here every eight minutes. "

An render of what the stadium is expected to look like when finished. (Supplied: Cox Architecture)

Premier Jeremy Rockliff described the occasion as a "new era of economic opportunity for Tasmania".

"Clearly the diggers have arrived, the builders are here and [it's] time to get on with the job," Mr Rockliff said.

"And it's so important for not only … bringing to life a four-decade-old dream when it comes to our own Tasmanian team … but also the significant opportunity economically [for] our visitor economy and all associated with such a significant event here today."

An artist's impression of the indoor playing area at the Macquarie Point stadium, during a football match. (Supplied: MPDC)

The Tasmania Devils club, which recently selected Ken Hinkley as its inaugural coach, will enter the AFL in 2028.

The stadium is not expected to be completed until late 2030, meaning the Devils will initially play Hobart-based games at Bellerive Oval.

Loading...

Two firms are currently vying for the right to build the stadium: Besix Watpac and Constructure Joint Venture, a collaboration between WeBuild and China Construction Oceania.

Both firms are expected to submit their bids to the Macquarie Point Development Corporation (MPDC) next month.

"They'll tell us their team, their capacity, their experience, their methodology, and they'll give us a target price for delivering this exciting project," MPDC chief executive Anne Beach said.

A preferred contractor is then likely to be chosen in October.

"We'll go through a pretty hefty assessment process and then we'll move into what we refer to as stage two, and that is when the price is locked down and a lot more local engagement is just cemented," Ms Beach said.

The final contract is expected to be signed at the end of the year.

An artist's impression of the Macquarie Point stadium entry gate 1 and retail precinct. (Supplied: Mac Point Site Master Plan Report)

WeBuild charges 'not a reason for us to not proceed'

WeBuild has come under scrutiny in recent months following revelations it is facing charges interstate relating to alleged workplace safety breaches.

SafeWork NSW has launched two separate criminal proceedings against the Italian infrastructure firm in the NSW Industrial Court alleging it put several workers at risk of death or serious injury.

WeBuild has pleaded not guilty to the charges.

Treasurer Eric Abetz (left) was at the site for the occasion. (ABC News: Mitchell Woolnough)

An artist's impression of Macquarie Point stadium entry gate 4 in Hobart. (Supplied: Mac Point Site Master Plan Report)

The Tasmanian Greens and independent MP Kristie Johnston have previously said WeBuild should have disclosed the charges during the expression of interest process, and that it should not have been selected as a tenderer.

Ms Beach said today WeBuild had declared all it was required to and that there was no reason to remove it from the process.

"The things that have been raised are allegations … are untested before the court," she said.

"They are not a reason for us to not proceed with a qualified party for a project in a different jurisdiction for a different project and they're untested in the court.

"So we're comfortable that we've gone through a thorough assessment process."

World.title: Sydney shark attack hero wins world paddleboarding championship
World.content:
A volunteer lifeguard who helped save a woman attacked by a shark on a Sydney beach has won the world paddleboarding championship amid hurricane conditions.

Charlie Verco competed in the 27th Moloka'i 2 O'ahu Paddleboard World Championships in Hawaii on Sunday.

Almost 100 participants from around the world paddleboarded a 52-kilometre stretch of open ocean from Moloka'i to O'ahu in the central Pacific.

It included crossing the Kaiwi Channel, known as the "Channel of Bones", which is home to sharks, jellyfish and other marine life.

The organisers described it as being "widely regarded as the sport's ultimate open-ocean endurance challenge", testing paddlers' skills, endurance and ocean knowledge.

The 24-year-old from Sydney won the event for the fourth time, finishing in 4 hours, 18 minutes and 3 seconds, breaking the world record.

The elite paddleboarder walked out of the water on foot smiling after finishing the race. (Supplied: Moloka'i 2 O'ahu Paddleboard World Championships)

"I'm so stoked, it's so incredible. I've never felt so good in body and mind after the race and it's extra special that I was able to set a record at the same time," he said in a post-race interview.

"I've put years and years of work into it, training two to three time a day, six days a week."

Verco, who regularly trains in the northern beaches and Sydney's east, was training when he helped save shark attack survivor Leah Stewart at Coogee Beach in June.

"It has definitely helped remind me that the ocean is something you have to respect," he said.

Shark attack victim update The 34-year-old's brother said she was awake, speaking with loved ones and her medical team and "remembers the whole event in detail".

" I'm hoping Leah is doing alright and I feel incredibly grateful that I get to have an experience like this in the ocean. "

Hurricane conditions

Verco had to navigate through "really big swells" and "strong winds" caused by category one Hurricane Fausto, which was heading towards the Hawaiian Islands.

Throughout the week, organisers had been monitoring the hurricane forecasts from the Central Pacific Hurricane Center in coordination with the United States Coast Guard and local emergency management partners.

"I think with the cyclone we were a little worried about impacting, but it managed to stay far enough away that there was just good wind behind us," Verco said.

Supporting him along the way in the escort boat was his brother and his father, Jamie Verco, who said the beginning of the race was "quiet".

Mr Verco was supported by his father and brother in the escort boat. (Supplied: Moloka'i 2 O'ahu Paddleboard World Championships)

"The swell wasn't lining up with the wind at all and you have to be very patient not to burn a lot of energy trying to chase the swell that would take you in the wrong direction," he said.

"Through the middle of the channel he started to speed up and by the end he was really flying.

" About an hour and a half out he said he'd have a crack at the record and his brother just said, 'Yeah, go for it'. "

The paddleboarder's mother and sister were watching from home.

Jamie Verco said he was "so proud" of his son.

"He's worked so hard and he's a humble kid who's put in the hard yards and does all the work and he's got the rewards today," he said.

"He's been quietly pleased with himself, I think."

Race organisers said more than 35 Australians competed in the prone paddleboard competition with Verco, with 38-year-old Stewart Mclachlan coming in second and 28-year-old Stone Harrison in third.

Verco said this year's focus was to not "get ahead of himself".

"My goal was just to have fun with it. It was the same attitude I had throughout all my training, is not to be so stressed out."

World.title: Quick hits: Wiggles star's daughter shines, netball 'cleaner' goes viral
World.content:
Two Aussie besties share a podium, a hometown hero fights his way to the final, and a very famous face wiggles his way into the stands.

Here are the quick hits from day three of the Commonwealth Games.

1. Cleaning up never looked so good

Every major sporting event has its surprise star.

Sometimes it's an underdog athlete. Sometimes it's a mascot. And sometimes it's a cleaner with a mop and a sense of rhythm.

A short clip from the Commonwealth Games netball venue has captured exactly why sport is about more than the result.

Loading Instagram content

A cleaner who danced as he mopped the court has become an unexpected crowd-pleaser on social media.

The routine, which was done to I Want To Break Free by Queen, had it all: the splits, the worm and twerking. If there were judges, he would have scored 10 out of 10.

Was the "cleaner" just a dancer with a mop employed to entertain the crowd?

That's for you to judge. Either way, he brought a lot of joy to people in the stadium.

2. Brilliant besties prove the power of friendship is real

With a medal each to their names, attention turned to Aussies Gemma Sellick and Victoria Belando Nicholson as they stepped up to be interviewed after the women's 100m backstroke S9 event.

But the pair had eyes only for each other, their friendship taking centre stage as they gushed about sharing a podium.

"This is my best friend," Sellick said, grinning ear to ear, a question from the media suddenly feeling rather inconsequential.

"This was not even a thought I had; I was not expecting this at all," Belando Nicholson told the ABC.

"To do it with my best friend is actually insane."

As they headed to pick up their medals, the pair were already planning a "debrief later tonight" to celebrate their silver and bronze medals.

3. Silver is sweet for Canada's Dolci after epic gymnastics comeback

The Arena in Glasgow was the venue for one of the maddest competitions at the Games so far: the men's all-around final at the artistic gymnastics.

At the end of the day, Flower of Scotland was on full blast (followed by the latest rendition of The Proclaimers' 500 Miles) as Reuben Ward became the first Scots gymnast to win the competition in Commonwealth Games history.

Jesse Moore also flew the flag, so to speak, as he became the latest Australian gymnastic medal-winner at these Games with a bronze, coming after he had to withdraw halfway through the Games four years ago with a shoulder injury.

But with respect, both these performances were left in the dramatic shadows by the competition of Canada's Felix Dolci.

Felix Dolci was down in 17th place in the men's all-around gymnastics final after falling off the pommel horse twice, before the Canadian made a miraculous recovery. (Getty I,mages: Francois Nel)

The men's all-around features all six disciplines: vault, rings, pommel horse, parallel bars, horizontal bars and floor exercise. Gymnasts are split into groups doing the six in different orders, maximising the drama.

Dolci was in a decent spot when he went on the pommel horse, but everything went pear-shaped as he fell off, twice. He ended up 17th out of 18 competitors after two rounds.

Game over, right? Wrong. A score of 14.200 on the vault, followed by 13.950 on the parallel bars, left him in with a vague hope.

And then he delivered on the horizontal bars, absolutely nailing his landing and scoring a whopping 14.500 to finish with the silver medal. Amazing stuff.

4. Hometown hero Goodburn not done yet

The men's 50m breaststroke is a fairly stacked event, with English legend Adam Ramsay-Peaty, Australia's Sam Williamson and South African speedster Michael Houlie all in the field.

But if you look beyond the very top times, you find Scottish swimmer Archie Goodburn.

The Edinburgh-born Goodburn was the British champion in 50 breaststroke in 2023, and had a chance of going to the Paris Olympics. But then he was diagnosed with three inoperable brain cancers in early 2024.

He was in the eighth and final heat on day three, up against Williamson.

Archie Goodburn of Scotland during the men's 50m breaststroke semifinals in Glasgow yesterday. (Getty: Rob Casey)

The 50m breaststroke is not quite the same "splash-and-dash" as the 50 freestyle, but it's not slow.

Williamson surged through to win in 26.75, with South Africa's Chris Smith second, and Goodburn made the home fans happy coming through for third.

He backed it up in the semifinal to squeeze into the final tomorrow morning (AEST) in lane one.

Regardless of his eventual placing, you could argue that no-one is flying the Saltire higher at these Games than Goodburn.

5. The Red Wiggle watches daughter star in wheelchair basketball

The Red Wiggle was wearing green and gold in support of daughter Georgia Munro-Cook. (ABC)

The Australian women's wheelchair basketball team notched its first win of the Games on day three, downing South Africa 20-5.

Georgia Munro-Cook was the star for the green and gold, finishing with 10 points in a dominant performance.

Watching on in Glasgow was her father, Murray, who, despite not sporting his famous red skivvy, will be a familiar face to many Australians.

The Red Wiggle was as proud as punch after his daughter's performance.

"She's worked so hard, the whole team has worked so hard, to see them get a win like that is just really exciting," he told ABC Sport.

Munro-Cook was over the Moon to have her mum and dad in the crowd, and said it was an interesting role reversal for the family.

"I think it's so funny, I used to go around watching him on stage, and now he's here watching me," she said.

World.title: Mayo wins All-Ireland title, ending 75-year 'curse'
World.content:
In one of the greatest upsets in Gaelic football history, Mayo has beaten Kerry in the All-Ireland football final in Dublin to break a 75-year title drought and end what some people call "the Mayo curse".

Whether the curse was hokum, a story or a real psychological issue that had simply bedevilled generations of Mayo footballers, the victory by 1-20 (23 points) to 1-17 (20 points) at Croke Park immediately drew a line under three quarters of a century of heartbreak and became one of the biggest headlines in Gaelic games history.

And one of the stars of the unlikely victory is a footballer who many think could be a generational talent although he has only just finished school, and is headed to the AFL.

The story goes that after beating Meath at Croke Park in the 1951 All-Ireland final, a jubilant Mayo team travelled home to the western province of Connacht on the back of a truck, celebrating the whole way.

While passing through the village of Foxford though, the players passed by a funeral that was taking place.

The local priest apparently took a dim view of the players continuing to celebrate while the funeral was taking place, placing a "curse" on the county, that it would not win the title again until all the team that played that day had died.

Mayo's 70-year wait goes on amid All-Ireland 'curse' Sporting curse or psychological barrier? Whatever it is, Mayo's All-Ireland Gaelic football title drought reaches 70 years after another final of blown chances against Tyrone at Croke Park.

After 1951, it took the Mayo senior team 38 years to return to the All-Ireland final. In total, before this year, it had played in 11 All-Ireland finals since 1951 and lost them all.

In 2016, Mayo conceded two own goals against Dublin, forcing a draw and a replay, which it lost.

The last of these finals, in 2021, came a few weeks before the final playing member of the original team, Paddy Prendergast, died aged 95.

The team did not make it back to Croke Park for the All-Ireland final until Sunday's decider against defending champions Kerry, who were trying to extend their record by winning a 40th All-Ireland crown.

So this year was the first opportunity to win the biggest game of the season since the elements of the "curse" had been met.

Things did not start well, with Kerry superstar forward David Clifford burying a shot in the net in the 15th minute.

But Mayo fought back to be a point down at half-time, 1-8 (11) to 0-10 (10).

Manager Andy Moran had backed young talent, with 18-year-old Kobe McDonald and 19-year-old Darragh Beirne key to the team's success.

McDonald, who was selected by St Kilda late last year as a Category B rookie and is expected to head Down Under shortly to join the team, would score three points in the final

Beirne's brilliant finish scored Mayo's only goal that sparked the county's run to victory.

Rollercoaster ride to All-Ireland title for Mayo

It had not been an auspicious start to the football season for Mayo, as it was beaten by 10 points by Roscommon in the Connacht provincial championship. The team in red and green was all but written off for the All-Ireland.

Andy Moran (right) got stuck into the media for laughing at long-suffering fans' celebrations. (Getty Images: Sportsfile/Ramsey Cardy)

It entered the All-Ireland Championship series still looking shaky, beating Monaghan by a point before a single-point loss to Tyrone left it on its final chance.

Mayo bounced back with a win over Meath to reach the quarter-finals, then downed Cork at Croke Park to make the last four.

The semi-final turned out to be a one-sided affair against Louth, with Mayo winning by 17 points. But the run was expected to end against Kerry. The questions started after the semi, with Moran asked if fans would lose the run of themselves celebrating given the county's horror record in finals.

Moran hit back hard.

"You laugh at that, lads. I don't laugh at that," Moran said at the press conference.

"I find it very, actually, dismissive, if I'm being honest. I think it's a bullshit question. I think it's a disrespectful question.

"Our county has been starved the last four or five years. If they [fans] go a bit nuts, let them."

He then set his sights on the football reporters present.

"You're going to go to a game tomorrow. Every single one of ye, you're going to write that Kerry or Dublin will go to win the All-Ireland final, right? Right?

"Does anyone here think we're going to win the All-Ireland final? No. Thank you."

Kobe McDonald has just finished school, but the Mayo young gun now has an All-Ireland medal and is set to come to the AFL. (Getty Images: Sportsfile/David Fitzgerald)

When the final siren went on Sunday, it set off emotional scenes at Croke Park among the 80,000-plus crowd.

The Saw Doctors' hit The Green and Red of Mayo, written by a group of Galway musicians about what Mayo means to the people, blasted out of the speakers at the stadium as joy mixed with disbelief for the fans.

After the game, McDonald, like his teammates, was elated and he was trying to focus on the now, rather than what's next.

"Look, to be honest I'm not thinking about Australia right now. I'm just going to soak in every minute of this. To give the people of Mayo something to celebrate, it's special," he told Irish broadcaster RTE.

ABC Sport Daily podcast ABC Sport Daily is your daily sports conversation. We dive into the biggest story of the day and get you up to speed with everything else that's making headlines.

"I know every team probably says it but we're like a family. When we're in training three days a week it's like 40 brothers.

"We know every single person in there has each other's back and whatever is being said outside the group doesn't affect us."

Gaelic games, football and hurling, are amateur sports, and there has been plenty of debate over the years about the loss of talent to the AFL.

The rest of Mayo, and quite possibly the rest of Irish Gaelic games, hopes that McDonald stays with Mayo and doesn't take his skills to Australia.

But whatever happens from here, McDonald and the rest of the team have written their names in Irish sporting history and moved their county forever beyond the ghosts of losses past.

A huge crowd of Mayo supporters travelled to Dublin and were overjoyed after their team's shock win. (Getty Images: Sportsfile/David Fitzgerald)

World.title: Scottish-blooded Anderson thrilled to win gold in Glasgow instead of Victoria
World.content:
There are a lot of Australians bemoaning the 2026 Commonwealth Games being held in Glasgow instead of regional Victoria, but don't make the mistake of thinking Iona Anderson is one of them.

Anderson emerged as Australia's biggest backstroke star of these Games when undisputed queen Kaylee McKeown withdrew due to glandular fever.

In the 200m, she finished sixth, over two seconds slower than the time she swam at the Australian trials in June.

But in the 100m, she touched first and it could not have been a better place for her first individual gold medal at a senior meet, storming past Canadian veteran and nine-time Commonwealth medallist Kylie Masse.

360 moment for Vicky Belando Nicholson Victoria Belando Nicholson was a baby when she was pulled lifeless from the water after falling from a refugee boat. Now she's a swimming bronze medallist for Australia.

Anderson got it done in the home of her forebears, if not herself, welcoming the controversial late change to the Scottish capital.

"Personally, for me, I think Glasgow's better than Victoria. Sorry," she laughed.

"I love the Scottish. I've got quite a few friends here and obviously my family. So it was great to come back here and do it."

Basically her entire family is from Scotland, Grangemouth on her mum's side and Dumfries and Galloway on her dad's.

Anderson was even named after the small island of Iona off the west coast of the country.

As she took her victory lap, the 20-year-old found her grandma Pam, who had been riding every drop of water displaced by Anderson's furious charge home.

"She was pretty emotional, there wasn't many words," she said.

"She's just really happy and stoked for me. She's always messaging me and always giving me good luck wishes, so that was really special to see her after the race."

The victory was comfortably the tightest of the night by any of the Australian swimmers as the Dolphins took home five more golds and 14 medals in total.

Cam McEvoy completed the full set of 50m freestyle titles by adding Commonwealth gold to Olympic and world titles, baton bearer Tim Hodge enjoyed another moment in the sun with gold in the 100m backstroke S9, Kai Taylor swam a glorious final leg to win the men's 4x200m relay, and Lani Pallister romped home in the women's 1,500m final for her second gold of the Games with the 200m and 800m to come.

Her victory gap of almost 18 seconds was 299 times bigger than Anderson's 0.06 margin over Masse.

A teenage Iona Anderson finished fifth as Kaylee McKeown completed the third leg of her double-double in Paris. (Getty Images: Maddie Meyer)

"I kept my blinders on so I'm really happy I got my hand on the wall," Anderson said.

"I could see some splashes, but to be honest, I closed my eyes at the end and hoped for the best."

The difficulty for Anderson is the spectre of McKeown.

The 25-year-old's double-double – winning the 100m and 200m backstroke at successive Olympics – has raised the bar for how greatness is defined in that discipline for the entire swimming world.

Perhaps that is why Anderson's distant finish in the longer race did not stay with her too long.

"I know I'm capable of more in the 200m but I've got to take away the positive that that's my third best swim ever," she said.

"I really just picked myself up and moved on."

Tech.title: With smart glasses, Meta holds all the cards but fails to play them well
Tech.content:
Across New York City, London, and Washington, DC, ads for Meta’s smart glasses have been plastered over with satirical posters from activist groups. One guerrilla ad calls these “the biggest advancement in pervert technology since the trenchcoat.” Another transposes the words “mass surveillance predator glasses” over influencer Kylie Jenner’s face, calling her out for partnering with the company as a glasses ambassador.

The message of these ads is clear. These glasses may violate your privacy — and would you trust Meta?

Meta seems spooked. For so long, the company’s privacy efforts for smart glasses have essentially relied on a single LED light and a policy that could be summed up as “don’t be a jerk.” Unfortunately, plenty of Meta glassholes have emerged over the last three years, filming often-sexualized videos of others without their consent, sometimes with the LED disabled. In a recent conversation with The Verge, Meta’s VP of wearables, Alex Himel, acknowledged that the company has become aware that an increasing number of people have tampered with the devices.

This explains why the company recently announced a mandatory software update that will disable the camera on all its glasses if the privacy light is physically tampered with. This week, Instagram head Adam Mosseri said that the social media platform will take down videos taken with Meta’s glasses that depict harassment. Instagram might have opened a can of worms concerning content moderation, but attempts to curtail misuse are good. The problem is Meta could have been doing this all along.

Activist groups have plastered satirical anti-Meta Ray-Ban ads across New York City, Washington D.C., and London.

We can’t talk about the current era of smart glasses without acknowledging that Meta has made a series of savvy decisions. Where Google Glass was loud, the Ray-Ban Meta glasses were normal and discreet. Bose beat Meta to the idea of audio glasses by a few years, and Snap was first to the idea of glasses recording POV content for social platforms. But Meta was the one that executed on making affordable, name-brand, and genuinely stylish glasses by partnering with EssilorLuxottica. It’s a model that Google and Samsung are now emulating by partnering with Warby Parker and Gentle Monster. Other companies may have been first to the concept of smart glasses, but Meta notably has been the closest to making these genuinely mainstream.

Except, in recent months, Meta’s been playing its cards all wrong. First there was the NYT report that Meta was looking to roll out facial recognition tech for the glasses while privacy advocates were distracted. Then there was the Wired report that said Meta had silently shipped — but not activated — that tech to existing glasses. Now, there’s a Financial Times report that alleges Meta wants these glasses to record 24/7. Outside these larger beats, Meta has done things like remove the ability to opt out of voice recordings training its AI. Its executives occasionally say tone-deaf things like those who eschew smart glasses will be at a “cognitive disadvantage.” And amid legitimate privacy concerns following bad actors misusing the tech, the company has seeded these glasses to content creators alongside a splashy campaign with Kylie Jenner — one of the most visible but polarizing celebrities.

In a vacuum, a gaffe or two happens. When you screw up this many times, it starts to look like you’re purposefully missing the point.

Focusing on the privacy LED light, experts say, isn’t enough on its own.

“You cannot hinge your entire privacy policy on a single light. You can’t expect everyone in the world to know that and react to that,” says Uttara Ananthakrishnan, a technology professor at the University of Washington who specializes in how online interactions affect platforms, markets, and social behaviors. “It puts a lot of pressure on the person who isn’t even wearing the glasses to be aware of what another person is going to do.”

Ananthakrishnan is skeptical that smart glasses will take off outside specific workplaces, not just because of social stigma, but because societal attitudes toward Big Tech companies and what’s shared online have shifted. Case in point, Meta’s executives have often pointed to the early days of the smartphone in defense of smart glasses. Back then, the public was unsure about these devices, but eventually, everyone figured out what the acceptable social norms ought to be. Ananthakrishnan disagrees.

“You cannot hinge your entire privacy policy on a single light. ”

“Tech companies are not at all looked upon with favor right now. Compounded with the fact that we live in an age of social media, where anything that we say and everything that we do — we could be liable for it. There’s a lot more awareness that there are bad people on the internet who could do really terrible things compared to the smartphone era,” says Ananthakrishnan. She also points out how people feel about individual privacy is different than when you are responsible for others’ privacy.

Take smartwatches. Ananthakrishnan notes that people are willing to risk their own health data privacy because there’s a clear benefit to their goals. However, if there are negative outcomes — for example, your health data getting leaked to your employer — you’re the only one who suffers, and you’re the only victim. With smart glasses, the privacy calculus changes. You’re the person risking others’ privacy, possibly without consent — the perpetrator.

Wearing smart glasses forces you to wonder: who else’s privacy am I putting at risk?

So is it even possible for Meta — or any other smart glasses company — to reassure a skittish public? Or are its recent attempts simply too little, too late?

“There’s not much Meta can do to convince me they genuinely care about user privacy when their whole business model is built on invading it,” says Kendall Schrohe, executive director of the Attention Sphere, one of the advocacy groups affiliated with the anti-Meta glasses ads in DC and New York City. “At the end of the day, there is nothing privacy-preserving about sunglasses with a built-in camera. This is surveillance technology and no amount of tweaking changes that.”

Schrohe says that Meta’s credibility is further undermined by the fact that it, along with other tech companies, reportedly lobbied to weaken state privacy bills.

“I think this moment has passed for them,” agrees Ananthakrishnan, noting that Meta isn’t known as a company that effectively communicates privacy policies. “Maybe Apple can, but I don’t think either Google or Meta could pull this off given their history. It’s not going to be reassuring if they put out a statement that says, ‘Hey we are doing everything we can; this is our privacy policy.’ People are still not going to believe that.”

The societal stigma, plus fatigue with Big Tech, is one reason for the backlash against smart glasses. Meta’s reputation is another.

Barring a dramatic overhaul, it’s going to be hard for Meta and Big Tech at large to change the current narrative. And it’s tempting to think that, perhaps, some tech execs might throw up their hands and give up on pursuing proactive privacy at all. To lean into the surveillance dystopia until external actors, like legislators and private businesses, force their privacy hand.

But the reality is that we’re all watching to see what card Meta — the current leader in this space — plays next. Continuing to run the same strategy all but ensures the company will either hand the mantle to Google or Apple, or tank smart glasses as a whole. If Meta wants even the smallest chance of succeeding, it simply has to do something different.

Tech.title: Champagne and Bullets belongs on the Mount Rushmore of bad movies
Tech.content:
is the Verge’s weekend editor. He’s covered the tech industry for over 18 years and knows a thing or two about synths.

There’s something about a movie like The Room, Troll 2, or Fateful Findings that I find irresistible. These sorts of “so bad they’re good” films are marvelous curiosities where ambition far outstrips resources, ability, and self-awareness to become something much greater than the sum of their parts. Champagne and Bullets (also released as GetEven and Road to Revenge) is a film on par with those classics of outsider cinema.

The movie is almost entirely the work of one man, John De Hart. Hart wrote, directed, and stars as Rick Bode in the film. He even performs a musical number early in the proceedings — the bizarre “Shimmy Slide.” During the performance, Hart, who was reportedly pumped full of painkillers after throwing out his back, is stiff and looks around the room as if he’s only performing under threat of violence. And somehow, this lifeless performance of a cringey country rocker isn’t the most awkward scene in the movie.

The relationships and interactions between characters in Champagne and Bullets are just as inexplicable and unnatural as those in The Room. Bode and his partner Huck Finney are cops who lose their badges five minutes into the movie. This precipitates the alarmingly quick mental decline of Finney, who is also going through a divorce after discovering his wife has been sleeping around. He fires a handgun through his bills, drinks bleach to get out of prison, and seemingly starts a cult.

Oh, and speaking of cults, a good portion of the plot revolves around the reemergence of Bode’s old girlfriend Cindy, who is fleeing a satanic coven that “sacrificed a human baby.”

While ostensibly an action film, the fight scenes are few and far between, and staged with all the believability of a theme park stunt show. Hart seemed far more interested in cramming in as much gratuitous nudity as possible. There are three uncomfortably long sex scenes with costar Pamela Bryant, who plays Cindy, all set to songs sung by Hart. In total, they take up 12 minutes of runtime in a movie that is only 90 minutes long. One scene that takes place in a Jacuzzi apparently even led Hart’s girlfriend at the time to break up with him. (Warning: One scene not involving Hart and Bryant does depict a sexual assault.)

If you’re a fan of bad movies, cult classics, or the podcast How Did This Get Made?, you owe it to yourself to go watch Champagne and Bullets. It’s available on Hoopla, Amazon Prime, and Tubi.

Tech.title: Apple is banking on privacy to set its smart glasses apart
Tech.content:
is the Verge’s weekend editor. He’s covered the tech industry for over 18 years and knows a thing or two about synths.

Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

According to Mark Gurman, Apple is planning to reveal its first smart glasses at WWDC next June, with an expectation that they’ll launch by the end of 2027. Part of the hold-up may be around the company’s efforts to get its privacy features and messaging in order. Smart glasses in general, and Meta’s in particular, have ignited controversy over their ability to stealthily capture photos and videos. As Gurman points out:

The company has spent more than a decade making privacy one of its defining product messages. Simply entering the same category as Meta risks undermining that reputation, regardless of how Apple’s approach differs.

Apple is likely to rely on on-device processing and skip out on more controversial features like facial recognition or an always-on-recording similar to Meta’s “super sensing.” Gurman also believes Apple will avoid using customer recordings to train AI models.

Other hardware and software privacy features are also reportedly in the works. It’s also possible that Apple could eventually release a version of its smart glasses without a camera, or with a camera that is exclusively for sensing and won’t be able to capture video or photos at all, similar to what is rumored for Apple’s AI-enabled AirPods.

Tech.title: The US is charging an American citizen for wiping his phone at the border
Tech.content:
is the Verge’s weekend editor. He’s covered the tech industry for over 18 years and knows a thing or two about synths.

The government is prosecuting US citizen Sam Tunick for allegedly providing authorities with a “duress password” that wiped his phone when they tried to seize it at Atlanta’s Hartsfield-Jackson airport on January 24th, 2025. Federal agents detained Tunick at the airport, allegedly questioning him about child exploitation images. However, a motion filed by Tunick’s lawyers argues this was simply “a pretext for a fishing expedition into Mr Tunick’s connections” to the Stop Cop City movement in Atlanta.

The government is turning to a little-known and rarely used statute that makes it illegal to destroy or damage property to stop authorities from seizing it. They allege that Tunick used a feature of the privacy-focused GrapheneOS to wipe his phone by giving authorities a duress password, instead of the actual passcode to unlock the phone. The defense has argued that the detention and seizure were unlawful, and therefore all evidence should be tossed.

According to Tunick’s attorneys, agents refused him access to a lawyer, did not provide a warrant, or inform him of his legal rights. They also allege that access to his phone was sought under false pretenses. The government has countered that they were not required to produce a warrant because Tunick had not yet been granted permission to enter the US.

Marlon Kautz, a member of the Atlanta Solidarity Fund, told The Guardian earlier this week that, “we all have a right to secure our private data against unconstitutional searches. And we should — especially in a time of rising authoritarianism.” Under the Trump administration, entering the US has become a much more fraught process, even for citizens who can face hours-long detention and scrutiny of social media accounts. Most agree the only way to protect your data is to delete it.

Tech.title: Carrie is just trying to make a friend in the new trailer
Tech.content:
is the Verge’s weekend editor. He’s covered the tech industry for over 18 years and knows a thing or two about synths.

Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

Mike Flanagan’s latest Stephen King adaptation, Carrie (this will be his fourth), is slated to make its debut on Amazon Prime on October 7th. The new trailer dropped at Comic-Con 2026 and doesn’t contain many surprises. If you’re familiar with Carrie at all, it hits all the expected notes, though it’s clearly been updated for the modern era.

According to Deadline, Flanagan’s take on the classic King novel will tackle very modern teen challenges like active shooter drills and bullying on social media. The director apparently invited high schoolers into the writers’ room, using their real-life traumas to inform the script:

“They shared shocking one-off situations or constant treatment and microaggressions and things that are not necessarily present themselves as targeted harassment. [We will dive into] the cruelty in today’s world and how the internet has encouraged cruelty, rewards and celebrates and amplifies it. This is awful for adults to deal with, and for teenagers even more so.”

Brian De Palma’s iconic 1976 adaptation of Carrie is iconic and features an unimpeachable performance from Sissy Spacek. But it’s undeniable that Summer H. Howell, who was 21 at the time of shooting, is much more believable as a high school student than Spacek, who was 26 at the time.

Tech.title: You can get three months of Xbox Game Pass Ultimate for almost half off
Tech.content:
is an editor covering deals and gaming hardware. He joined in 2018, and after a two-year stint at Polygon, he rejoined The Verge in May 2025.

Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

Subscribing to Xbox Game Pass Ultimate on a recurring basis has been tough to justify recently, even after Microsoft reduced the monthly cost from $29.99 to $22.99. But you can get a better deal on a three-month subscription (valued at $69) by grabbing a digital code at Eneba that costs $39.01 at the time of publication.

Game Pass Ultimate grants you access to the full Game Pass library on Xbox (compared to a more limited slice with Premium), including first-party titles and online multiplayer access. The subscription also gives PC gamers access to Microsoft’s catalog of Game Pass games through the Xbox app, though the selection differs a bit between console and desktop.

You don’t need me to tell you why deals like these are nice. The costs of subscriptions generally only go in one direction over time, and it is becoming more rare to find worthwhile discounts that give you a break. If you want to jump into Halo: Campaign Evolved when it launches July 28th on Xbox and PC, all you need is this subscription instead of buying the $49.99 re-remake.

Tech.title: The vertical video takeover is here
Tech.content:
This is The Stepback, a weekly newsletter breaking down one essential story from the tech world. For more on all things vertical video, follow David Pierce. The Stepback arrives in our subscribers’ inboxes on Sunday at 8AM ET. Opt in for The Stepback here.

How it started

For a while, every social and media platform had its own identity. YouTube was for clips of TV shows and movies, and the home of so many members of a burgeoning creator community. Instagram was mostly pictures. Netflix was trying to be the on-demand HBO. Facebook was about friends. Twitter was about news. Snapchat was a messaging app.

All these apps did have one important thing in common, though: They were growing up alongside the smartphone. Billions of new people were coming online for the first time, and they began to make content that made sense for the tall, skinny new devices in their hands. Selfies were a vertical art form, both because the photos filled the screen better and because it was just easier to hold the phone and take the photo that way. Some resisted the idea of vertical video for years — they’d argue that our eyes are meant to scan horizontally rather than vertically, and that vertical video looked bad on widescreen laptops. But ultimately phones won, and we hold our phones upright, so our phone experiences turned upright. That includes entertainment.

As has been true so many times, Snap figured this out before anyone. It launched Stories in late 2013 as a slightly more relaxed way to see what your friends are up to. CEO Evan Spiegel called it a “totally new way to share your day with friends — or everyone.” It took off in a massive way, and by the middle of 2014 was the most popular feature on Snapchat. That’s the kind of virality that Mark Zuckerberg tends to notice, and by August of 2016, the feature had been copied more or less exactly into Instagram. Kevin Systrom, then the CEO of Instagram, said of Spiegel and Snapchat that “they deserve all the credit” for Stories. The implication? That this was no longer a proprietary feature of a single social network; it was just in the air. Stories were for everyone. They started showing up on LinkedIn, Tinder, Medium, and so many other places.

Stories weren’t always video, but as cameras and upload speeds improved, video became the dominant medium in many ephemeral spaces. And video stories had two semi-magical properties: They were perfectly suited to endless, mindless scrolling, and they made it really easy to integrate ads. Only a few months after turning on Stories in Instagram, by which point half the platform’s users were already using Stories, Facebook began flooding ads into the product. The semi-randomness of Stories made ads actually seem less intrusive — you’d see a photo of a dog, a video of a hike, an ad for jeans, your friend’s makeup routine, brunch pics, an ad for blush. Video ads felt more premium, took up the whole screen, and were thus far more lucrative for the social platforms.

With apologies to the short, brilliant life of Vine, the six-second video platform that helped invent so much about the video-first social network, it wasn’t until TikTok took off that things really turned again. The platform launched in the US in 2018, but had been popular for a few years in China as Douyin and elsewhere as Musical.ly. TikTok combined the vertical-first format of Stories with the permanence of YouTube, but it also made video easier than ever. It had filters like Instagram and Snapchat, but also supplied a steady stream of video ideas through the platform’s many trends, offered access to music and sound effects, and made it easy to stitch or duet a video.

By defaulting to the purely algorithmic For You page, TikTok also freed creators from caring about curating their profile or worrying about posting too much — you could just pump out videos and trust the algorithm to deliver them. And so that’s what people did. Pretty quickly, TikTok became one of the fastest growing apps on the planet, and its daily usage numbers became the envy of the industry. Instagram may have had more users, but TikTok users spent far more time TikToking.

When TikTok became a phenomenon, just about everyone jumped on the vertical video bandwagon. Reels launched in 2020 and became a core feature of both Instagram and Facebook; YouTube created Shorts a year later. By the end of 2021, Twitter had both launched and killed a similar feature called Fleets. By this point, this kind of full-screen, vertical-scrolling video was part of the lingua franca of the smartphone. At the same time, in a search for ever more engagement, these platforms were learning another lesson from TikTok: to stop relying on your friends to post interesting content, and instead to show you whatever the algorithm thinks you might like. Social networks were gone, replaced by social media — entertainment with a comments section.

How it’s going

Short-form, vertical video has effectively won the internet. Business is booming, and viewers show no sign of tuning out. Meta said in 2024 that Instagram users were spending more than half their time in Reels, and said in 2025 the feature was turning into a $50 billion annual business across Meta’s apps. About 63 percent of young adults and teens are on TikTok, per Pew Research Center, and one in five teens reported being on the app “almost constantly.” YouTube reported 200 billion daily views of Shorts at the end of 2025, and said that Shorts earned more money per watch hour than standard YouTube videos.

The last three or four years have been about relentless standardization in social media. The pace with which these products copy each other, and regress back toward parity, has been absolutely astonishing. First, Shorts and Reels both aped TikTok’s design, its duetting and stitching, and its close relationship with sounds and music. Then they bought into TikTok’s idea of prioritizing content over connection — followers are dead, long live the algorithm. TikTok pushed hard into shopping, then suddenly Reels and Shorts became a lot more shoppable. YouTube began to grow on TVs, and suddenly TikTok and Instagram started investing in its own TV apps. Videos got longer and longer across platforms, to allow more ads. All the apps got really into livestreaming for a while. And micro dramas. They’ve relentlessly copied each other on big things like letting users control their algorithm, and small things like Clear Mode.

There are two reasons for the ongoing onslaught of short-form vertical video: time spent and advertising. The endlessly scrolling video feed turns out to be one of the most engrossing forms of entertainment ever devised (to the point that it has become a regulatory problem for the social platforms), and in a relentless competition for eyeballs and attention, it has become everyone’s best idea. In 2024, when Meta switched its default video player to a vertical-first layout across all platforms, the race was officially won.

Meanwhile, as those platforms have captured more of our time and attention, short-form video has become a dominant force of advertising on the internet, which means advertisers are already comfortable making ads designed to go between videos in the feed. And as so many companies turn to AI to do their ad targeting, all they really need is the creative to get started. “So long as clients give us different assets — a six-second ad, a 15-second ad, a long-format, a vertical ad — AI is essentially powering everything else,” YouTube’s Brian Albert told me last year. “From the audiences you’re reaching, to the contextual placements, to the ad that’s actually showing.” The combination of AI and vertical video has become a self-fulfilling prophecy: The more it wins, the easier it becomes for everyone else to get on board, and so it just keeps winning.

What happens next

Vertical video haters, I have bad news: It’s only going to get worse. TikTok, YouTube, and Instagram are if anything going to become more short-form and vertical, since those short videos are easier to make and easier to load into endlessly scrolling feeds. Video services used to require you to pick something and press play, but now all they need is for you to open the app and they can start showing you ads. They’re not going to want to go back. Here’s how dominant video is: Facebook is testing a new version of the app that loads a full-screen video feed when you open the app. If that happens, there will be no Facebook — only Reels. After all this time, they’ve trained users to want and expect this kind of fast-paced, instant-gratification entertainment, to the point where even a full-length movie can feel like a chore.

Meanwhile, after years of raising prices, streaming services around the world are hoping they can turn to advertising to keep growing. For a while, they could coast on the back of linear TV, borrowing those ads to run on digital platforms. But a TikTok ad won’t make any sense on Netflix, so Netflix decided the best thing to do is build something that looks more like TikTok. A recent HubSpot report found that short-form video was by a wide margin both the most-used and most successful form of marketing content in 2025, and that it was the format in which marketers planned to invest the most this year.

All that said, there are glimmers of a bigger shift beginning to happen. Fed up with the algorithm, some users are starting to demand the return of friends and family in social media. But more broadly, more and more young people are deciding to put down their phones, resist the invasion of AI into their lives, and look for different kinds of entertainment. Movie theaters are having a big year; one of the year’s most exciting new phones is a flip phone. As long as we live in this era of social media and entertainment, vertical video is going to win. It would take a cultural revolution to stop it — and there might just be one brewing.

By the way

The best way to understand TikTok, Instagram, and Snapchat in particular right now is as a combination of two things: a streaming service and an inbox. Studies have found that the most popular thing to do is watch videos, and the second most popular thing is to send videos to someone else. Actually posting? Way down the list. (YouTube, by the way, is desperately trying to make DMs happen .)

If you’ve made it this far and you’re thinking, no way, you’re way overstating it? I’m so sorry to say this, but you might just be old. At this point, YouTube and Facebook cross generations and demographics, but Pew and others have found that TikTok, Snapchat, and Instagram are effectively ubiquitous among young people in particular.

It’s important to remember that views are lies . Everyone on the internet has an incentive to make their platform seem big and vibrant and popular, and they will invent whatever new metrics they need to do so.
